=== Possessory credits ===
Depending on their standing, the director may be granted an extra, prominent credit before the film's title (as in "A [[Ridley Scott]] Film"); this practice began with directors such as [[Otto Preminger]], [[David Lean]], and [[John Frankenheimer]] in the mid-1960s. Sometimes the producer or writer may also get a possessory credit. Up until the establishment of the director's possessive credit, in the early 1970s, some directors were so highly regarded that they received what seems to be a producer's credit, even if they did not produce the film. [[Victor Fleming]] was one such director: his films usually featured the credit "A Victor Fleming Production", even when someone else produced the film. [[James Whale]] was similarly credited.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0001843/ |title = James Whale - IMDb| website=[[IMDb]] }}</ref>

Director [[Kevin Smith]] refuses to use a possessory credit, such as "A Kevin Smith Film", feeling that a movie is made by everyone involved and not the product of just the director.<ref>{{cite video
| people = Enhanced Playback Trivia Track
| title = [[Clerks (film)#Clerks. X|Clerks. X]] Tenth Anniversary Edition
| medium =  DVD
| publisher = [[Buena Vista Home Entertainment]]
| date = 2004 
}}</ref>

=== Top and above-title billing ===
{{redirect|Top billing|other uses|Top Billing (disambiguation)}}{{more citations|date=December 2009}}
The [[actor]]s whose names appear first are said to have "top billing". They usually play the principal characters in the film and have the most screen time. Frequently, top-billed actors are also named in advertising material such as [[trailer (Movie)|trailers]], [[movie poster|posters]], [[billboard (advertising)|billboards]], and [[Television advertisement|TV spots]].

The two or three top-billed actors in a movie will usually be announced prior to the title of the movie; this is referred to as "above-title billing". For an actor to receive it, he/she will generally have to be well-established, with box-office drawing power. Those introduced afterward are generally considered to be the supporting cast. Well-known actors may be given top billing for publicity or contractual purposes if juvenile, lesser-known, or first-time performers appear in a larger role: e.g., [[Marlon Brando]] and [[Gene Hackman]] were both credited before the title in ''[[Superman (1978 film)|Superman]]'' (1978), while [[Christopher Reeve]], the then-unknown actor who played the title character and protagonist, was not, even though Brando only appears in the introduction while Hackman was the main antagonist. Similarly in ''[[Apocalypse Now]]'', Brando was billed first even though he only appears at the end as the film's chief antagonist, while [[Robert Duvall]] was billed second despite a brief supporting role that earned him an Oscar nomination for Best Supporting Actor, and [[Martin Sheen]], who portrayed the main character, was billed third.

It used to be common practice to give top billing based on a person's level of fame, regardless of the significance of their role in the film. For example, Marlon Brando received top billing in ''[[The Godfather]]'' (although he had less on-screen time than [[Al Pacino]]'s character; Pacino was displeased that he was only nominated for the Best Supporting Actor Oscar while Brando received the Oscar for Best Actor in a Leading Role), ''[[Apocalypse Now]]'' (see above), and ''[[Superman (1978 film)|Superman]]'' (also see above). [[Maximilian Schell]] was billed fifth in ''[[Judgment at Nuremberg]]'' after [[Spencer Tracy]], [[Burt Lancaster]], [[Richard Widmark]], and [[Marlene Dietrich]], yet Schell went on to win the Oscar for Best Actor in a Leading Role.  In recent decades, however, the practice of giving top billing to a star actor has largely been discontinued especially if they only play a [[bit part]] (see [[#Last billing|Last billing]]); some major actors may have a [[Cameo appearance|cameo]] where they are only noted within the other cast during the end credits.

If an unfamiliar actor has the lead role, they may be listed last in the list of principal supporting actors, their name prefixed with "and introducing" (as [[Peter O'Toole]] was in ''[[Lawrence of Arabia (film)|Lawrence of Arabia]]''). However "and introducing" is now mostly used in feature films by a young actor (usually a child) who appears for the first time in a motion picture. Sometimes, they may not receive special billing even if their role is crucial. For example, the then-unknown [[William Warfield]], who played Joe and sang "[[Ol' Man River]]" in the [[Show Boat (1951 film)|1951 film version]] of ''[[Show Boat]]'', received tenth billing as if he were merely a bit player, while [[Paul Robeson]], an established star who played the same role in the [[Show Boat (1936 film)|1936 film version]] of the musical, received fourth billing in the 1936 film.

If more than one name appears at the same time or of a similar size, then those actors are said to have "equal billing", with their importance decreasing from left to right. However, an instance of "equal importance" is ''[[The Towering Inferno]]'' (1974) starring [[Steve McQueen]] and [[Paul Newman]]. The two names appear simultaneously with Newman's on the right side of the screen and raised slightly higher than McQueen's, to indicate the comparable status of both actors' characters (this also features on the advertising poster). A similar situation occurred in 2002 with ''[[Chicago (2002 film)|Chicago]]'', where [[Renee Zellweger]] and [[Catherine Zeta-Jones]] received "stacked billing" on the film's poster, where a person reading from left to right would read Zeta-Jones' name first and a person reading from top to bottom would read Zellweger's name first.

If a film has an [[ensemble cast]] with no clear lead role, it is traditional to bill the participants alphabetically or in the order of their on-screen appearance. An example of the former is ''[[A Bridge Too Far (1977 film)|A Bridge Too Far]]'' (1977), which featured 14 roles played by established stars, any one of whom would have ordinarily received top billing as an individual.{{Citation needed|date=December 2009}} The cast of the ''[[Harry Potter (film series)|Harry Potter]]'' films includes many recognized stars in supporting roles who are billed alphabetically, but after the three principals who were initially child actors.

In the case of the [[Kenneth Branagh]] ''[[Hamlet (1996 film)|Hamlet]]'', there were many famous actors playing supporting or bit roles, and these actors were given prominent billing in the posters along with the film's actual stars: Branagh, [[Derek Jacobi]], [[Julie Christie]], and [[Kate Winslet]]. In the actual film's credits, they (along with the other actors in the film) were listed in alphabetical order and in the same size typeface.

If an actor is not an established star, he or she may not receive above-the-title billing, or even "star" billing; they may just be listed at the head of the cast. This is the way that all of the actors were listed in the opening credits to ''[[The Wizard of Oz (1939 film)|The Wizard of Oz]]''; [[Judy Garland]], although listed first, was given equal billing to all the others, with the cast list reading "with Judy Garland, Frank Morgan, Ray Bolger, Bert Lahr, Jack Haley", etc. [[F. Murray Abraham]], a supporting actor at the time of ''[[Amadeus (film)|Amadeus]]'', did not receive special star billing although he played the lead role of [[Antonio Salieri]]; his onscreen credit reads "with F. Murray Abraham", although his name does appear first in the cast.

In some cases, the position of a name in the credits roll can become a sticking point for both cast and crew. Such was the case on the 1960s TV [[sitcom]] ''[[Gilligan's Island]]'', where two of the stars were only mentioned by name in the closing credits. In fact, the characters of The Professor ([[Russell Johnson]]) and Mary Ann ([[Dawn Wells]]) were the only ones whose mention in the opening theme song was abbreviated simply as "the rest" in the show's first season. [[Bob Denver]], who played Gilligan, was so upset with this treatment that he reportedly told the producers that since his contract stipulated that his name could appear anywhere in the credits that he wished, he wanted to be moved to the end credits with his co-stars. From the show's second season, the studio capitulated, and moved Denver's co-stars to the opening credits of the show, and also changed the theme song's lyrics to include "The Professor and Mary Ann" instead of saying "and the rest".{{Citation needed|date=December 2009}}

====Competitive top billing====
Sometimes actors can become highly competitive over the order of billing. For example:

[[Spencer Tracy]] was originally cast to play the lead opposite [[Humphrey Bogart]] in ''[[The Desperate Hours (1955 film)|The Desperate Hours]]'' (1955), but when neither actor would relinquish top billing, Tracy withdrew and was replaced by [[Fredric March]], who took second billing to Bogart. Bogart's role in the film had earlier been played on [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]] by [[Paul Newman]] but the young actor was not considered for the movie version since Newman, viewed by studios at the time as mainly a stage and television actor only beginning his movie career, was in no position to compete with Bogart. Tracy would also later back out of costarring in the 1965 film ''[[The Cincinnati Kid]]'' when he learned he would have to take second billing behind the film's star, [[Steve McQueen]]. The role Tracy had been cast in went instead to [[Edward G. Robinson]], whom McQueen had idolized from childhood. Whenever it was pointed out to Tracy that he routinely took top billing in his films with [[Katharine Hepburn]], he responded, "It's a movie, not a lifeboat."

[[Clark Gable]] had a top billing clause written into his [[MGM]] contract and made three major films in the 1930s with Tracy in supporting roles (''[[San Francisco (1936 film)|San Francisco]]'', ''[[Test Pilot (film)|Test Pilot]]'', and ''[[Boom Town (film)|Boom Town]]''), but when Tracy renegotiated his contract during [[World War II]], he had a similar clause included in his own contract, effectively ending the hugely popular Gable-Tracy team.

In the opening credits of ''[[The Bridge on the River Kwai]]'' (1957), [[Alec Guinness]], who is generally regarded as the main character in the film, receives third billing, after [[William Holden]] (who demanded top billing) and [[Jack Hawkins]] (who does not even appear until halfway through the picture). In the closing credits, Guinness is billed second, with Hawkins third.
[[File:The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance (1962 poster).jpg|thumb|John Wayne was billed second on posters and in trailers but first in the film itself for ''The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance'' (1962).]]
For ''[[The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance]]'' (1962), [[James Stewart]] was given top billing over [[John Wayne]] in the movie's posters and the previews (trailers) shown in [[cinemas]] and on television prior to the film's release, but in the film itself, Wayne is accorded top billing. Their names are displayed on pictures of signposts, one after the other, with Wayne's name shown first with his sign mounted slightly higher on its post than Stewart's. Director [[John Ford]] remarked in an interview with [[Peter Bogdanovich]] that he made it apparent to the audience that [[Vera Miles]]' character had never entirely recovered from an abortive romance with Wayne's gunslinging rancher because "I wanted Wayne to be the lead."<ref>''Who The Devil Made It: Conversations with Legendary Film Directors'' by [[Peter Bogdanovich]]</ref> [[Dustin Hoffman]] and [[Robert Redford]] used precisely the same billing formula for ''[[All the President's Men (film)|All the President's Men]]'' (1976), with Redford receiving top billing in posters and trailers while Hoffman was billed over Redford in the film itself.<ref>{{cite web |title= All the President's Men Movie Poster |url= http://www.impawards.com/1976/all_the_presidents_men.html |website= [[ImpAwards.com]] }}</ref> In 2021, ''[[Don't Look Up (2021 film)|Don't Look Up]]'' used exactly the same approach, with [[Leonardo DiCaprio]] receiving top billing on the posters and in the trailers while [[Jennifer Lawrence]] was accorded top billing at the beginning of the film itself.<ref>{{cite AV media
 | people = [[Adam McKay|McKay, Adam]] (director)
 | date = 5 December 2021
 | title = Don't Look Up
 | type = Motion picture
 | url = https://www.netflix.com/br/title/81252357?s=i&trkid=13747225&vlang=pt&clip=81522111
 | access-date = 26 April 2022
 | time = 11:28
 | publisher = [[Netflix]]
 | url-access = subscription
}}</ref>

As both [[Tony Curtis]] and [[Jerry Lewis]] wanted top billing for ''[[Boeing Boeing (1965 film)|Boeing Boeing]]'' ([[1965 in film|1965]]), their animated names appeared in a spinning, circular fashion in front of an airplane engine's [[nacelle]].<ref name="tcmcurtis">''Private Screenings: Tony Curtis''. [[Turner Classic Movies]], 19 Jan 1999.</ref> For the trailer, the circular animation of the two names was repeated and neither name was spoken aloud. For the posters, the names made an X, Lewis' going up from the bottom left and Curtis' going down from the upper left.

For the film ''[[The Towering Inferno (film)|The Towering Inferno]]'' (1974), [[Steve McQueen]], [[Paul Newman]] and [[William Holden]] all tried to obtain top billing. Holden was refused as his diminished star power was no longer considered to be in the league of McQueen's and Newman's. To provide dual top billing and mollify McQueen, the credits were arranged diagonally, with McQueen at the lower left and Newman at the upper right. Thus, each actor appeared to have top billing depending on whether the poster was read from left to right or top to bottom.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.art.com/asp/sp-asp/_/pd--10134441/The_Towering_Inferno_Style_A.htm |title=The Towering Inferno Masterprint at Art.com<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=2010-01-09 |archive-date=2004-12-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20041228081439/http://www.art.com/asp/sp-asp/_/pd--10134441/The_Towering_Inferno_Style_A.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref> Technically, McQueen has top billing and is mentioned first in the film's trailers; however, at the end of the movie, as the cast's names roll from the bottom of the screen, Newman's name is fully visible first, giving him top billing in the closing credits. This was the first time that this type of "staggered but equal" billing had been used for a movie, although the same thing had been discussed for the same two actors five years earlier when McQueen was going to play the [[Harry Longabaugh|Sundance Kid]] in ''[[Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid]]'' (1969). McQueen ultimately passed on the part and was replaced by [[Robert Redford]], who did not enjoy McQueen's status and took second billing to Newman. Today, it has become understood that whoever's name appears to the left has top billing,{{citation needed|date=August 2012}} but this was by no means the case when ''The Towering Inferno'' was produced. This same approach has often been used subsequently, including ''[[Cruel Intentions]]'' (1999), ''[[Sky Captain and the World of Tomorrow]]'' (2004), and ''[[Righteous Kill]]'' (2008) starring [[Robert De Niro]] and [[Al Pacino]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.impawards.com/2008/righteous_kill.html|title = Righteous Kill Movie Poster (#1 of 9)}}</ref>

In ''[[The Bonfire of the Vanities (film)|The Bonfire of the Vanities]]'' (1990), [[F. Murray Abraham]] asked for above-title billing. This was rejected as too many other stars were getting it ([[Tom Hanks]], [[Bruce Willis]], [[Melanie Griffith]]). Thus, Abraham asked for his name to be completely removed, even from the closing credits. That same year, [[Raúl Juliá]] requested above the title billing alongside Robert Redford and Lena Olin for the drama ''[[Havana (film)|Havana]]''. When the producers rejected this, he decided to go uncredited. Eleven years later, [[Don Cheadle]] did exactly the same thing when his name was not allowed to appear above the title in ''[[Ocean's Eleven (2001 film)|Ocean's Eleven]]'' (2001), presumably because his name would have alphabetically preceded [[George Clooney]]'s and, unlike with the later sequels, the cast above the title was presented alphabetically (Clooney, [[Matt Damon]], [[Andy García]], [[Brad Pitt]], and [[Julia Roberts]]). Cheadle removed his name from the credits.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.impawards.com/2001/oceans_eleven_ver2.html|title = Ocean's Eleven Movie Poster (#2 of 5)}}</ref> The producers apparently wanted Clooney, not Cheadle, to be the first name a casual viewer of the advertising would see.

In ''[[Batman (1989 film)|Batman]]'' (1989), [[Jack Nicholson]] demanded top billing and a share of the film's earnings (including associated merchandise), even though [[Michael Keaton]] played the [[Batman|titular character]] while Nicholson's [[Joker (character)|Joker]] was the antagonist.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.thetimes.com/article/top-ten-batman-villains-on-screen-c9xwz76jg6q|title=Top ten Batman villains on screen|date=July 17, 2012|website=[[The Times]]|access-date=January 16, 2020|quote=Nicholson... demanded top-billing and a deal that gave him royalties on merchandise.}}{{Subscription required}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://ew.com/article/2000/03/03/biggest-movie-payoffs/|title=The biggest movie payoffs|last=Hochman|first=David|date=March 3, 2000|magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]]|access-date=January 16, 2020|archive-date=January 2, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230102102305/https://ew.com/article/2000/03/03/biggest-movie-payoffs/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In the film ''[[Miami Vice (film)|Miami Vice]]'' (2006), [[Colin Farrell]] originally received top billing. However, after [[Jamie Foxx]] won an [[Academy Award]] he demanded top billing and received it despite his role actually being much smaller than Farrell's. Foxx's name appears first in the opening credits, while Farrell still receives top billing in the closing credits.

In a comedic commercial for ''[[Michael and Michael Have Issues]]'' (2009), the aforementioned characters mock-argue over who gets top billing for their show.

===Last billing===
An actor may receive "last billing", which usually designates a smaller role played by a famous actor. They are usually credited after the rest of the lead cast, prefixed by "and" or "with". In some cases, for extra emphasis the actor's name is followed by "as" and the name of the character (thus called an "and-as" credit).

An early example of last billing is found in the 1931 classic ''[[Frankenstein (1931 film)|Frankenstein]]'', which simply listed a question mark (?) as portraying the monster. Reissued prints add actor [[Boris Karloff]] to the end credit listings, as the film made him a huge star, such that the credits of the film's first sequel ''[[The Bride of Frankenstein]]'' credits him only by his last name.{{Citation needed|date=August 2021}}

One of the first "and-as" credits was given to [[Spencer Tracy]] ("as Lieutenant Colonel [[James H. Doolittle]]") in the 1944 World War II film ''[[Thirty Seconds Over Tokyo]]'', since another top box office star of the time, [[Van Johnson]], had top billing, but Tracy was too big a star to receive second billing. In promotional posters and screen credits, Tracy's name is displayed in larger letters than Johnson's.

Occasionally, films have both an "and-as" credit and a separate last billing credit, such as the [[Irwin Allen]] 1978 disaster film ''[[The Swarm (1978 film)|The Swarm]]'', the opening credits of which, after listing a large cast of stars, concludes with "[[Fred MacMurray]] as Clarence ... and [[Henry Fonda]]".

===Unbilled appearances===
An actor may choose to go unbilled (i.e., [[wikt:uncredited|uncredited]]) and not be listed, either being entirely omitted from screen credits, or only listed in the closing credits. Reasons for this vary.

Unbilled roles often feature [[cameo appearance]]s by famous actors or actresses who pop up in a movie as a face in a crowd, a man on a bench, or other 'background' characters, who are given screen time for a brief, but recognizable, moment. For example, [[Bing Crosby]] and [[Bob Hope]] appeared momentarily in a circus audience during ''[[The Greatest Show on Earth (film)|The Greatest Show on Earth]]''.

Sometimes, actors can be recognized, but are not credited for contractual and/or financial reasons; if they receive credit, they would be due payment commensurate with their fame.{{citation needed|date=January 2020}} For example, [[James Cagney]] is clearly glimpsed during the opening scenes of ''[[Mutiny on the Bounty (1935 film)|Mutiny on the Bounty]]'' (1935) starring [[Charles Laughton]] and [[Clark Gable]]. Cagney was contracted to [[Warner Bros.]] at the time and was arguably their biggest star, but he only appears briefly as an unbilled and presumably unpaid extra at the beginning of the rival [[MGM]] studio's seagoing epic.

Examples of reasons why an actor is not credited follow.
* As [[Gary Oldman]] appeared under heavy make-up in ''[[Hannibal (2001 film)|Hannibal]]'', he requested that his name be completely removed from the billing and credits in order to "do it anonymously".<ref>[http://uk.movies.ign.com/articles/035/035937p1.html Interview with Gary Oldman] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090226192110/http://uk.movies.ign.com/articles/035/035937p1.html |date=2009-02-26 }} from [[IGN]]</ref> However, Nathan Murray is still credited as "Mr. Oldman's assistant" and Oldman's name was added to the end credits upon the film's home video release.{{Citation needed|date=December 2009}}
* Even though [[Gene Hackman]] had a prominent role in ''[[The Firm (1993 film)|The Firm]]'' he chose not to receive any billing credit because [[Tom Cruise]] was afforded sole, above the title, top billing with the letters of his name equal to that of the film title.
* For suspense purposes, [[Kevin Spacey]], in ''[[Seven (1995 film)|Seven]]'', requested not to be credited in the opening titles or in any advertising for the film.<ref>''Seven'' [https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0114369/trivia?tr=tr0734334 Trivia] – [[IMDb]]</ref> His name appears in the closing credits.
*In the 1995 ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine]]'' episode "[[Heart of Stone (Star Trek: Deep Space Nine)|Heart of Stone]]," [[Salome Jens]] agreed to be listed in the end credits (rather than in the opening credits as usual) to avoid spoiling the [[twist ending|surprise]] that her recurring character was impersonating one of the lead characters. She was listed as "Special Guest Star" rather than "Guest Star."<ref name="erdmannblock">{{cite book|last=Erdmann|first=Terry J.|author2=Block, Paula M.|title=Star Trek: Deep Space Nine Companion|year=2000|publisher=Pocket Books|location=New York|isbn=9780671501068|page=208}}</ref>
* Also on ''Star Trek: Deep Space Nine'', [[Frank Langella]] declined to be credited in three episodes despite playing a central guest role. He did not want to give the impression he had taken the role for money or exposure, as he had actually taken it to please his children.<ref name="erdmannblock" />
* In the opening of 1931's ''[[Frankenstein (1931 film)|Frankenstein]]'', the credit for "The Monster" is a question mark. [[Boris Karloff]] is named in the closing credits.
* [[Ashton Kutcher]] appears as Hank in the 2003 family comedy ''[[Cheaper by the Dozen (2003 film)|Cheaper by the Dozen]]'' and is uncredited, although he is one of the film's main characters.
* In the 1974 film ''[[Earthquake (1974 film)|Earthquake]]'', [[Walter Matthau]] agreed to provide a cameo performance without compensation on the condition that he not be credited under his real name; he was credited under a fictitious name of his choosing, "Walter Matuschanskayasky".
* Because he played the part without pay, [[Bruce Willis]] is not credited for his prominent role in the portion of ''[[Four Rooms]]'' directed by [[Quentin Tarantino]].
* [[Owen Wilson]] does not receive credit for his "Jedidiah" character in ''[[Night at the Museum]]'', though he receives credit in the sequel, ''[[Night at the Museum: Battle of the Smithsonian|Battle of the Smithsonian]]''.
* [[John Wayne]] was billed as "Michael Morris" in two cameo television appearances directed by [[John Ford]], an episode of ''[[Wagon Train]]'' titled "[[The Colter Craven Story]]" and an anthology installment called ''[[Flashing Spikes]]'' starring [[James Stewart]]. Wayne's real name, before it was changed for the 1930 [[widescreen]] film ''[[The Big Trail]]'', was Marion Robert Morrison (his widely reported middle name of Michael was apparently a change made by studio publicists after he became famous as Wayne).
* For his cameo appearances in ''[[Cabin Boy]]'' and ''[[Beavis and Butt-head Do America]]'', [[David Letterman]] was billed as "Earl Hofert".
* In ''[[Interstellar (film)|Interstellar]]'', [[Matt Damon]]'s casting was kept secret during production, and he is not credited in the film. This was a deliberate decision by the director [[Christopher Nolan]], as he uses the audience's familiarity with Matt Damon as a 'good guy' actor to hide his character's true intentions.<ref>{{cite web |date= November 14, 2014 |last= Nepales |first= Ruben V. |title= Chris Nolan explains why he kept actor's casting a secret |url= http://entertainment.inquirer.net/156463/chris-nolan-explains-why-he-kept-actors-casting-a-secret |website= Inquirer.net }}</ref>
* [[David Hyde Pierce]] declined to be credited for his voice-acting role in ''[[Hellboy (2004 film)|Hellboy]]'' because he felt it was the physical performance of [[Doug Jones (actor)|Doug Jones]], and not his own voice, which ultimately brought the character of Abe Sapien to life.<ref>{{cite interview|first=Doug |last=Jones|interviewer=Staci Layne|url=http://www.horror.com/php/article-1596-1.html|title=Doug Jones – Exclusive Interview|type=transcript|work=Horror.com|date=May 11, 2007|access-date=2008-06-11}}</ref>

===Screenwriters billing===
{{main|WGA screenwriting credit system}}
Writing credits for films and TV shows written under the jurisdiction of the [[Writers Guild of America]] (WGA) use the [[WGA screenwriting credit system]]. For writers who belong to the WGA, the writing credits affect reputation, union membership, and income. Under the rules, the film producer must first submit the proposed writing credits for the project to both the WGA and all the participating writers. If any participating writer objects to the proposed credits, it then enters arbitration, with the WGA being the final arbiter.

The WGA rules help dictate whether a screenplay should be classified as "original" or is instead based on another source. If based on another source, an additional "Based on a book/play/other source by" is generally required. In the case of a sequel to the film, the credited writers of the original motion picture may be entitled to a "Based on characters created by" credit.

The WGA's rules also outlines when credits can be apportioned separately for the story, and for the screenplay itself when all writers were not equally involved in the creation of both. When the same writers are entitled to both "Screenplay by" and "Story by" credit, they will instead by listed under one "Written by" credit.

For writing teams of two, they are credited as one, separated on the credits by an ampersand ("X & Y"). If each works independently on the script (the most common system), they are separated by an "and". If more than two persons worked on the screenplay, the credits may read like "screenplay by X & Y and Z and W", where X and Y worked as a team, but Z and W worked separately.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.salon.com/entertainment/feature/1998/10/09feature.html|title=Glatzer (October 1998) "Movie credits 101"|access-date=2017-02-04|archive-date=2010-12-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101220075448/http://www.salon.com/entertainment/feature/1998/10/09feature.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The WGA system also puts limits on the number of writers: on films, "Screenplay by", "Teleplay by", and "Written by" credit each can list no more than three writers (or writing teams).

===Director billing===
The [[Directors Guild of America]] (DGA) requires that a film lists only one director, even if more than one director has worked on the film,<ref name="Glatzer" /> with few exceptions, such as for directing teams like the [[Coen brothers]].<ref name="Engber" /> If the main credits occur at the beginning, then the director's name is last to be shown before the film's narrative starts, as a result of an agreement between the DGA and motion picture producers in 1939. If all billing is shown at the end, the director's name will be displayed first, immediately followed by the writing credits.

* In 1980, [[George Lucas]] resigned from the DGA after it insisted, against his wishes, that [[Irvin Kershner]], the director of ''[[The Empire Strikes Back]]'', be credited at the beginning of the film because the company name [[Lucasfilm]] was there; it had previously allowed the original ''[[Star Wars (film)|Star Wars]]'' (1977), which had a similar opening sequence, to go unchallenged because the writer-director credit (George Lucas) matched the company name Lucasfilm Ltd.
* ''[[Ben-Hur (1959 film)|Ben-Hur]]'' is one of the few MGM films in which the director receives very prominent billing in the posters advertising the movie – the posters state "[[William Wyler]]'s Production of", although the same credit does not appear in the actual on-screen credits.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r4Vqh-dOq04 |title=YouTube |website=[[YouTube]] |access-date=2016-12-01 |archive-date=2017-02-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170210050554/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r4Vqh-dOq04&feature=related |url-status=dead }}</ref> A similar example is [[David Lean]], whose ''[[Doctor Zhivago (1965 film)|Doctor Zhivago]]'' and ''[[Ryan's Daughter]]'' both carry the credit "David Lean's Film of" (followed by the title). [[Stanley Kubrick]] received prominent title billing from ''[[Dr. Strangelove]]'' (1964) onwards, and from ''[[A Clockwork Orange (film)|A Clockwork Orange]]'' (1971) he generally received main billing, with the actors only listed in the billing block. Advertising materials for Kubrick's ''[[Eyes Wide Shut]]'' featured the billing "[[Tom Cruise|CRUISE]] / [[Nicole Kidman|KIDMAN]] / KUBRICK".
* Filmmaker and playwright [[Tyler Perry]] always inserts his name into the title of each of his films and television shows. For instance: ''Tyler Perry's Why Did I Get Married?'' or ''Tyler Perry's Meet the Browns''. To date, the only film he has not done this with is ''[[For Colored Girls]]'', which is an adaptation of the [[Ntozake Shange]] play ''[[For Colored Girls Who Have Considered Suicide When the Rainbow Is Enuf]]''.{{citation needed|reason=Tyler Perry's For Colored Girls can easily be misread – this could be a factor |date=May 2012}}
* In 2004 [[Robert Rodriguez]] quit the DGA because he wanted to credit [[Frank Miller]] as "co-director" on the film ''[[Sin City (film)|Sin City]]''.<ref>{{cite web |first= Jake |last= Coyle |title= When Robert Rodriguez approached Frank Miller about adapting Sin City, he knew he needed a great pitch |url=http://www.kentucky.com/mld/kentucky/entertainment/movies/11272792.htm |website= Lexington Herald |publisher= [[Associated Press]] |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20050419094558/http://www.kentucky.com/mld/kentucky/entertainment/movies/11272792.htm |archive-date= 2005-04-19 |url-status= dead }}</ref><ref name="Engber">{{cite web |date= 8 April 2005 |last= Engber |first= Daniel |title= Why not quit the Directors Guild? |url= https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2005/04/why-not-quit-the-directors-guild.html |website= Slate Magazine }}</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Escuela Internacional de Cine y Televisión
======================================================================

{{Short description|Film school in Cuba}}
{{Infobox university
| name              = Escuela Internacional de Cine y Televisión
| native_name       = 
| image             = 
| caption           = 
| motto             = Aprender haciendo (Learning by doing)
| established       = {{Start date|1986|12|15}}
| founders          = [[Gabriel García Márquez]], [[Fernando Birri]], [[Julio García Espinosa]]
| type              = Private / NGO Film School
| director          = Susana Molina
| location          = [[San Antonio de los Baños]], [[Artemisa Province|Artemisa]], [[Cuba]]
| students          = 
| language          = Spanish
| affiliations      = Fundación del Nuevo Cine Latinoamericano, CILECT
| website           = {{URL|http://www.eictv.org}}
}}

The '''Escuela Internacional de Cine y Televisión''' ('''EICTV''') is an internationally recognized film and television school located in [[San Antonio de los Baños]], [[Artemisa Province]], [[Cuba]]. The institution was founded on December 15, 1986, by the Colombian journalist and Nobel laureate [[Gabriel García Márquez]], Argentine filmmaker [[Fernando Birri]], and Cuban theoretician and filmmaker [[Julio García Espinosa]]. It was established under the auspices of the Fundación del Nuevo Cine Latinoamericano (Foundation of New Latin American Cinema) and received logistical support and land from the Cuban government under Fidel Castro.<ref name="eictv_history">{{cite web |title=Historia de la EICTV |url=http://www.eictv.org/la-escuela/historia/ |publisher=Escuela Internacional de Cine y Televisión |access-date=1 October 2026 |language=es}}</ref> 

Often referred to as the "School of Three Worlds" (''Escuela de Todos los Mundos''), the EICTV originally aimed to provide rigorous cinematic training to students from [[Latin America]], [[Africa]], and [[Asia]]. Today, it has opened its doors to aspiring filmmakers globally, maintaining its status as a vital hub for independent cinema, critical thinking, and international co-production.

== History ==
=== Foundation and Early Years ===
The establishment of the EICTV was a manifestation of the [[Third Cinema]] movement and the broader goals of the Fundación del Nuevo Cine Latinoamericano. The founders envisioned an audiovisual training center for creatives from developing nations, free from the commercial pressures of Hollywood.<ref name="guardian_marquez">{{cite news |last=Carroll |first=Rory |date=18 April 2014 |title=Gabriel García Márquez: the writer who survived and styled out the critics |url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2014/apr/18/gabriel-garcia-marquez-writer-survived-critics |work=[[The Guardian]] |access-date=1 October 2026}}</ref> García Márquez, who was deeply passionate about cinema and had previously worked as a screenwriter, utilized his international prestige to secure funding and resources. Fernando Birri, often considered the father of the New Latin American Cinema, served as the school's inaugural director, instilling a manifesto of "socially conscious but artistically free" filmmaking.<ref>{{cite news |last=Riding |first=Alan |date=1988-02-04 |title=Cuba Film School's Quest: A Third World Cinema |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1988/02/04/movies/cuba-film-school-s-quest-a-third-world-cinema.html |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=1 October 2026}}</ref>

=== The Special Period and Resilience ===
Following the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, Cuba entered a severe economic crisis known as the [[Special Period]]. The EICTV faced significant shortages in film stock, equipment, electricity, and basic necessities. Despite these immense challenges, the school remained operational, largely sustained by international donations, tuition fees from European students, and the relentless advocacy of García Márquez.<ref>{{cite news |last=Kettleday |first=Richard |date=2006-12-14 |title=Cuba's film school celebrates 20th anniversary |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/americas/6179455.stm |work=[[BBC News]] |access-date=1 October 2026}}</ref> The resourcefulness demanded during this era became deeply embedded in the school's teaching philosophy, teaching students to create impactful cinema with minimal resources.

== Campus and Facilities ==
Situated approximately 40 kilometers from [[Havana]], the EICTV is located on a former agricultural estate in San Antonio de los Baños. The isolated, rural setting is a deliberate choice, creating an immersive, "monastic" environment where students and faculty live together and focus entirely on filmmaking. 

The campus operates as a boarding school and is equipped with soundstages, editing suites, a mixing theater, and specialized camera equipment. Its library, the ''Mediateca André Bazin'', is one of the most comprehensive audiovisual archives in Latin America, containing thousands of films, screenplays, and theoretical texts.<ref>{{cite web |title=Mediateca André Bazin |url=http://www.eictv.org/mediateca/ |publisher=EICTV |access-date=1 October 2026 |language=es}}</ref>

== Academic Programs ==
=== Regular Course (Curso Regular) ===
The cornerstone of the EICTV's educational model is its three-year Regular Course (''Curso Regular''). The program is highly selective, admitting a small cohort of students each year based on rigorous portfolio reviews and exams. 

* '''Year 1:''' Students undergo a multidisciplinary polyvalent training program, learning the basics of all cinematic trades.
* '''Years 2 and 3:''' Students declare a specialization and engage in advanced theoretical and practical training. The specializations include Documentary Direction, Fiction Direction, Sound, TV and New Media, Screenwriting, Cinematography, Editing, and Production.<ref name="eictv_academics">{{cite web |title=Curso Regular |url=http://www.eictv.org/formacion/curso-regular/ |publisher=EICTV |access-date=1 October 2026 |language=es}}</ref> 

=== International Workshops and Master's Degrees ===
In addition to the Regular Course, the school offers short-term International Workshops (''Talleres Internacionales'') and advanced Master's programs. These courses attract working professionals looking to hone specific skills, such as underwater cinematography, advanced color grading, or documentary pitching.

== Educational Philosophy ==
The EICTV operates under a distinctive "learning by doing" (''aprender haciendo'') philosophy. The curriculum dictates that practical execution is as important as theoretical study. Students are required to conceptualize, shoot, and edit a multitude of short films, documentaries, and thesis projects on strict deadlines. 

Crucially, the school employs very few permanent academic faculty. Instead, it relies on a rotating roster of active industry professionals from around the globe who travel to Cuba to teach intensive modules ranging from one to four weeks. This ensures the curriculum remains grounded in contemporary, real-world cinematic practices rather than purely academic theory.<ref>{{cite web |title=Inside the world’s most utopian film school |url=https://www.dazeddigital.com/artsandculture/article/33946/1/inside-the-world-s-most-utopian-film-school-cuba-eictv |publisher=[[Dazed]] |date=2016-12-08 |access-date=1 October 2026}}</ref>

== Visiting Faculty and Guest Lecturers ==
Because of its unique pedigree and the influence of Gabriel García Márquez, the EICTV has historically attracted some of the most revered figures in world cinema to hold workshops, give masterclasses, or simply interact with students. 

Notable visiting faculty and guests have included:
* '''[[Francis Ford Coppola]]''', who frequently visited in the school's early years, occasionally cooking pasta for the entire student body while teaching screenwriting and directing.<ref>{{cite news |last=Hopewell |first=John |date=2015-12-10 |title=Cuba’s EICTV Film School: A Talent Pipeline For The Global Industry |url=https://variety.com/2015/film/festivals/cubas-eictv-film-school-a-talent-pipeline-for-the-global-industry-1201658428/ |work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |access-date=1 October 2026}}</ref>
* '''[[Werner Herzog]]''', who has conducted his renowned "Rogue Film School" seminars at the EICTV, teaching students about perseverance and ecstatic truth in documentary filmmaking.
* '''[[Abbas Kiarostami]]''', the legendary Iranian auteur who hosted an intensive practical workshop in San Antonio de los Baños, guiding students in making shorts over a ten-day period.<ref>{{cite web |title=Abbas Kiarostami in Cuba |url=https://www.screendaily.com/news/kiarostami-to-host-cuba-workshop/5099238.article |publisher=[[Screen International]] |date=2016-01-26 |access-date=1 October 2026}}</ref>
* Other notable visitors have included [[Steven Spielberg]], [[George Lucas]], [[Brian De Palma]], [[Emir Kusturica]], and [[Agnès Varda]].

== Global Impact and Partnerships ==
Over the decades, the EICTV has grown into a crucial institution for international cooperation and cinematic diversity. It is a full member of [[CILECT]] (The International Association of Film and Television Schools). Thousands of professionals from over 50 countries have graduated, creating a vast global alumni network known informally as "la mafia de San Antonio."

The school maintains partnerships with numerous international institutions, allowing for student exchanges and co-productions. For instance, [[Concordia University]]'s Mel Hoppenheim School of Cinema in Canada and several European film academies hold formal collaborative agreements with the EICTV.<ref name="concordia_eictv">{{cite web |title=Art History & Film Studies Degree (BFA) - Internships and other study opportunities |url=https://www.concordia.ca/academics/undergraduate/art-history-filmstudiesbfa.html |publisher=[[Concordia University]] |access-date=1 October 2026}}</ref>

== Notable Alumni ==
The EICTV has produced a significant number of award-winning directors, producers, writers, and cinematographers who have premiered works at major festivals like Cannes, Venice, and Berlin. 
* '''[[Amat Escalante]]''' (Mexico) – Director and screenwriter, known for critically acclaimed films such as ''[[Heli (film)|Heli]]'' (Best Director at the Cannes Film Festival) and ''[[The Untamed (2016 film)|The Untamed]]''.
* '''[[Benito Zambrano]]''' (Spain) – Film director and screenwriter, highly celebrated for his multi-Goya-winning debut feature ''[[Solas (film)|Solas]]''.
* '''[[Mariana Rondón]]''' (Venezuela) – Film director and visual artist, best known for her coming-of-age drama ''[[Bad Hair (film)|Bad Hair]]'' (''Pelo Malo''), which won the Golden Shell at the San Sebastián International Film Festival.
* '''[[Jaime Rosales (director)|Jaime Rosales]]''' (Spain) – Film director whose film ''[[Solitary Fragments|La Soledad]]'' won the Goya Award for Best Director and Best Film.
* '''[[Estibaliz Urresola Solaguren]]''' (Spain) – Basque filmmaker, director of the acclaimed feature ''[[20,000 Species of Bees]]'' which premiered at the Berlinale.<ref name="urresola_bio">{{cite web |title=Estibaliz Urresola Solaguren - Biography |url=https://www.kino-zeit.de/personen/estibaliz-urresola-solaguren |publisher=Kino-Zeit |access-date=1 October 2026 |language=de}}</ref>
* '''[[Kiro Russo]]''' (Bolivia) – Director and cinematographer known for ''[[Dark Skull]]'' (''Viejo Calavera'') and ''The Great Movement'', which won the Special Jury Prize in the Orizzonti section at the Venice Film Festival.
* '''[[Anne von Petersdorff]]''' (Germany) – Scholar, writer, and filmmaker known for her documentary work and collaborative, border-crossing projects, including the acclaimed film ''Wanderlust, female bodies in transit''.<ref name="anne_vp">{{cite web |title=Anne von Petersdorff: hello |url=https://www.annevonpetersdorff.com/ |publisher=Anne von Petersdorff Official Website |access-date=1 October 2026}}</ref>
* '''[[Miguel Coyula]]''' (Cuba) – Independent filmmaker and writer, noted for his rebellious, non-linear cinematic style in films like ''[[Memories of Overdevelopment]]'' and ''[[Blue Heart (film)|Blue Heart]]''.
* '''[[Bettina Blümner]]''' (Germany) – Director and academic, renowned for her acclaimed documentary film ''[[Prinzessinnenbad]]'' (Pool of Princesses).
* '''[[Juan Carlos Valdivia Galdo|Juan Carlos Valdivia]]''' (Bolivia) – Director of ''Zona Sur'', which won Best Direction and Best Screenplay in the World Cinema Dramatic Competition at Sundance.
* '''[[Jorge Molina Enríquez|Jorge Molina]]''' (Cuba) – Actor and cult independent filmmaker.
