Color|url=https://www.studiodaily.com/2019/11/dp-mihai-malaimare-jr-capturing-dark-comedy-jojo-rabbit-living-color/|access-date=2021-03-30|website=Studio Daily|language=en|archive-date=January 29, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210129204944/https://www.studiodaily.com/2019/11/dp-mihai-malaimare-jr-capturing-dark-comedy-jojo-rabbit-living-color/|url-status=live}}</ref> The actors described having a fun experience on set, saying Waititi was engaging to work with.<ref>{{Cite web|title='Jojo Rabbit' Cast Scarlett Johansson, Rebel Wilson on Working with Director Taika Waititi|date=January 21, 2020|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/video/jojo-rabbit-cast-scarlett-johansson-rebel-wilson-working-director-taika-waititi-1270719|access-date=2021-02-19|website=The Hollywood Reporter|language=en|archive-date=February 19, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210219170900/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/video/jojo-rabbit-cast-scarlett-johansson-rebel-wilson-working-director-taika-waititi-1270719|url-status=live}}</ref> McKenzie further elaborated that it was "easy-going and fun", as it allowed her to "explore the character and try different things".<ref>{{Cite web|title='Jojo Rabbit' Will Teach Trump A Lesson Says Roman Griffin Davis with Taika Waititi {{!}} TIFF 2019|date=September 7, 2019|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/video/jojo-rabbit-young-star-teaches-trump-a-lesson-skills-watch-1237780|access-date=2021-02-19|website=The Hollywood Reporter|language=en|archive-date=April 15, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200415084915/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/video/jojo-rabbit-young-star-teaches-trump-a-lesson-skills-watch-1237780|url-status=live}}</ref> These, along with doing rehearsals, were part of an effort to make the child actors feel comfortable so they would act more naturally.<ref name="Studio Daily-2019" />

Reshoots were done starting in February 2019.<ref>{{cite web|last=Topel|first=Fred|date=February 4, 2019|title=Taika Waititi is Finishing 'Jojo Rabbit' Reshoots, Movie Will Be Released This Fall [TCA 2019]|url=https://www.slashfilm.com/jojo-rabbit-reshoots/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190606001435/https://www.slashfilm.com/jojo-rabbit-reshoots/|archive-date=June 6, 2019|access-date=September 5, 2019|website=[[/Film]]}}</ref> They mainly focused on scenes set during winter.<ref name="Grobar-2019a">{{Cite web|last=Grobar|first=Matt|date=2019-10-29|title=Cinematographer Mihai Malaimare Jr. On His "Classical" Cinematic Approach To The Tonally Complex 'Jojo Rabbit'|url=https://deadline.com/2019/10/jojo-rabbit-cinematographer-mihai-malaimare-jr-taika-waititi-interview-news-1202771500/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201028054317/https://deadline.com/2019/10/jojo-rabbit-cinematographer-mihai-malaimare-jr-taika-waititi-interview-news-1202771500/|archive-date=October 28, 2020|access-date=2021-02-16|website=[[Deadline Hollywood]]|language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Cinematography and visual effects ===
[[File:Jojo_Rabbit_chroma_key_extension.jpg|thumb|upright=1.4|The pavement and buildings further away were in reality [[Blue screen process|blue screens]]. ''Jojo Rabbit'' was shot in a [[1.85:1]] [[aspect ratio]], as there are many scenes with two people indoors. A lively color palette is used to symbolize Jojo's amusement towards the Nazi regime.|alt=A view of Jojo running enthusiastically through a long, crowded pavement at a sunny day.]]
[[Mihai Mălaimare Jr.]] was enlisted as the film's cinematographer while he was doing reshoots for ''[[The Hate U Give (film)|The Hate U Give]]'' in [[Atlanta]], and he joined the project five days later. He agreed to depict ''Jojo Rabbit'' in a colorful and vibrant way, a primary motif of the film,<ref name="Grobar-2019a" /> taking inspiration from several colorized documentaries.<ref name="Mălaimare Jr.-2019">{{Cite interview|last=Mălaimare Jr.|first=Mihai|subject-link=Mihai Mălaimare Jr.|interviewer=Sim, Ted|title=The Cinematography of JoJo Rabbit {{!}} Camera & Lighting Breakdown w/ Mihai Malaimare Jr.|type=[[YouTube]] video|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_OgBDRPoIcA|access-date=2021-03-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200620061941/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_OgBDRPoIcA|archive-date=2020-06-20|url-status=live|work=[[Indy Mogul]]|publisher=[[YouTube Next Lab and Audience Development Group]]|date=2019-11-10}}</ref> He also took inspiration from a film he had previously worked on, ''[[Youth Without Youth (film)|Youth Without Youth]]'' (2007), which featured colorful World War II footage, contrasting the typical desaturated and grayscale historical footage. ''[[Cabaret (1972 film)|Cabaret]]'' (1972) was also a visual reference used for the cinematography. Despite this, Mălaimare arranged for the melancholic scenes to look more desaturated, corresponding to Jojo's emotions and showing the passage of time. He and Waititi also agreed not to visually exaggerate scenes with Adolf. [[Henri Cartier-Bresson]] and [[Robert Capa]]'s images of children during World War II also served as inspiration for the cinematography style: "They were still playing, and they were still doing normal kid stuff, [but] the closer you look at the photo, [...] you realize something is wrong—like, 'Oh, in this one, they are wearing gas masks,' or 'They are playing close to a pile of bomb'—all these situations that we felt were very close to [''Jojo Rabbit'']." Around 60 similar stills from [[Magnum Photos]] and [[Flickr]] were also printed to be analyzed for inspiration.<ref name="Grobar-2019a" /><ref>{{Cite podcast|url=https://ascmag.com/podcasts/jojo-rabbit-mihai-m%C4%83laimare-jr|title=Jojo Rabbit / Mihai Mălaimare Jr., Episode #102|website=[[American Cinematographer]]|publisher=[[American Society of Cinematographers]]|last=Hemphill|first=Jim|date=2019-11-28|access-date=2021-03-21|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200927001637/https://ascmag.com/podcasts/jojo-rabbit-mihai-m%C4%83laimare-jr|archive-date=2020-09-27|last2=Mălaimare Jr.|first2=Mihai|author2-link=Mihai Mălaimare Jr.}}</ref>

Mălaimare and Waititi also agreed on the decision not to use [[hand-held camera]]s, in order to retain the film's classical style. Equipped with a [[Camera dolly|dolly]]<ref name="Film School Rejects-2020" /> (a golf cart for scenes in the forest),<ref name="Mălaimare Jr.-2019" /> an [[Arri Alexa]] SXT and Mini with [[Super 35]] format was used.<ref name="Leitz Cine">{{Cite web |title=Jojo Rabbit |url=https://www.leitz-cine.com/production/jojo-rabbit-2019 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211027132538/https://www.leitz-cine.com/production/jojo-rabbit-2019 |archive-date=October 27, 2021 |access-date=2022-06-16 |website=Leitz Cine }}</ref><ref name="NoFilm" /> Around five tests were implemented to determine the [[aspect ratio]] for the film; a [[1.85:1]] [[anamorphic format]] was chosen, considering that there were lots of scenes with two people indoors.<ref name="Film School Rejects-2020">{{Cite web|last1=Olthof |first1=Samantha |date=2020-02-13|title=How 'Jojo Rabbit' Went from Bleak Novel to Vibrant Satire|url=https://filmschoolrejects.com/jojo-rabbit-cinematography-mihai-malaimare-jr/|access-date=2021-02-23|website=Film School Rejects|language=en-US|archive-date=September 18, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200918145804/https://filmschoolrejects.com/jojo-rabbit-cinematography-mihai-malaimare-jr/|url-status=live}}</ref> The anamorphic format was favored due to its "velvety" tone, [[focus breathing]], as well as authentic [[bokeh]].<ref name="Mălaimare Jr.-2019" /> Lenses include the Hawk V-Lite 1.3x [[anamorphic]], Vantage One T1 [[Spherical lens|spherical]],<ref name="Film School Rejects-2020" /> and Leitz Summilux-C.<ref name="Leitz Cine" /> The [[Stopping down|stopped down]] T1 was used for scenes in small or [[Low-light photography|low-light]] areas, in order to give them a wide feel. Mălaimare worked with [[digital imaging technician]] (DIT) Eli Berg to seamlessly transition between scenes using different lenses.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Hawk V-Lites Strike Perfect Tone: Jojo Rabbit Gets 1.3x Squeeze For 1.85|url=http://www.vantagefilm.com/en/news/hawk-v-lites-strike-perfect-tone-11209|url-status=live|access-date=2021-03-30|website=Vantage Hawk|language=en|archive-date=January 2, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210102180545/https://www.vantagefilm.com/en/news/hawk-v-lites-strike-perfect-tone-11209}}</ref> Though point-of-view shots were used, the main approach in making the film first-person on Jojo is to lower the camera to Davis's height. Waititi also allowed the actors to also give cinematographic advice, some of which were better than Waititi's suggestions, per Mălaimare. Symmetry and horizons are the main composition approaches to the cinematography, a major contributor to the narrative flow.<ref name="Grobar-2019a" /> The film was mostly shot using a [[multiple-camera setup]] so that [[close-up]] and [[wide shot]]s could be done simultaneously.<ref name="Film Doctor-2020" /> These camerawork techniques were used as a way to show Jojo's emotions and what he was feeling throughout the entirety of Jojo Rabbit. In the Mirror scene, for example, the camera, in this instance acts as a powerful tool, peeling back the surface of Jojo's outward display to expose the underlying vulnerability and the insidious grip of indoctrination. Exterior scenes rarely used [[artificial lighting]]: scenes in the forest, for example, solely used the sun. The interplay of light and shadow in the forest is crucial for conveying mood. Scenes where Jojo is fearful or uncertain might feature more prominent shadows, creating a sense of unease or the unknown. Conversely, moments of budding connection or understanding might be bathed in softer, more even light. The final sequence of the battle scene, which took five or six takes to accomplish, used three extra lights, but they were merely supplements to the sun. The scene where Jojo is having dinner with Rosie used an extensive lighting kit, mainly consisting of a [[chandelier]] and two practical lights, lighting the entirety of the setting; one of them dimmed, and [[tungsten lights]] to give the characters a softer and warmer lighting in the close-up shots.<ref name="Mălaimare Jr.-2019" /> Small five-[[watt]] [[LED]] lights were used as lighting for the actors in scenes at Elsa's [[Secret passage|secret room]].<ref name="NoFilm">{{Cite web|date=2019-12-19|title=How 'Jojo Rabbit' DP Mihai Mălaimare Uses Color to Create Perspective|url=https://nofilmschool.com/jojo-rabbit-cinematography|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201027155126/https://nofilmschool.com/jojo-rabbit-cinematography|archive-date=October 27, 2020|access-date=2021-02-23|website=No Film School|language=en}}</ref> In that setting, Mălaimare decided to use a medium-bright petrol lamp as the [[key light]], whereas a lighting was used to indicate [[dusk]];<ref name="Mălaimare Jr.-2019" /> candles act as supplements.<ref name="Fox Searchlight Pictures" />{{Rp|20}}

[[Visual effects supervisor]] Jason Chen had previously worked with Waititi.<ref name="Hart-2019">{{Cite web|last=Hart|first=Hugh|date=2019-10-22|title=How Jojo Rabbit's VFX Supervisor Helped Taika Waititi Create the Year's Wildest Comedy {{!}} The Credits|url=https://www.motionpictures.org/2019/10/how-jojo-rabbits-vfx-supervisor-helped-taika-waititi-create-the-years-wildest-comedy/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200926085332/https://www.motionpictures.org/2019/10/how-jojo-rabbits-vfx-supervisor-helped-taika-waititi-create-the-years-wildest-comedy/|archive-date=September 26, 2020|access-date=2021-02-17|website=Motion Picture Association|language=en-US}}</ref> He joined the project after working on ''[[Bumblebee (film)|Bumblebee]]''. The goal was to create a "seamless illusion", balancing realism and surrealism. In total, there were about 200 visual effects shots, "about half of which were big invisible [[set extension]]s and often done by a [...] team of [[in house]] compositors" led by previous Chen collaborator Kenneth Quinn Brown.<ref name="fxguide-2019">{{Cite web |date=2019-11-05 |title=Jojo Rabbit |url=https://www.fxguide.com/quicktakes/jojo-rabbit/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201101060110/https://www.fxguide.com/quicktakes/jojo-rabbit/ |archive-date=November 1, 2020 |access-date=2021-03-22 |website=fxguide |language=en-US}}</ref> Chen worked with Clear Angle Studios to set up 3D scanners on tripods at Žatec. The scanners shoot laser beams, rotating 360 degrees, scanning the surrounding architecture in order to give an accurate representation of them. They also scanned Czech streets with historical relevance to ''Jojo Rabbit'', especially the square used for Jojo's town, which was once a frequent place for Hitler to hold rallies.<ref name="Hart-2019" /> A major contributor to the visual effects was [[Luma Pictures]], which split work between [[Los Angeles]] and [[Melbourne]].<ref name="fxguide-2019" /> Luma used [[Blue screen process|blue screens]] to incorporate elements like explosions, tanks, smoke, and gunfire in [[post-production]].<ref name="Hart-2019" /> The glow of bombs going off in the distance, meanwhile, used [[matte painting]]s.<ref name="Fox Searchlight Pictures" />{{Rp|22}} They also incorporated snow into scenes that were actually shot during the summer, but were supposed to depict winter in ''Jojo Rabbit''<nowiki/>'s universe. This was achievable by photographing snow on the streets and adding it to the film, a technique known as "background plate."<ref name="Hart-2019" /> Additional effects were done by Picture Shop VFX.<ref name="Fox Searchlight Pictures" />{{Rp|52}} In total, visual effects took a year to finish.<ref name="fxguide-2019" />

=== Fashion design ===
[[Mayes C. Rubeo]], who had previously collaborated with Waititi in ''Ragnarok'', became ''Jojo Rabbit''<nowiki/>'s costume designer. In an "intensive" conversation about the costumes, Waititi favored "formal, elegant" fashion, as it matched the kind of clothing people wore in that era, according to his research. He also wanted a design that symbolized the joy of childhood: bright, vivid colors, stressing the ambition to contrast typical [[historical films]]. Rubeo interpreted these as [[Italian neorealism]], a filmmaking style popular in the 1940s.<ref name="Fox Searchlight Pictures" />{{Rp|20}}<ref name="Whitlock-2019">{{Cite web|date=2019-10-18|title=How 'Avatar's' Costume Designer Mayes C. Rubeo Dressed the Satirical World of Taika Waititi's 'JoJo Rabbit'|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/how-avatars-costume-designer-dressed-satirical-world-jojo-rabbit-1248598|first=Cathy|last=Whitlock|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191020175540/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/how-avatars-costume-designer-dressed-satirical-world-jojo-rabbit-1248598|archive-date=October 20, 2019|access-date=2021-02-16|website=The Hollywood Reporter|language=en}}</ref>

Rubeo thought of Rosie's character as open: "She represents [...] life, [and] she doesn't want to hide [that]."<ref name="Walt Disney Studios Home Entertainment-2020" /> Rubeo started by scouring [[Vintage clothing|vintage]] Italian houses for Rosie's wardrobe, though she also created several blouses and dresses by herself. She wanted Rosie's clothing to be distinctive so it would resonate with the audience throughout the film and assist them in the scene where Rosie is found hanged.<ref name="Fox Searchlight Pictures" />{{Rp|21}} Concerning that specific scene, Rubeo chose a pair of single lace-up red and white [[spectator shoe]]s made by the [[Toronto]] shoemaker Jitterbug, based on a sketch she made. Imagining Rosie as "the friend of [[Elsa Schiaparelli]]", Rubeo flew to New York City, where she discussed the costume with actor Johansson. Rosie's short-sleeved sweater was characterized by "plaid and zigzag [[Missoni]]-style patterns". She was completed with high-waist baggy pants and several other accessories, offering her character a "chic" look.<ref name="Whitlock-2019" /> This is in stark contrast to Elsa's clothing palette which, being a confined character, was made [[Monochromatic color|monochromatic]].<ref name="Tangcay-2020">{{Cite web|last=Tangcay|first=Jazz|date=2020-01-31|title=Mayes C. Rubeo on Storytelling Through Costume Design|url=https://variety.com/2020/artisans/awards/mayes-rubeo-jojo-rabbit-costume-design-1203487510/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200820221215/https://variety.com/2020/artisans/awards/mayes-rubeo-jojo-rabbit-costume-design-1203487510/|archive-date=August 20, 2020|access-date=2021-02-16|website=Variety|language=en-US}}</ref>

Jojo's ''Jungvolk'' uniform was based on the assumption that he is "trying to be the policeman of his household", especially when he wears it even in his house. Though Rubeo found vintage ''Jungvolk'' uniforms in Berlin, she noted the need for more sizes for the [[Extra (acting)|extras]], causing her and the clothing department to sew them, a total of 250, themselves. For Adolf, Rubeo chose the typical brown [[Nazi Party]] style, in order to highlight the absurdities of his character, though a "voluminous" pair of riding pants was used to highlight his imaginary state and insecurities. ''[[The Hollywood Reporter]]'' described it as "paper-bag colored", "[[khaki]]", and "safari-style". In total, three Adolf uniforms were sewn.<ref name="Fox Searchlight Pictures" /><ref name="HR-11nov-2019" /><ref name="Whitlock-2019" /> Portraying Captain Klenzendorf, Rockwell reached out to Rubeo and showed her a photo of Murray on ''[[Saturday Night Live]]'', saying that he wanted such design. For an experimental uniform Klenzendorf was written to wear in the screenplay, Rubeo went for a "glitzier", "heroic", and "flamboyant" approach, creating for him an "unorthodox" outfit, showcasing the character's creativity despite "know[ing] almost nothing about the rules of design." She said that creating Klenzendorf's outfit "was fun to do".<ref name="Fox Searchlight Pictures" />{{Rp|21}}

Rubeo made six different versions for a paper uniform Yorki wears in the final battle scene. She made it out of paper and cardboard, with some cotton. As the war ensues, Yorki's uniform degrades, with only a [[Waistcoat|vest]] left as the war concludes.<ref name="Tangcay-2020" />

The film's [[make-up artist]] was Danelle Satherley, also a frequent collaborator of Waititi's. On Adolf's looks, she envisioned them to be those of a 10-year-old imagination and not an exact replica of Hitler's looks. Despite this, they had some similarities for familiarity purposes. The hair, mustache, and ears shared similarities with Hitler's, whereas the skin and eyes had some alterations. Waititi's skin, specifically, was toned down a bit to not make his character look [[Caucasian race|Caucasian]]. Blue eyes were chosen to match the propaganda Jojo saw.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2019-10-15|title=Interview: How Danelle Satherley Turned Taika Waititi Into Hitler For 'Jojo Rabbit'|url=https://www.awardsdaily.com/2019/10/15/interview-how-danelle-satherley-turned-taika-waititi-into-hitler-for-jojo-rabbit/|access-date=2021-03-04|website=Awards Daily|language=en-US|archive-date=October 29, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191029063224/http://www.awardsdaily.com/2019/10/15/interview-how-danelle-satherley-turned-taika-waititi-into-hitler-for-jojo-rabbit/|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Production design ===
[[File:Úštěk,_2020_(08).jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|A row of houses in [[Úštěk]] that was used in the film]]
Vincent, who lived in New Zealand, was flabbergasted to be offered the role of the film's production designer,<ref name="Licuria-2020" /> but he had read the script when it was still unproduced and already had some ideas for the set design.<ref name="Film Doctor-2020">{{Cite web|date=2020-01-16|title=EXCLUSIVE: 'Jojo Rabbit' production designer – Ra Vincent – In Conversation|url=http://filmdoctor.co.uk/2020/01/16/exclusive-jojo-rabbit-production-designer-ra-vincent-in-conversation/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201225233920/https://filmdoctor.co.uk/2020/01/16/exclusive-jojo-rabbit-production-designer-ra-vincent-in-conversation/|archive-date=December 25, 2020|access-date=2021-03-06|website=Film Doctor|language=en-US}}</ref> He stayed in the Czech Republic for some time to get a feel for [[European architecture]], and took to locals who told generational stories about World War II in order to depict wartime Europe authentically, while giving aesthetic touches to symbolize the joy Jojo's character feels about Nazi Germany. Vincent recalled that the interaction with locals was easier than one might think because they see their Nazi history as something it is important to remember, not cover up.<ref name="Licuria-2020">{{Cite web|last=Licuria|first=Rob|date=2020-01-23|title=Production designer Ra Vincent ('Jojo Rabbit') on the challenges of Nazi imagery on location in Europe [EXCLUSIVE VIDEO INTERVIEW]|url=https://www.goldderby.com/article/2020/production-designer-ra-vincent-jojo-rabbit-video-interview/|access-date=2021-03-06|website=GoldDerby|language=en-US|archive-date=January 24, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200124195431/https://www.goldderby.com/article/2020/production-designer-ra-vincent-jojo-rabbit-video-interview/|url-status=live}}</ref> He also said that he thinks the locals might have even felt sad when the set decorations were torn away, since his team had "transformed the village back into its former glory days, when it was a beautifully unsullied town."<ref name="Grobar-2019b" /> Mălaimare commented that the practice in the Czech Republic of being very cautious about installing air conditioners and antennas on historical buildings – things that would have ruined the historical look of the film – allowed for a 360-degree set without having to remove much other than cars and street signs.<ref name="Studio Daily-2019"/> Helping the research were [[military advisor]]s and specialists;<ref name="Film Doctor-2020" /> Filip Stiebitz was officially credited as one.<ref name="Fox Searchlight Pictures" />{{Rp|42}}

The fully handcrafted<ref name="Licuria-2020" /> [[set design]] for the Betzlers' house, a Baroque stone cottage<ref>{{cite news|date=2020-01-07|title=How 'Irishman,' 'Jojo Rabbit' and 'Little Women' Set Designs Brought Fresh Takes to Period Looks|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/lists/how-irishman-jojo-rabbit-little-women-set-designs-brought-fresh-takes-period-looks-1266199|access-date=2025-03-13|first=Carolyn|last=Giardina|newspaper=The Hollywood Reporter|language=en|archive-date=August 15, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200815060430/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/lists/how-irishman-jojo-rabbit-little-women-set-designs-brought-fresh-takes-period-looks-1266199|url-status=live}}</ref> filmed at a {{Convert|7,000|sqft|m2|abbr=}} Barrandov Studios [[soundstage]], is characterized by elegant details, such as thick door frames, windows recessed deeply into the [[stone wall]]s, a wood-paneled hallway, and a curved staircase. Broadly, it features [[Art Deco architecture]] popular in the 1930s. [[Victorian architecture]] and a muted color palette were used for Inge's bedroom in order to provide a neutral space in which Jojo and Elsa could bond. According to Vincent's research, Inge's bedroom being in the attic is historically accurate, because certain families in World War II had new types of [[Building insulation|insulation]] replacing the method of [[pitched roof]]s, meaning they could build rooms up to the attic. This makes Elsa's hideout "obvious, but not-so-obvious". It is conceptualized that the Betzlers are a [[middle-class]] family, wealthy enough to own a two-floored, three-bedroom house.<ref name="Reinstein-2019" /><ref name="Grobar-2019b">{{Cite web|last=Grobar|first=Matt|date=2019-12-18|title='Jojo Rabbit' Production Designer Ra Vincent On Crafting Stylish, Baroque Home For Unconventional World War II Film|url=https://deadline.com/2019/12/jojo-rabbit-production-designer-ra-vincent-taika-waititi-interview-news-1202807207/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201006141925/https://deadline.com/2019/12/jojo-rabbit-production-designer-ra-vincent-taika-waititi-interview-news-1202807207/|archive-date=October 6, 2020|access-date=2021-02-15|website=[[Deadline Hollywood]]|language=en-US}}</ref> With a more modernized interior, another notion is also formed that the house was at some point renovated.<ref name="Licuria-2020" /> Creating the house was said to be the trickiest thing throughout the film's production design. To not make it [[claustrophobic]], the house was given an [[Open plan|open layout plan]], "and one with viewing portals through to other spaces so that you never felt like you were going to individual little sets. We wanted you to feel you were journeying through a proper house." The house was built on a stage to allow for adequate space to film using a multi-camera setup.<ref name="Film Doctor-2020" />

According to Vincent, a woman named Cheng Liang, who was the film's art department assistant, drew ''Yoohoo Jew''. She took inspiration from some of the artwork from the screenplay, as well as Waititi and Vincent's descriptions. Though the book was planned to be about 12 pages long, Liang ended up drawing 42 pages. Her drawings also became inspirations for the cast's acting style, according to Vincent.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Gates|first=Christopher|date=2020-01-30|title=The Truth About Jojo Rabbit's Most Important Prop – Exclusive|url=https://www.looper.com/186093/the-truth-about-jojo-rabbits-most-important-prop/|url-status=live|access-date=2021-03-03|website=Looper|publisher=[[ZergNet]]|language=en-US|publication-place=[[Indianapolis]]|archive-date=January 31, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200131123234/https://www.looper.com/186093/the-truth-about-jojo-rabbits-most-important-prop/}}</ref>

=== Editing ===
[[File:Jojo_Rabbit_reverb.ogv|thumb|277x277px|This dialogue of Adolf scolding Jojo in Adolf's penultimate speaking scene has [[reverb]] added (starting with "wolf!") to evoke a sense of rallying and tension as it closely mimics the real Hitler's speeches.]]
Editor [[Tom Eagles]] said that Waititi had been talking to him about the project "for a long time", though he read the screenplay much later.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Grobar|first=Matt|date=2019-12-12|title=How 'Jojo Rabbit' Editor Tom Eagles Pulled Off Satire's Tricky Tonal Balance — Production Value Video Series|url=https://deadline.com/video/jojo-rabbit-editor-tom-eagles-taika-waititi-production-value-interview-news/|access-date=2021-03-11|website=[[Deadline Hollywood]]|language=en-US|archive-date=January 18, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210118055150/https://deadline.com/video/jojo-rabbit-editor-tom-eagles-taika-waititi-production-value-interview-news/|url-status=live}}</ref> He recalled that Waititi did not sit by his side to judge his editing while it was ongoing. "He's interested in what you have to say and what you might bring to the edit," Eagles said. Eagles was given two weeks to edit ''Jojo Rabbit'' after being given some initial suggestions, which Eagles "cautiously" implemented. The film was edited using [[Avid Media Composer]]. Eagles used ScriptSync to compare scenes with the screenplay.<ref name="Randi Altman-2020" /> He stated that the main challenge in editing the film was to give it a tonal balance for every transition between scenes:<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-01-21|title=The Tonal Trick of Editing "Jojo Rabbit"|url=https://www.creativeplanetnetwork.com/news/the-tonal-trick-of-editing-jojo-rabbit|access-date=2021-03-11|website=Creative Planet Network|language=en-US}}</ref> The [[rough cut]] was 165 minutes, with the [[director's cut]] being the finalized,<ref name="Randi Altman-2020">{{Cite web|last=Randi Altman|date=2020-01-29|title=Oscar-nominated Jojo Rabbit editor Tom Eagles: blending comedy and drama|url=https://postperspective.com/oscar-nominated-jojo-rabbit-editor-tom-eagles-blending-comedy-and-drama/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210216114751/https://postperspective.com/oscar-nominated-jojo-rabbit-editor-tom-eagles-blending-comedy-and-drama/|archive-date=February 16, 2021|access-date=2021-02-16|website=postPerspective|language=en-US}}</ref> 108-minute version.<ref name="BBFC">{{cite web|title=Jojo Rabbit (2019)|url=https://bbfc.co.uk/releases/jojo-rabbit-2019|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191222045412/https://bbfc.co.uk/releases/jojo-rabbit-2019|archive-date=December 22, 2019|access-date=December 21, 2019|publisher=[[British Board of Film Classification]]}}</ref> Eagles said that "We didn't want it to look like ''Titanic''". Trimming took eight months, with [[test screening]]s implemented: "We needed to test different versions of things and iterations of jokes." It was also observed that some audiences were shocked by a scene when Hitler is scolding Jojo over his degrading patriotism; one person began quietly reciting a prayer.<ref name="HR-11nov-2019" /> [[Dailies]] were also screened to the entire film team once or twice a week in a "small" screening room to let everyone judge the film's qualities, something said to be rare in modern filmmaking.<ref name="Studio Daily-2019" />

The film's [[title sequence]] was created by the New Zealand production company Assembly.<ref name="www.assemblyltd.com">{{Cite web|title=Jojo Rabbit – Main titles {{!}} Assembly|url=https://www.assemblyltd.com/work/jojo-rabbit---main-titles|access-date=2021-03-27|website=www.assemblyltd.com|archive-date=October 19, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201019154100/http://www.assemblyltd.com/work/jojo-rabbit---main-titles|url-status=live}}</ref> It features footage from the 1935 Nazi [[Propaganda documentaries|propaganda documentary]] ''[[Triumph of the Will]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Adams|first=Sam|date=2019-09-09|title=Disney's Hitler Movie Mocks Nazis Without Making Light of Them|url=https://slate.com/culture/2019/09/jojo-rabbit-hitler-movie-taika-waititi-disney.html|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210302183217/https://slate.com/culture/2019/09/jojo-rabbit-hitler-movie-taika-waititi-disney.html|archive-date=March 2, 2021|access-date=2021-03-12|website=Slate Magazine|language=en}}</ref> The text [[letterform]]s were handcrafted to correspond to the film's historical aesthetic.<ref name="www.assemblyltd.com" /> The film's [[end titles]] were created by Scarlet Letters.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Jojo Rabbit|url=https://www.artofthetitle.com/title/jojo-rabbit/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200808040141/https://www.artofthetitle.com/title/jojo-rabbit/|archive-date=August 8, 2020|access-date=2021-03-27|website=[[Art of the Title]]|language=en}}</ref>

[[Ai-Ling Lee]] was the film's [[Sound editor (filmmaking)|sound editor]], [[Sound design|designer]], and [[Sound mixer|mixer]]. With the [[digital audio workstation]] (DAW) [[Pro Tools]], she used "subliminal sonic enhancements" to strengthen the sense that the film was portraying Jojo's point of view. In an interview with ''Variety'', she referenced a scene in Jojo's kitchen where Waititi wanted to evoke the sound of Adolf rallying to reflect the character acting progressively more like the real Hitler. To increase the tension in the scene, she added [[reverb]] to Adolf's dialogue as if he were speaking in front of a microphone to a large crowd.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Valentini|first=Valentina I.|date=2020-01-16|title=Sound Mixers, Designers Talk About the Nuances of This Season's Top Movies|url=https://variety.com/2020/artisans/production/sound-mixers-designers-movies-1203468608/|access-date=2021-03-01|website=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|archive-date=July 26, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200726040735/https://variety.com/2020/artisans/production/sound-mixers-designers-movies-1203468608/|url-status=live}}</ref> Accompanying Lee as sound editor was Tobias Poppe.<ref>{{Cite news|last1=Ramos|first1=Dino-Ray|date=16 December 2019|title=Motion Picture Sound Editors Unveil 67th Annual Golden Reel Nominations|work=[[Deadline Hollywood]]|url=https://deadline.com/2019/12/motion-pictures-sound-editors-67th-annual-golden-reel-nominations-1202809902/|url-status=live|access-date=9 January 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191217145832/https://deadline.com/2019/12/motion-pictures-sound-editors-67th-annual-golden-reel-nominations-1202809902/|archive-date=17 December 2019}}</ref> Paul Apelgren was the film's [[music editor]].<ref>{{cite news|last1=Ramos|first1=Dino-Ray|date=19 January 2020|title=MPSE Golden Reel Awards: 'Ford V Ferrari', '1917', 'Parasite', 'The Mandalorian' Among Winners|work=[[Deadline Hollywood]]|url=https://deadline.com/2020/01/golden-reel-awards-2020-winners-list-motion-picture-sound-editors-1202835466/|url-status=live|access-date=19 January 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201116174704/https://deadline.com/2020/01/golden-reel-awards-2020-winners-list-motion-picture-sound-editors-1202835466/|archive-date=16 November 2020}}</ref> Steve Baine of Foley One was the [[Foley artist]], with Peter Persaud and Gina Wark mixing and assisting with the Foley, respectively.<ref>{{cite web|title=Steve Baine|url=http://dev.tcm.com/tcmdb/person/705649%7C0/Steve-Baine|access-date=2021-03-01|website=[[Turner Classic Movies]]|language=en|archive-date=March 1, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210301082753/http://dev.tcm.com/tcmdb/person/705649%7C0/Steve-Baine|url-status=dead}}</ref> Bob Industries was credited for post-production services.<ref name="Fox Searchlight Pictures" />{{Rp|44}}

[[Digital intermediate]] work, specifically [[color grading]], was done by [[Company 3]]'s senior colorist Tim Stipan.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hemphill |first=Jim |date=2019-11-28 |title=Jojo Rabbit / Mihai Mălaimare Jr. – The American Society of Cinematographers |url=https://ascmag.com/podcasts/jojo-rabbit-mihai-m%C4%83laimare-jr |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200927001637/https://ascmag.com/podcasts/jojo-rabbit-mihai-m%C4%83laimare-jr |archive-date=September 27, 2020 |access-date=2021-03-12 |website=[[American Cinematographer]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Jojo Rabbit {{!}} |url=https://www.company3.com/videos/jojo-rabbit/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210117103644/https://company3.com/videos/jojo-rabbit/ |archive-date=January 17, 2021 |access-date=2021-03-12 |language=en-US}}</ref>

===Music===
{{main|Music of Jojo Rabbit|l1 = Music of ''Jojo Rabbit''}}
{{Listen|filename=Michael Giachinno - Jojo's Theme.ogg|title="Jojo's Theme"|pos=right|description=The [[theme music]] of ''Jojo Rabbit'', which depending on the film's mood comes in different tones, from joyful to depressing. This clip—part of the longer, ambivalent "Jojo's Theme", which was the [[end titles]]' music—represents the latter.}}

''Jojo Rabbit''<nowiki/>'s original score is composed by [[Michael Giacchino]], in his maiden collaboration with Waititi. Giacchino used the approach of a melodious fairy-tale like score,<ref name="Desowitz-2019">{{Cite web|last=Desowitz|first=Bill|date=2019-10-18|title='Jojo Rabbit': Michael Giacchino's Score Is a Bold Statement Against Hate|url=https://www.indiewire.com/2019/10/jojo-rabbit-michael-giacchino-score-music-oscars-1202182993/|url-status=live|access-date=2021-03-29|website=[[IndieWire]]|publisher=[[Penske Media]]|archive-date=November 28, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201128140527/https://www.indiewire.com/2019/10/jojo-rabbit-michael-giacchino-score-music-oscars-1202182993/}}</ref> evoking themes of love and losses after Waititi insisted to score similarly to what he did in ''[[Up (2009 film)|Up]]'',<ref name="HR-11nov-2019" /> Giacchino pledged to use music to emphasize the film's deep emotions instead of its humor, in order to retain the film's message,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gray |first=Tim |date=2019-10-18 |title=Composer Michael Giacchino on Setting the Right Tone for 'Jojo Rabbit' |url=https://variety.com/2019/music/features/jojo-rabbit-composer-michael-giacchino-1203374528/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210216042025/https://variety.com/2019/music/features/jojo-rabbit-composer-michael-giacchino-1203374528/ |archive-date=February 16, 2021 |access-date=2021-02-15 |website=Variety |language=en-US}}</ref> and to try to musicalize Nazi Germany from Jojo's perspective, who recalled this being a challenge.<ref name="Fox Searchlight Pictures" /> The score was recorded in December 2018 at the [[Abbey Road Studios]], London, with the choir portions for the 11-minute suite (which was the film's [[theme music]]), composed by Giacchino, was the first to be recorded. Caludia Vašeková coordinated the choir, while the vocals, done by [[Trinity Boys Choir]], were contracted by Susie Gillis for Isobel Griffiths Ltd.<ref name="Fox Searchlight Pictures" />{{Rp|23, 56}} Freddie Jemison, part of Trinity Boys,<ref name="Desowitz-2019" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-01-10 |title=Trinity Boys Choir enjoy busy festive season |url=https://trinity-school.org/trinity-boys-choir-enjoy-busy-festive-season/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210328145204/https://trinity-school.org/trinity-boys-choir-enjoy-busy-festive-season/ |archive-date=March 28, 2021 |access-date=2021-03-27 |website=Trinity School |language=en-US}}</ref> was the vocal soloist in another version of the suite and adult vocalists were from [[London Voices]].<ref name="Fox Searchlight Pictures" />{{Rp|56}}

Apart from contemporary [[German music]], the score consisted of old-time [[European classical music]], such as that of [[Frédéric Chopin]], [[Franz Liszt]], and [[Erik Satie]]. Instead of a 100-piece orchestra, the score was composed with a 22-piece orchestra, featuring [[string quartet]] and various instruments including [[guitar]], [[brass]] and [[percussion]], as according to Giacchino, "the smaller the orchestra, the more emotional the sound."<ref name="Fox Searchlight Pictures" />{{Rp|23–24}}

Incorporated music in the film was packaged as a [[soundtrack album]], notably "{{-'}}Helden{{'-}}", the German version of "[["Heroes" (David Bowie song)|{{-'}}Heroes{{'-}}]]" by [[David Bowie]], and "[[Komm, gib mir deine Hand]]", the German version of "[[I Want to Hold Your Hand]]" by [[the Beatles]]. While watching documentaries on the Hitler Youth during research, Waititi noted "similarities between the crowd at Hitler's rallies and the frenzy at Beatles concerts". Giacchino helped secure the rights to the song by contacting [[Paul McCartney]], with whom he had previously worked.<ref name="HR-11nov-2019" /> Both this soundtrack and the original score soundtrack were released on October 18, 2019, the day of ''Jojo Rabbit''<nowiki/>'s theatrical release, by [[Hollywood Records]], [[Fox Music]], and [[Universal Music Canada]], with the [[Vinyl record|vinyl]] version of the soundtrack released on November 22.<ref>{{cite press release|title=Jojo Rabbit Digital Soundtrack Featuring Songs and Score, Plus Digital Score Album by Oscar®-Winning Composer Michael Giacchino, Out Now|url=http://www.umusic.ca/press-releases/jojo-rabbit-digital-soundtrack-featuring-songs-and-score-plus-digital-score-album-by-oscar-winning-composer-michael-giacchino-available-today/|date=2019-10-31|access-date=2025-03-13|publisher=Umusic|language=en-US|archive-date=November 14, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191114002224/http://www.umusic.ca/press-releases/jojo-rabbit-digital-soundtrack-featuring-songs-and-score-plus-digital-score-album-by-oscar-winning-composer-michael-giacchino-available-today/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Apple">{{Cite web |last=Giacchino |first=Michael |author-link=Michael Giacchino |date=2019-10-18 |title=Jojo Rabbit (Original Score) |url=https://music.apple.com/us/album/jojo-rabbit-original-score/1482698267 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200623103523/https://music.apple.com/us/album/jojo-rabbit-original-score/1482698267 |archive-date=June 23, 2020 |access-date=2021-02-15 |website=[[Hollywood Records]]; [[Fox Music]] |via=[[Apple Music]]}}</ref>

== Themes and analysis ==
Waititi described the moral of ''Jojo Rabbit'' as "about learning to think for yourself and not falling into the trap of just following the group".<ref name="Nulman-2021" />

A dominant theme within this film is Nazism. According to GradeSaver, a study guide, the film uses humor to reveal the stakes of the regime's impact on the characters and their freedom. Specifically in Jojo, whose loyalty towards Nazism shifts throughout the film due to a clash with innocence, the film also shows the dangers of propaganda to those who blindly abide by it, especially children.<ref name="GradeSaver">{{cite web|title=Jojo Rabbit Themes|url=https://www.gradesaver.com/jojo-rabbit/study-guide/themes|url-status=live|access-date=2021-03-17|publisher=GradeSaver|language=en|archive-date=April 30, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210430151332/https://www.gradesaver.com/jojo-rabbit/study-guide/themes}}</ref> The film also focuses on the individual characters and their traits, highlighting their bravery and strength to show "how strong they were even in the face of horror"; this is most distinct in Elsa's character, who has been compared to [[Anne Frank]].<ref>{{Cite conference|last1=Motl|first1=Ryan|last2=Pemberton|first2=Barbara|date=2020-04-14|title=Jewish Representation in Modern Film and Television|url=https://scholarlycommons.obu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1039&context=scholars_day_conference|format=PDF|conference=Virtual Scholars Day 2020|publisher=[[Ouachita Baptist University]]|pages=9|access-date=2021-04-30|via=Scholarly Commons|archive-date=August 6, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200806170139/https://scholarlycommons.obu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1039&context=scholars_day_conference|url-status=live}}</ref> Thus, the film centers around the concept of how ideologies can affect people and society. It is also a message that fascist groups, such as the Nazis, are harmful to everyone, supporters and opposition.<ref>{{Cite thesis|last=Ma'ruf|first=Rizqi|title=The Effects of Nazi Dogma on the Main Children Characters Development in Taika Waititi's ''Jojo Rabbit''|date=2021-02-19|degree=Undergraduate|publisher=[[Sanata Dharma University]]|url=https://repository.usd.ac.id/39277/2/174214157_full.pdf|place=[[Yogyakarta]]|url-status=live|access-date=2021-04-30|archive-date=April 30, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210430151329/https://repository.usd.ac.id/39277/2/174214157_full.pdf}}</ref> It also sends a message that war takes joy away from people and is "painstakingly ugly"; the ''Annals of the Romanian Society for Cell Biology'' described it as "a moral to the present uncertainties in the modern world."<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Pillai|first1=Shamy Sobha|last2=Kurup|first2=Parvathi M.|last3=Chellarian|first3=B. Sonia|date=2021-03-04|title=War And Psyche: An Examination Of Psychoanalytic Theory In The Movies "Jojo Rabbit" And "Dunkirk"|url=https://www.annalsofrscb.ro/index.php/journal/article/view/7862/5808 |format=PDF|journal=Annals of the Romanian Society for Cell Biology|location=[[Kochi]]|publisher=[[Vasile Goldiș Western University of Arad]]|volume=25|issue=4|pages=5–6|issn=1583-6258|access-date=2021-07-09}}</ref>

[[Hegemonic masculinity|Hegemonic]] and [[toxic masculinity]] are also themes expressed in ''Jojo Rabbit''. The main example lies in Jojo's desire to be a Nazi, which to do so he was taught to act fierce. It also shows how such mentality harms everyone, men and women. Jojo's clumsy attitude as seen throughout the film shows how he is inherently incompatible with the ideology. This also allows the other characters as well as the audiences who "eventually overlook his avowed Nazism and instead view him as a sympathetic, misguided character who should be allowed redemption." Adolf's buffoonish attitude is a way of showcasing how hegemonic masculinity can attack itself subversively.<ref>{{Cite thesis|last=Lippert|first=Christian W.|title=Snake Mind, Wolf Body, Panther Courage: Jojo Rabbit as a Critique of Hegemonic Masculinity|date=2021|degree=Master's|publisher=[[Utah State University]]|url=https://www.proquest.com/openview/f5e6510582c254485b6c7ede86285ff5 |place=[[Logan, Utah]]|access-date=July 2, 2021|archive-date=July 3, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210703113723/https://www.proquest.com/openview/f5e6510582c254485b6c7ede86285ff5/1?pq-origsite=gscholar&cbl=18750&diss=y|url-status=live}} Retrieved June 3, 2021</ref> There's also the suggestion that "[[Komm, gib mir deine Hand]]" is used to compare the obsessive behavior of the Beatles' fans ([[Beatlemania]]) to that of the prejudicial behavior of the Nazis.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Froio|first=Nicole|date=2020-02-11|title=Review: Taika Waititi's Jojo Rabbit, White Masculinity and Fascism|url=https://medium.com/academica-feminista/review-taika-waititis-jojo-rabbit-white-masculinity-and-fascism-a2cd6e24eece|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200831003913/https://medium.com/academica-feminista/review-taika-waititis-jojo-rabbit-white-masculinity-and-fascism-a2cd6e24eece|archive-date=August 31, 2020|access-date=2021-07-03|website=Academia Feminista|publisher=[[Medium (website)|Medium]]}}</ref><!-- Froio is an author at The Guardian, which is a reliable source. The style of the article is also on par with scholarly articles. -->

Irony runs throughout the film. In the opening scene, Jojo motivates himself to be "a man," yet is nervous.<ref name="Buchleiter-2020">{{Cite magazine|last=Buchleiter|first=Jon|date=2020-06-08|title=Film Review – Jojo Rabbit (Dir: Taika Waititi, 2019)|url=https://repositories.lib.utexas.edu/bitstream/handle/2152/83312/Film%20Review%20-%20Jojo%20Rabbit%20%28Dir_%20Taika%20Waititi%2C%202019%29%20-%20Not%20Even%20Past.pdf?sequence=2|magazine=Not Even Past|publisher=[[University of Texas at Austin]]|access-date=2021-07-02}}</ref> According to Tony S.L. Michael of the ''[[Journal of Religion and Film]]'', the way Falkenheim literature is German but the character dialogues are mostly English "sets up the dichotomy between the fact that what is outside may separate us, but what is inside should bring us altogether." This leads to another suggested theme of the film: human interaction.<ref name="Michael-2019">{{Cite journal|last=Michael|first=Tony S.L.|date=2019-10-01|title=Jo Jo Rabbit|url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/2313018922 |journal=[[Journal of Religion and Film]]|publisher=[[University of Nebraska Omaha]]|volume=23|issue=2 |id={{ProQuest|2313018922}} }}</ref> For example, as Elsa and Rosie began stressing to Jojo the importance of love and compassion in various dialogues, his viewpoint of Nazism begin to subtly shift, shown by the darkening attitude of Adolf. Klenzendorf's character, meanwhile, most embodies the film's use of [[hyperbole]] and [[sarcasm]]—seen in his distinct use of [[dry humor]]—which makes him important to the over-the-top portrayals of Nazism.<ref name="Buchleiter-2020" />

A main motif of ''Jojo Rabbit'' is shoes. They feature frequently in the film, either visually or audibly. According to Michael, it is a metaphor symbolizing Jojo's coming-of-age journey. During the scene where Jojo finds Rosie hanged, it suggests to Jojo that he should become more mature.<ref name="Michael-2019" /> Other motifs include the rabbit, symbolizing Jojo's inability to live up to the Nazis' expectations, and the dagger, symbolizing toxic masculinity.<ref name="GradeSaver" /> Meanwhile, dancing represents "pleasure in the face of adversity, relief when it is over, and hope for the future", as well as freedom.<ref name="GradeSaver" /> Nulman compares this to the misquoted phrase by [[Emma Goldman]], "If I can't dance, it's not my revolution."<ref name="Nulman-2021">{{Cite book|last=Nulman|first=Eugene|title=Coronavirus Capitalism Goes to the Cinema|date=2021-07-09|publisher=[[Routledge]]|isbn=978-1-003-17347-2|location=New York City|lccn=2021001599|oclc=1240828478}}</ref>

==Marketing and release==
[[File:Jojo_Rabbit_01_(48810532492).jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|Premiere of the film at the [[44th Toronto International Film Festival]]|alt=Entrance of a theater, with the film's poster showcased above.]]
In March 2019, [[Disney]] completed [[Acquisition of 21st Century Fox by Disney|its acquisition]] of [[Film distributor|distributor]] Fox Searchlight's parent company [[21st Century Fox]].<ref name="BOM" /> As ''Jojo Rabbit'' featured mature themes, several Disney executives worried that releasing the film would ruin their reputation as a family-friendly studio; it was also said to be "too edgy" for Disney, as stated in ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]''. However, they remained optimistic about the film's success,<ref>{{Cite web|last=Sharf|first=Zack|date=2019-08-13|title=Disney Executive Fears Taika Waititi's Nazi Satire 'Jojo Rabbit' Is Too Edgy For Studio Image — Report|url=https://www.indiewire.com/2019/08/disney-fears-taika-waititi-nazi-jojo-rabbit-edgy-studio-1202165495/|access-date=2021-02-18|website=IndieWire|language=en|archive-date=January 25, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210125141727/https://www.indiewire.com/2019/08/disney-fears-taika-waititi-nazi-jojo-rabbit-edgy-studio-1202165495/|url-status=live}}</ref> with CEOs [[Bob Iger]] and [[Alan Horn]] arguing that it has a good message and would diversify their scope.<ref>{{cite web|date=2019-10-04|title=Fox Searchlight Bosses Say Disney Had No Problems With 'Jojo Rabbit'|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/fox-searchlight-bosses-say-disney-had-no-problems-jojo-rabbit-1245619|first=Alex|last=Ritman|access-date=2021-02-18|website=The Hollywood Reporter|language=en|archive-date=December 8, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191208012152/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/fox-searchlight-bosses-say-disney-had-no-problems-jojo-rabbit-1245619|url-status=live}}</ref>

To market the film, Fox Searchlight released a scene from the German World War II film ''[[Downfall (2004 film)|Downfall]]'', which had been a popular asset for [[Internet meme|memes]], wherein [[subtitles]] would mistranslate the dialogue to something humorous, mostly known as the Angry Hitler meme. In the ''Jojo Rabbit'' version, Hitler is driven insane with the news of Waititi, a [[Polynesians|Polynesian]] Jew, creating a film poking fun at Hitler.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Crucchiola|first=Jordan|date=2019-07-26|title=Jojo Rabbit Movie Finds the One True Perfect Use Case for Screaming Hitler Meme|url=https://www.vulture.com/2019/07/the-screaming-hitler-meme-is-now-jojo-rabbit-marketing.html|access-date=2021-02-18|website=Vulture|url-access=limited|language=en-us|archive-date=December 24, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201224024127/https://www.vulture.com/2019/07/the-screaming-hitler-meme-is-now-jojo-rabbit-marketing.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Additionally, a [[Teaser campaign|teaser]] was released on July 24, 2019,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.vox.com/culture/2019/7/24/20707834/jojo-rabbit-trailer-taika-waititi|title=Thor: Ragnarok director Taika Waititi made an "anti-hate" satire about Hitler. Here's the trailer.|date=July 24, 2019|first=Alissa|last=Wilkinson|website=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210430131324/https://www.vox.com/culture/2019/7/24/20707834/jojo-rabbit-trailer-taika-waititi|archive-date=April 30, 2021|url-status=live|access-date=April 30, 2021}}</ref> and a [[Trailer (promotion)|trailer]] was released on September 3, 2019.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://deadline.com/video/jojo-rabbit-trailer-taika-waititi-imaginary-hitler-german-monkees-david-bowie/|title='Jojo Rabbit' Trailer: Imaginary Hitler, German Monkees & David Bowie Add To Satire|date=September 3, 2019|first=Greg|last=Evans|website=[[Deadline Hollywood]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210430131551/https://deadline.com/video/jojo-rabbit-trailer-taika-waititi-imaginary-hitler-german-monkees-david-bowie/|archive-date=April 30, 2021|url-status=live|access-date=April 30, 2021}}</ref> Smith Brothers Media was in charge of making visual advertisements, including posters and web banners, primarily for Australia. Due to the film's quirky nature, a "vibrant" theme was chosen to "make the character images 'pop' for potential audiences."<ref>{{Cite web|title=Jojo Rabbit|url=https://smithbrothersmedia.com.au/projects/jojo-rabbit/|access-date=2021-03-18|website=Smith Brothers Media|language=en-AU|archive-date=January 16, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210116085341/https://smithbrothersmedia.com.au/projects/jojo-rabbit/|url-status=live}}</ref> The poster was unveiled on September 5.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2019-09-05|title=Jojo Rabbit Cast Poster Features Famous People Dressed as Nazis|first=Matt|last= Goldberg|url=https://collider.com/jojo-rabbit-cast-poster/|access-date=2021-02-18|website=Collider|language=en-US|archive-date=January 10, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200110190553/https://collider.com/jojo-rabbit-cast-poster/|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Reception==
===Box office===
During its original theatrical run, ''Jojo Rabbit'' grossed $33.4&nbsp;million in the United States and Canada, and $57&nbsp;million in other territories (including $4&nbsp;million in New Zealand), for a worldwide total of $90.3&nbsp;million.<ref name="BOM">{{cite Box Office Mojo |id=2584384 |title=Jojo Rabbit |access-date=March 29, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210329072916/https://www.boxofficemojo.com/title/tt2584384/ |archive-date=March 29, 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref> A 2023 re-release in New Zealand brought its total box office gross up to $93.6&nbsp;million.<ref name="BOM"/>

In its domestic limited opening weekend, the film made $349,555 from five theaters, an average of $69,911 per venue (the fourth-best of 2019).<ref name="opening">{{cite web |url=https://deadline.com/2019/10/maleficent-mistress-of-evil-zombieland-double-tap-weekend-box-office-1202763525/ |title='Maleficent: Mistress Of Evil' No Magic With $36M+, 'Joker' Still Stealing 2nd Place From 'Zombieland 2' With $28M+ |last=D'Alessandro |first=Anthony |work=[[Deadline Hollywood]] |date=October 20, 2019 |access-date=October 20, 2019 |url-status=live }}</ref> On its opening day alone it earned an average of $70,000,<ref name="HR-11nov-2019" /> The film expanded to 55 theaters in 10 cities the following week, making $1&nbsp;million,<ref name="expand">{{cite web |url=https://deadline.com/2019/10/synonyms-nadav-lapid-kanye-west-jesus-is-king-frankie-ira-sachs-isabelle-huppert-specialty-box-office-1202769933/ web |last=Brueggemann |first=Tom |url=https://www.indiewire.com/2019/11/waves-a24-box-office-arthouse-1202190157/ |title='Waves' Makes Box Office Splash as Amazon and Netflix Stay Quiet in 230 theaters.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Ramos|first=Dino-Ray|date=2019-12-22|title='Uncut Gems' Crosses $1 Million In Second Limited Weekend, 'Jojo Rabbit' Hops Past $20 Million, 'Invisible Life' Debuts In the immediate aftermath of its [[Academy Award for Best Picture]] nomination, the film experienced a box office boost, with 895 more theaters screening it. On January 19, 2020, it was being screened at 1,005 American theaters, "the largest expansion of any Oscar contender" according to ''[[TheWrap]]''. During the weekend, it earned $1.8 million, bringing its total to $23.8 million.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-01-19|title='Parasite' and 'Jojo Rabbit' Score Oscar Rebound at Indie Box Office|url=https://www.thewrap.com/parasite-and-jojo-rabbit-score-oscar-rebound-at-indie-box-office/|access-date=2021-02-24|website=TheWrap|language=en-US|archive-date=April 25, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200425140120/https://www.thewrap.com/parasite-and-jojo-rabbit-score-oscar-rebound-at-indie-box-office/|url-status=live}}</ref> Over the [[Oscar season|Oscar weekend]], the film's 17th week of release, it made $1.5&nbsp;million from 1,096 theaters, for a running total of $30.3&nbsp;million.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://deadline.com/2020/02/birds-of-prey-weekend-box-office-margot-robbie-1202853768/|title=How 'Birds Of Prey' Went Astray With $33M+ Opening|last=D'Alessandro|first=Anthony|website=[[Deadline Hollywood]]|date=February 9, 2020|access-date=February 9, 2020|archive-date=February 8, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200208173530/https://deadline.com/2020/02/birds-of-prey-weekend-box-office-margot-robbie-1202853768/|url-status=live}}</ref> Demand dropped during the rise of the COVID-19 pandemic by as much as 68%,<ref>{{Cite web|last=Robbins|first=Shawn|date=2020-03-14|title=Weekend Box Office Estimates: I Still Believe Could Top $10M, But Onward and Holdovers Down 60%+ in Wake of COVID-19|url=https://www.boxofficepro.com/weekend-estimates-still-believe-bloodshot-the-hunt-onward/|url-status=live|access-date=2021-03-29|website=[[Boxoffice Pro]]|language=en-US|archive-date=July 20, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200720021234/https://www.boxofficepro.com/weekend-estimates-still-believe-bloodshot-the-hunt-onward/}}</ref> with its rank at the box office dropping from 21 to 32 between February 21, 2020, and its closing date. Its peak period was November 8–14, its fourth weekend, when it earned $5,603,616 (average: $7,022) from 798 theaters, experiencing a 70.3% increase in demand and ranking 11th place at the U.S. box office.<ref name="BOM" />

On February 23, 2020, its third week of release on home video, 14,277 DVD copies were sold ($208,046) and 47,036 Blu-ray copies were sold, making a total profit of $1,365,588. The latter type saw fewer purchases the following month.<ref name="NUM">{{cite the numbers|id=Jojo-Rabbit-(Germany)-(2019)|title=Jojo Rabbit|access-date=March 29, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191227203733/https://www.the-numbers.com/movie/Jojo-Rabbit-(Germany)-(2019)|archive-date=December 27, 2019|url-status=live}}</ref>

Outside of the United States and Canada, ''Jojo Rabbit'' did the best in the United Kingdom, where it grossed $10,450,169, followed by Australia ($7,020,681) and Mexico ($4,952,293), as well as Italy, New Zealand, Japan, Spain, France, Germany, and the Netherlands. It performed the worst in [[Bulgaria]], where it earned a total of $39,181 as of March 11, 2020.<ref name="NUM" /> In [[India]], the film opened earning [[₹]] 1.2-1.5 million on the first day,<ref>{{cite news |date=2020-02-01 |title=Box office update: Saif Ali Khan's 'Jawaani Jaaneman' earns 2.75–3 crore while 'Jojo Rabbit', 'Happy Hardy Heer' and others fail to pull the audience on day 1 |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/entertainment/hindi/bollywood/box-office/h/d-box-office-update-saif-ali-khans-jawaani-jaaneman-earns-2-75-3-crore-while-jojo-rabbit-happy-hardy-heer-and-others-fail-to-pull-the-audience-on-day-1/articleshow/73834958.cms |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200202080111/https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/entertainment/hindi/bollywood/box-office/h/d-box-office-update-saif-ali-khans-jawaani-jaaneman-earns-2-75-3-crore-while-jojo-rabbit-happy-hardy-heer-and-others-fail-to-pull-the-audience-on-day-1/articleshow/73834958.cms |archive-date=February 2, 2020 |access-date=2021-03-29 |website=[[The Times of India]] |language=en}}</ref> [[₹]]6 million in the first 3 days, and closed after 28 days with a total of ₹34.3 million.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Jojo Rabbit (English) Box Office Collection till Now {{!}} Box Collection – Bollywood Hungama|url=https://www.bollywoodhungama.com/movie/jojo-rabbit-english/box-office/|url-status=live|access-date=2021-03-29|website=[[Bollywood Hungama]] |date=January 31, 2020 |language=en |archive-date=November 19, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201119171709/https://www.bollywoodhungama.com/movie/jojo-rabbit-english/box-office/}}</ref> As of July 15, 2020, the film had earned $36,000 ([[€]]30,614) in Italy from 37 theaters with a total of $4.4 million (€3,741,719), earning first place at the box office.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Tartaglione|first=Nancy|date=2020-07-15|title='Scoob!' Is Weekend Top Dog With $1.8M From 5 Overseas Markets; 'Peninsula' To Thrill Korea – International Box Office|url=https://deadline.com/2020/07/international-box-office-scoob-weekend-update-key-markets-coronavirus-peninsula-korea-1202986098/|url-status=live|access-date=2021-04-04|website=Deadline Hollywood|archive-date=December 7, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201207112550/https://deadline.com/2020/07/international-box-office-scoob-weekend-update-key-markets-coronavirus-peninsula-korea-1202986098/}}</ref> In China, where it was released the latest, it earned more: a total of $1,590,000 from 7,099 theaters, with an opening weekend gross of $730,000.<ref name="NUM" />

===Critical response===
The [[review aggregator]] website [[Rotten Tomatoes]] reported an approval rating of {{RT data|score}} with an average score of {{RT data|average}}, based on {{RT data|count}} reviews. The website's critical consensus reads, "''Jojo Rabbit''{{'}}s blend of irreverent humor and serious ideas definitely won't be to everyone's taste—but either way, this anti-hate satire is audacious to a fault."<ref name="RT">{{cite Rotten Tomatoes|id={{RT data|rtid|noprefix=y}}|type=m|title=Jojo Rabbit|access-date={{RT data|access date}}|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200125114152/https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/jojo_rabbit|archive-date=January 25, 2020|url-status=live}}</ref> [[Metacritic]], which uses a weighted average, assigned the film a score of 58 out of 100 based on 57 critics, indicating "mixed or average" reviews.<ref>{{cite Metacritic |id=jojo-rabbit |type=movie |title=Jojo Rabbit|access-date=March 29, 2021}}</ref> Audiences polled by [[CinemaScore]] gave the film an average grade of "A" on an A+ to F scale, and those at [[PostTrak]] gave the film a 96% overall positive score, with 87% saying they would definitely recommend it.<ref name="expand" />

Brian Truitt, writing for ''[[USA Today]]'' called it "brilliant Nazi-mocking satire", praising the performances, and writing: "As much as it makes you laugh, Waititi's must-watch effort is a warm hug of a movie that just so happens to have a lot of important things to say."<ref name="USAT">{{cite web|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/entertainment/movies/2019/10/17/jojo-rabbit-review-taika-waititi-mocks-hitler-brilliant-wwii-satire/3999929002/|title= Review:Love's at the heart of Taika Waititi's brilliant Nazi-mocking satire 'Jojo Rabbit'|last=Kohn|first=Eric|date=October 17, 2019|work=[[USA Today]]|access-date=October 18, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191018161531/https://www.usatoday.com/story/entertainment/movies/2019/10/17/jojo-rabbit-review-taika-waititi-mocks-hitler-brilliant-wwii-satire/3999929002/|archive-date=October 18, 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> In a positive review, Steve Pond of ''TheWrap'' wrote that "there's real heart in ''Jojo Rabbit'', too. This is a dark satire that finds a way to make a case for understanding. As circumstances slowly chip away at Jojo's hate-driven worldview, the black comedy finds room for some genuinely touching moments."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.thewrap.com/jojo-rabbit-film-review-taika-waititi-insists-that-nazis-can-be-funny/|title='Jojo Rabbit' Film Review: Taika Waititi Insists That Nazis Can Be Funny|last=Pond|first=Steve|date=October 16, 2019|website=[[TheWrap]]|access-date=October 23, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191023180828/https://www.thewrap.com/jojo-rabbit-film-review-taika-waititi-insists-that-nazis-can-be-funny/|archive-date=October 23, 2019|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Richard Roeper]] of the ''[[Chicago Sun-Times]]'' lauded it as "uncomfortably funny, unapologetically insensitive, cheerfully outrageous" and concluding that writer-director Waititi "delivers a timely, anti-hate fractured fairy tale."<ref name="SunTimes">{{cite news|url=https://chicago.suntimes.com/2019/10/24/20924323/jojo-rabbit-review-hitler-imaginary-friend-movie-taika-waititi-scarlett-johansson-sam-rockwell|title='JoJo Rabbit': Imagine that – in these sensitive times, a Hitler comedy that works|last=Roeper|first=Richard|date=2019-10-24|newspaper=[[Chicago Sun-Times]]|access-date=2020-01-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191218162803/https://chicago.suntimes.com/2019/10/24/20924323/jojo-rabbit-review-hitler-imaginary-friend-movie-taika-waititi-scarlett-johansson-sam-rockwell|archive-date=December 18, 2019|url-status=live|url-access=subscription}}</ref> In another positive review, Stephanie Zacharek of ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' wrote: "It's Waititi's ability to balance unassailable goofy moments with an acknowledgment of real-life horrors that makes the movie exceptional."<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://time.com/5709376/jojo-rabbit-movie-review/|title=''Jojo Rabbit'' Is a Tender Black Comedy About Dark Times|first=Stephanie|last=Zacharek|magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]]|date=October 24, 2019|access-date=2020-01-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191216111927/https://time.com/5709376/jojo-rabbit-movie-review/|archive-date=December 16, 2019|url-status=live|url-access=limited}}</ref> Adam Graham of ''[[The Detroit News]]'' called it an "enchanting, whimsical satire about the absurdity of war as seen through a child's eyes" as well as "a smart, accessible, inclusive film that opens doors at a time when many are slamming them shut."<ref name="Detroit">{{cite news|url=https://www.detroitnews.com/story/entertainment/movies/2019/10/30/review-jojo-rabbit-jubilant-comic-farce-takes-aim-hatred/2497376001/|title=Review: 'Jojo Rabbit' a jubilant comic farce that takes aim at hatred|newspaper=[[The Detroit News]]|first=Adam|last=Graham |access-date=2020-01-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191216112237/https://www.detroitnews.com/story/entertainment/movies/2019/10/30/review-jojo-rabbit-jubilant-comic-farce-takes-aim-hatred/2497376001/|archive-date=December 16, 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> Benjamin Franz of ''Film & History'' praised the film for its use of symmetrical cinematography and exaggerated German accents, equivalent to the styles of [[Wes Anderson]] films. The film also does not show liberating shots of the skies, offering a sense of tightness to the setting equivalent to the works of [[Fritz Lang]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Franz |first=Benjamin |date=2019 |title=Jojo Rabbit |url=https://muse.jhu.edu/article/744572 |journal=Film & History |volume=49 |issue=2 |pages=34–36 |doi=10.1353/flm.2019.0028 |s2cid=258058608 |issn=1548-9922|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

''Variety''{{'}}s [[Owen Gleiberman]] said that the film "creates the illusion of danger while playing it safe" and wrote that "it lacks the courage of its own conventionality. It's a feel-good movie, all right, but one that uses the fake danger of defanged black comedy to leave us feeling good about the fact that we're above a feel-good movie."<ref name=VarietyReview/> Eric Kohn of [[IndieWire]] wrote that "Despite a few flashes of tragedy, ''Jojo Rabbit'' lingers in a charming muddle of good vibes without really confronting their implications. [Waititi] may be one of the few working directors capable of injecting quirky scenarios with real depth, but in this case, he reduces the underlying circumstances—you know, that [[Holocaust]] thing—to a superficial prop."<ref name=kohn>{{cite web|url=https://www.indiewire.com/2019/09/jojo-rabbit-review-taika-waititi-tiff-1202172024/|title='Jojo Rabbit' Review: Taika Waititi's Nazi Satire Is a Charming Muddle of Good Intentions|last=Kohn|first=Eric|date=September 9, 2019|website=[[IndieWire]]|access-date=October 18, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191112181450/https://www.indiewire.com/2019/09/jojo-rabbit-review-taika-waititi-tiff-1202172024/|archive-date=November 12, 2019|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[A.&nbsp;O. Scott]] of ''[[The New York Times]]'' wrote that "The particulars of the evil can seem curiously abstract, and the portrayal of goodness can feel a bit false, and forced" and that "Elsa's [[Jewishness]] has no real content. She exists mainly as a teaching moment for Johannes. Her plight is a chance for him to prove his bravery."<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/10/17/movies/jojo-rabbit-review.html|title='Jojo Rabbit' Review: The Third Reich Wasn't All Fun and Games|last=Scott|first=A.O.|author-link=A. O. Scott|date=October 17, 2019|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|url-access=limited|access-date=October 22, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191022110429/https://www.nytimes.com/2019/10/17/movies/jojo-rabbit-review.html|archive-date=October 22, 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> Keith Uhlich of ''[[Slant Magazine]]'' criticized the film's premise, lack of historical accuracy and realism, and use of anti-semitic canards and [[Stereotypes of Jews|stereotypes]], and wrote that Waititi's performance as Hitler is "aiming for ''[[The Great Dictator]]'' but barely hitting ''[[Ace Ventura: Pet Detective|Ace Ventura]]''."<ref name=uhlich>{{cite web|url=https://www.slantmagazine.com/film/review-jojo-rabbit-is-taika-waititis-marvel-presents-mein-kampf/|title=Marvel Presents Mein Kampf|last=Uhlich|first=Keith|date=September 9, 2019|work=Slant Magazine|access-date=October 22, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191117221157/https://www.slantmagazine.com/film/review-jojo-rabbit-is-taika-waititis-marvel-presents-mein-kampf/|archive-date=November 17, 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> ''[[Little White Lies (magazine)|Little White Lies]]''{{'}} Hannah Woodhead criticized the film for its inclusion of a sympathetic ''[[Wehrmacht]]'' officer, Captain Klenzendorf, writing that it "feels oddly impartial, keen to note that actually, there were some Nice Nazis Too. That's not really something we need to hear in 2019, with [[white nationalism]] back in vogue and on the march across much of western civilisation."<ref name=woodhead>{{cite web |last1=Woodhead |first1=Hannah |title=Jojo Rabbit- First Look |url=https://lwlies.com/festivals/jojo-rabbit-toronto-film-festival-review-taika-waititi-scarlett-johansson/ |website=Little White Lies |access-date=October 22, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190926024347/https://lwlies.com/festivals/jojo-rabbit-toronto-film-festival-review-taika-waititi-scarlett-johansson/ |archive-date=September 26, 2019 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The film received a negative critical reception in the UK, with [[Robbie Collin]] saying that he was "aghast": the scenes at the camp were "the laziest rip-off of ''[[Moonrise Kingdom]]'' I've seen in my life", and "there's no sense that anything is at stake [...] it sentimentalises and [[Holocaust trivialization|trivialises the Holocaust]] [...] the stuff that JoJo is indoctrinated with is made up of old ''[[Borat]]'' lines, and that's not what anti-Semitism is."<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kEsCdoLLHg8 |title=Jojo Rabbit reviewed by Robbie Collin |access-date=October 31, 2020 |archive-date=February 16, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210216042058/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kEsCdoLLHg8 |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Peter Bradshaw]] agreed: "There are no insights to be had – and no laughs", and calling it "weirdly redundant".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2019/dec/20/jojo-rabbit-review-taika-waititi-hitler-comedy|title=Jojo Rabbit review – Taika Waititi's Hitler comedy is intensely unfunny|first=Peter|last=Bradshaw|date=December 20, 2019|newspaper=[[The Guardian]]|location=London|access-date=October 31, 2020|archive-date=January 9, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200109222959/https://www.theguardian.com/film/2019/dec/20/jojo-rabbit-review-taika-waititi-hitler-comedy|url-status=live}}</ref> [[Mark Kermode]] was slightly more positive, but still said that it was "neither sharp enough nor funny enough to cut to the heart of its subject matter."<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.theguardian.com/film/2020/jan/05/jojo-rabbit-review-taika-waititi-hitler-scarlett-johansson-sam-rockwell|title=Jojo Rabbit review – down the rabbit hole with Hitler|date=January 5, 2020|newspaper=The Guardian|location=London|first=Mark|last=Kermode|access-date=November 26, 2020|archive-date=February 16, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210216042130/https://www.theguardian.com/film/2020/jan/05/jojo-rabbit-review-taika-waititi-hitler-scarlett-johansson-sam-rockwell|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Historical accuracy ==
[[File:Bundesarchiv_Bild_133-151,_Worms,_Fanfarenkorps_des_Jungvolkes.jpg|thumb|upright=1.3|''Jungvolk'' boys fanfare trumpeters at a Nazi rally in the town of [[Worms, Germany|Worms]] in 1933|alt=Young boys marching with a trumpet at a garden.]]
Despite being a loose depiction of World War II, ''Jojo Rabbit'' accurately depicts various aspects of the era. Boys in the Hitler Youth did spread propaganda and collect scrap like Jojo does, and ''Stielhandgranaten'' were popularized during World War II. Several mentions of the [[Axis powers]] are also said to be accurate, although the film fictionalized a convergence of American and Soviet soldiers in the same battle. The "free Germany" sign style used in the film is also fictional, though other styles were present.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-01-20|title=Jojo Rabbit: 8 Real Historical Connections It Makes To World War II (& 2 Made Exclusively For The Movie)|url=https://screenrant.com/jojo-rabbit-historical-fictional-connections/|first=Paolo|last=Alfar|access-date=2021-02-19|website=[[Screen Rant]]|language=en-US|archive-date=January 25, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200125133520/https://screenrant.com/jojo-rabbit-historical-fictional-connections/|url-status=live}}</ref>

Bundling various historical sources, ''Time'' stated that the film depicted the Nazi regime, as seen from a child's perspective, accurately. Many ''Jungvolk'' children recalled the experience as being fun and looked upon the regime from an innocent perspective. A [[memoir]] by former member [[Alfons Heck]] described the program as "an exciting life, free from [[parental supervision]], filled with 'duties' that seemed sheer pleasure." Though female members did not do many physical activities, as seen in the film, they were given traditionally feminine duties, such as farming, cooking, cleaning, singing, swimming, gymnastics, and running, which had the purpose of keeping their bodies fit so they could find a husband and spread the Nazi ideology to their future children.<ref>{{Cite magazine|title=The History Behind ''Jojo Rabbit'' and What It Was Really Like to Be in the Hitler Youth|url=https://time.com/5700753/hilter-youth-jojo-rabbit/|first=Olivia B.|last=Waxman|date=October 17, 2019|access-date=2021-02-19|magazine=Time|url-access=limited|archive-date=February 19, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210219080600/https://time.com/5700753/hilter-youth-jojo-rabbit/|url-status=live}}</ref>

''Jojo Rabbit'' divided experts of the Holocaust at a panel discussion following a screening at the [[Museum of Tolerance]]. Rick Trank, producer of ''[[The Long Way Home (1997 film)|The Long Way Home]]'' (1997), felt that, while it has a creative premise, the lack of historical context makes the film detrimental to young viewers, who may misunderstand the premise and think the film's farcical elements are depicting historical reality. However, Claudia Wiedeman, director of education at the [[USC Shoah Foundation]], said that, with the right educational methods and tools, the film could be a useful resource for young people who are learning about World War II. Brian Levin, director of the Center for the Study of Hate & Extremism and professor of criminal justice at [[California State University, San Bernardino]], applauded the film for using sarcasm—an easy-to-understand modern language—to depict Nazi Germany.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Saval|first=Malina|date=2019-11-13|title=Holocaust Experts Debate 'Jojo Rabbit' at Museum of Tolerance Screening|url=https://variety.com/2019/scene/news/jojo-rabbit-debate-holocaust-museum-of-tolerance-1203403980/|access-date=2021-02-19|website=Variety|language=en-US|archive-date=October 3, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201003101144/https://variety.com/2019/scene/news/jojo-rabbit-debate-holocaust-museum-of-tolerance-1203403980/|url-status=live}}</ref>

{{External media|video1=[https://iwitness.usc.edu/sfi/Sites/JojoRabbit/ ''Jojo Rabbit'' Holocaust resources page] at the [[USC Shoah Foundation]]{{'s}} IWitness website.|title=External website}}
''Jojo Rabbit'' had an impact on teaching of the Holocaust on December 19, 2019, when the USC Shoah Foundation announced it worked together with Searchlight to develop a classroom curriculum regarding the depiction of Nazism in the film. According to the Foundation, it "demonstrates how individuals can overcome ingrained prejudices and hate" and significantly expands their catalog of Holocaust scholarly resources. This curriculum was combined with [[Holocaust survivors]] testimony videos from their Visual History Archive (VHA). These are all bundled into a landing page at the Foundation's IWitness website.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Ben-Moche|first=Erin|date=2019-12-19|title=Fox Searchlight and USC Shoah Foundation Partner on 'Jojo Rabbit' Education Initiative|url=https://jewishjournal.com/culture/arts/308765/fox-searchlight-and-usc-shoah-foundation-partner-on-jojo-rabbit-education-initiative/|url-status=live|access-date=2021-04-30|website=[[The Jewish Journal of Greater Los Angeles]]|archive-date=April 30, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210430142802/https://jewishjournal.com/culture/arts/308765/fox-searchlight-and-usc-shoah-foundation-partner-on-jojo-rabbit-education-initiative/}}</ref>

'''King Wallis Vidor''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|v|iː|d|ɔr}} {{respell|VEE|dor}}; February 8, 1894 – November 1, 1982) was an American film director, film producer, and screenwriter. His 67-year career spanned the silent and sound eras, with works distinguished by a sympathetic depiction of contemporary social issues. Considered an {{lang|fr|[[auteur]]}} director, Vidor approached multiple genres and allowed the subject matter to determine the style, often pressing the limits of film-making conventions.<ref>Berlinale Retrospective 2020: "...he was actively involved in making movies for 67 years." And "allowed the material to define the style." And on "auteur": "Vidor's status as an auteur is definitely underscored by his independence and by the passion he brought to films. ...Vidor was indeed at times something of an auteur filmmaker..." And on "humane": "There is also a whole series of motifs that repeatedly turn up in his films, and which reflect the things he cared about – issues of class, as well as the issue of race in the US, which he incorporated into his films with a humanist bent..." <br />WSWS Reinhardt 2020: "What distinguished him as an artist was his instinct for substantial and relevant social topics and conflicts."<br />Gustaffson 2016: "At his best, Vidor "made films about the human condition, about human's moral and physical battles, and the battle between us and nature.<br />Baxter 1976, p. 41: "...Vidor adapted well to sound."</ref>
