==Military==
*[[Gus George Bebas]] – naval aviator and a recipient of the [[Distinguished Flying Cross (United States)|Distinguished Flying Cross]]
*[[LTG Peter G. Burbules]] – retired [[United States Army]] [[Lieutenant General]]. U.S. Army Ordnance Hall of Fame.
*[[Matthew Bogdanos]] – colonel in the [[United States Marine Corps Reserves]]
*[[Chris Carr (Medal of Honor)|Chris Carr]] – United States Army soldier and a recipient of the United States military's highest decoration—the Medal of Honor
*[[Alden Partridge Colvocoresses]] – developer of the first satellite map of the United States
*[[George Colvocoresses]] – commander of the [[USS Saratoga (1842)|Saratoga]] during the [[American Civil War]]<ref>http://72.14.207.104/search?q=cache:SymsEkFOslcJ:www.hellenicnews.com/print.html?newsid%3D2885%26lang%3DUS+Maria+Stephanos+Greek&hl=en&gl=us&ct=clnk&cd=3{{dead link|date=December 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> [[File:George Musalas Colvocoresses (US Navy officer).jpg|thumb|[[George Colvocoresses]], enslaved during the [[Chios massacre]] he would after his freedom from slavery emigrate to the United States and become a US Naval Officer; commanded the [[USS Saratoga]] during the [[American Civil War]]]]
*[[George Partridge Colvocoresses]] – led a distinguished military career rising to the rank of [[Admiral]]
*[[George Dilboy]] – first [[Greek-American]] to receive [[Medal of Honor]] [[File:George Dilboy - WWI Medal of Honor recipient.png|thumb|[[George Dilboy]] – first [[Greek-American]] [[Medal of Honor]] recipient; served and died during his service in [[World War I]]]]
*[[Andrea Dimitry]] – Greek-American soldier in the [[War of 1812]] fought in the [[Battle of New Orleans]]
*[[George Doundoulakis]] – Greek-American soldier who worked under British Intelligence during World War II and served with the OSS in Thessaly, Greece. Later becoming a physicist, he is known by his twenty-six US patents in the fields of radar, electronics, and narrowband television.
*[[Helias Doundoulakis]] – served in the United States Army and the Office of Strategic Services — the OSS — as a spy during the Battle of Crete in WWII. Later becoming a civil engineer, he worked on many elite projects for the U.S. Navy and NASA as project leader at Grumman Aerospace.  Brother of [[George Doundoulakis]].
*[[Michel Dragon]] (1739–1821) Greek American Lieutenant in the [[Spain and the American Revolutionary War|American Revolution]] fought in the [[Siege of Pensacola]].
*[[Photius Fisk]] (1809–1890) American abolitionist, Chaplain U.S.N., lobbied to abolish flogging in the U.S. Navy
*[[Jack H. Jacobs]], Vietnam War veteran. Medal of Honor recipient (of [[Romaniote Jews|Romaniote Jewish descent]]).
*[[James G. Kalergis]] – U.S. Army officer who played a significant role in the post-Vietnam era reorganization of the U.S. Army
*[[George Marshall (gunner)|George Marshall]] (1781–1855) served in the U.S. Navy during the [[War of 1812]], he was a Master Gunner and wrote ''Marshall's Practical Marine Gunnery''.
*[[James Megellas]] – retired United States Army officer, the most decorated officer in the history of the 82nd Airborne Division, received a Distinguished Service Cross, a Silver Star, and been nominated for the Medal of Honor
*[[Charles Moskos]] – leading military sociologist in the [[US Military]]. Author of ''Greek Americans: Struggle and Success''.
*[[William Pagonis]] – retired three-star U.S. [[Lieutenant General (United States)|Army General]] and chairman of the board for [[RailAmerica]]
*[[Steve Pisanos]] – (November 10, 1919 – June 6, 2016) aka "The Flying Greek" - flying ace who served as a fighter pilot with the British Royal Air Force (RAF) and later in the United States Army Air Forces in World War II.  He retired in 1974 from the U.S. Air Force as a colonel. [[File:Steve Pisanos 2006 Gathering of Eagles Lithograph.jpg|thumb|Steve Pisanos]]
*[[Andrew P. Poppas]] – [[United States Army]] [[lieutenant general]] currently serving as the [[director of the Joint Staff]]
*[[George Sirian]] – served in the [[US Navy]] with distinction for nearly fifty years
*[[Alek Skarlatos]] – [[US Army National Guard]] soldier awarded the [[Soldier's Medal]] from US President [[Barack Obama]] and the [[Legion of Honor]] by French President [[François Hollande]] for his participation in the thwarting of terrorist train attack on the [[2015 Thalys train attack]]. Portrayed himself in Clint Eastwood's film [[The 15:17 to Paris]] (2018).[[File:Alek Skarlatos 2015.png|thumb|[[US Army National Guard]] soldier [[Alek Skarlatos]]]]
*[[James G. Stavridis]] – retired [[USN]] admiral, [[Supreme Allied Commander Europe]] July 2, 2009 - May 13, 2013 [[File:ADM James G. Stavridis.jpg|thumb|Admiral [[James G. Stavridis]], former [[Supreme Allied Commander Europe]]]]
*[[Peter G. Tsouras]] – retired [[Lieutenant Colonel (United States)|Lieutenant Colonel]] in the [[United States Army]]

=== Engineering ===
*[[Constantine A. Balanis]] – electrical engineer
*[[John Baras]] – electrical engineer
*[[George Doundoulakis]] – physicist and soldier who worked under British Intelligence during World War II and then served with the OSS in Thessaly, Greece. He is known by his twenty-six US patents in the fields of radar, electronics, and narrowband television.
*[[Helias Doundoulakis]] – civil engineer who was employed at Grumman Aerospace Corporation for over thirty five years and group leader on many USAF and NASA projects. These included the Apollo space missions and the Lunar Excursion Module, the F-14 Tomcat fighter jet, and the Space Shuttle. His design of the oxygen tanks on the ill-fated Apollo 13 mission was instrumental in the return of the Apollo 13 crew, for which Doundoulakis was given a plaque by Captain James Lovell, Fred Haise, and Jack Swigert. Served in the United States Army and the [[Office of Strategic Services]] (OSS) — as a spy during the Battle of Crete in WWII.
*[[Maria Flytzani-Stephanopoulos]] – chemical engineer
*[[Peter Karter]] – nuclear engineer and one of the pioneers of the modern recycling industry
*[[Ares J. Rosakis]] – engineer
*[[George Tchobanoglous]] – civil and environmental engineer, professor at University of California, Davis
*[[Michael Tsapatsis]] – chemical engineer and materials scientist

=== English, debate, speech ===
*[[Helena Zachos]] (March 5, 1856 – February 28, 1951) - American college professor and elocutionist, who was on the faculty at [[Cooper Union]] from 1897 to 1939. Daughter of educator and abolitionist Professor John Celivergos Zachos.
[[File:HelenaZachos.tif|thumb|HelenaZachos]]
*[[John Celivergos Zachos]] (December 20, 1820 – March 20, 1898) - worked as Library Curator and Professor of English Language at [[Cooper Union]] from 1872 until his death in 1898. In 1861 was named the first superintendent of the [[Port Royal Experiment]] where freed slaves were educated on the liberated islands off of Charleston, SC.

==Criminal figures==
*[[Gus Alex]] (April 1, 1916 – July 24, 1998) - high-ranking associate of the [[Chicago Outfit]]
*[[Joe Gallo|Peter "Pete the Greek" Diapoulas]] - body guard of NYC mobster [[Joe Gallo]], was present the night of Gallo's assassination.
*[[Fotios Geas]] – mobster involved with the [[Genovese crime family]] and murderer of [[Whitey Bulger]] in [[United States Penitentiary, Hazelton|Hazelton (WV) Federal Penitentiary]]
*[[Tom Kapatos]] – [[New York City]] mobster, also known as "The Greek"
*Dr. [[George C. Nichopoulos]] – personal physician to [[Elvis Presley]] from 1970 to 1977 (Presley's death). Although exonerated in the death of Presley, Dr. Nichopoulos was later stripped of his medical license due to overprescribing medications to many other patients in the state of Tennessee.
*[[Michael Thevis]] - mobster
*[[Velentzas crime family|Peter Kourakos]] "Pete The Greek" - founder of Greek-American organized crime in Astoria, Queens, New York.
*[[Velentzas crime family|Spyredon "Spiros" Velentzas]] – Spiros Velentzas, aka "Sakafias", expanded the activities of the Kourakos crime family in New York City in the 1980s-1990s.

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: List of South by Southwest Film Festival award winners
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}}

The following is a list of award winners at the [[South by Southwest]] Film & TV Festival. The festival presents jury awards across multiple competition categories, including Narrative Feature, Documentary Feature, and several short film programs (Narrative, Documentary, Animated, Midnight, Texas, and Music Video), as well as an Independent TV Pilot Competition, Poster Design Competition, and XR Experience Competition. In addition to jury awards, all festival selections are eligible for audience awards, with voting certified by the accounting firm Maxwell Locke & Ritter.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=SXSW Film & TV Festival Awards |url=https://www.sxsw.com/festivals/film-awards/ |access-date=2025-02-18 |website=SXSW |language=en-US}}</ref>

The festival also presents various special awards, which have changed over the years. Recurring special awards have included the Louis Black "Lone Star" Award (for films shot in Texas or directed by Texas residents, named for SXSW co-founder [[Louis Black]]), the Adam Yauch Hörnblowér Award (for unconventional filmmaking in the Visions section, named for [[Beastie Boys]] member [[Adam Yauch]]), and the ZEISS Cinematography Award.

Winners of the SXSW Narrative, Documentary, and Animated Short Film jury awards are eligible for [[Academy Awards]] consideration. British short films and animations screened at SXSW are eligible for [[BAFTA]] nomination, and feature films are eligible for the [[Independent Spirit Awards]].<ref name=":0" />

==2026 SXSW Film Awards==
The SXSW 2026 jury and special awards were announced March 19, 2026, in [[Austin, Texas]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=SXSW Film & TV Festival Awards |url=https://sxsw.com/festivals/film-awards/#twentysix/ |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=SXSW |language=en-US}}</ref>

==2020 SXSW Film Awards==
The 2020 SXSW Film Festival was canceled by the City of Austin due to concerns surrounding [[COVID-19 pandemic|COVID-19]]. Jury and special awards were still announced on March 24, 2020, after filmmakers opted in and juries were assembled. Due to the event cancellation, there were no audience awards for 2020.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Roberts |first=Jordan |date=2020-03-24 |title=The 2020 SXSW Film Festival Announces Jury and Special Awards |url=https://www.sxsw.com/film/2020/the-2020-sxsw-film-festival-announces-jury-and-special-awards/ |access-date=2024-03-17 |website=SXSW |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-03-24 |title=SXSW FILM FESTIVAL ANNOUNCES 2020 JURY AND SPECIAL AWARDS |url=https://www.sxsw.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/2020-SXSW-AWARDS-RELEASE-FINAL-2.pdf |access-date=2025-02-18 |website=SXSW}}</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: List of films considered as New Hollywood
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}}
This is the list of films considered by various sources as part of the [[New Hollywood]] era.

==Background==
The '''New Hollywood''', '''Hollywood Renaissance''', or '''American New Wave''', was a movement in [[Cinema of the United States|American film history]] from the mid-1960s to the early 1980s,<ref name=Britannica>Payne, Laura. "[https://www.britannica.com/art/New-Hollywood New Hollywood]", ''[[Encyclopædia Britannica]]''.</ref><ref>[https://thequietus.com/culture/books/we-are-the-mutants-new-hollywood-kelly-roberts-michael-grasso-richard-mckenna-interview/ New Hollywood Vs Mutant Cinema: The Flipside Of US Cinema, 1960s–80s|The Quietus]</ref> when a new generation of filmmakers came to prominence.<ref name="riseandreign">[https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/mar/03/the-last-kings-of-hollywood-by-paul-fischer-review-the-rise-and-reign-of-spielberg-lucas-and-coppola The Last Kings of Hollywood by Paul Fischer review – the rise and reign of Spielberg, Lucas and Coppola|Books|The Guardian]</ref> They influenced the types of film produced, their production and marketing, and the way the [[major film studios]] approached filmmaking.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://stacker.com/stories/1366/50-best-movies-1970s|title=50 best movies from the 1970s|website=Stacker}}</ref> In New Hollywood films, the film director, rather than the studio, took on a key [[Auteur theory|authorial]] role.<ref name="limitsofauteurism" />

The definition of "New Hollywood" varies, depending on the author, with some defining it as a movement and others as a period. The span of the period is also a subject of debate, as well as its integrity, as some authors, such as Thomas Schatz, argue that the New Hollywood consists of several different movements. The films made in this movement are stylistically characterized in that their narrative often deviated from [[Classical Hollywood Cinema|classical]] norms. After the demise of the [[studio system]] and the rise of television, the commercial success of films was diminished.<ref name="limitsofauteurism" />

Successful films of the early New Hollywood era include ''[[Bonnie and Clyde (film)|Bonnie and Clyde]]'',<ref name="ST">{{cite web|url=http://www.afi.com/silver/new/nowplaying/2011/v8i3/penn.aspx|title=AFI Silver Theatre and Cultural Center|website=www.afi.com}}</ref> ''[[The Graduate]]''{{sfn|Krämer|2005|p=8}}<ref name="10classicswedliketoforget">[https://lamag.com/news/the-top-10-underrated-movies-and-10-classics-wed-like-to-forget The Top 10 Underrated Movies ... and 10 Classics We'd Like to Forget – LAmag]</ref> and ''[[Easy Rider]]''<ref name="offscreen.com">[https://offscreen.com/view/seconds-john-frankenheimer-1967-and-point-blank-john-boorman-1968 Seconds (John Frankenheimer, 1967) and Point Blank (John Boorman, 1968) – Offscreen]</ref> while films whose box office failure marked the end of the era include ''[[New York, New York (1977 film)|New York, New York]]'', ''[[Sorcerer (film)|Sorcerer]]'', ''[[Heaven's Gate (film)|Heaven's Gate]]'', ''[[They All Laughed]]'', and ''[[One from the Heart]]''.<ref name="wildesteverthriller?"/><ref name="onemoviekilledthe80s">[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NM0VsX1mdL8 How One Movie Killed The 1980s – Patrick (H) Willems on YouTube]</ref><ref name="allpowerfuldirector">[https://www.theringer.com/2021/07/19/movies/heavens-gate-1970s-hollywood-auteur-directors The Death of the All-Powerful Director - The Ringer]</ref>

* [[Frank Yablans]]<ref name="postfordist">{{cite book | title=Post-Fordist Cinema: Hollywood Auteurs and the Corporate Counterculture | date=26 February 2019 | publisher=Columbia University Press | isbn=978-0-231-54508-2 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=P2NbDwAAQBAJ }}</ref>

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Luis Buñuel
======================================================================

{{short description|Spanish-Mexican filmmaker (1900–1983)}}
{{family name hatnote|Buñuel|Portolés|lang=Spanish}}
{{good article}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=December 2025}}
{{Infobox person

'''Luis Buñuel Portolés''' ({{IPA|es|ˈlwis βuˈɲwel poɾtoˈles|lang}}; 22 February 1900 – 29 July 1983) was a Spanish and Mexican filmmaker who worked in [[France]], [[Mexico]], and [[Spain]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Bauer |first1=Patricia |title=Luis Buñuel, Spanish director |url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Luis-Bunuel |access-date=29 January 2023 |website=Britannica}}</ref> He has been widely considered by many film critics, historians, and directors to be one of the greatest and most influential filmmakers of all time.<ref name="Encyclopædia Britannica">{{cite web |last=Kyrou |first=Ado |title=Luis Buñuel |url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Luis-Bunuel |access-date=9 October 2017 |website=Encyclopædia Britannica |publisher=Encyclopædia Britannica, Inc.}}</ref> [[Luis Buñuel filmography|Buñuel's works]] are known for their [[avant-garde]] surrealism which was also infused with [[political commentary]].

Often associated with the [[surrealist movement]], Buñuel's career spanned the 1920s through the 1970s. He collaborated with surrealist painter [[Salvador Dalí]] on ''[[Un Chien Andalou]]'' (1929) and ''[[L'Age d'Or]]'' (1930).<ref name="koller" /> Both are considered masterpieces of [[surrealist cinema]].<ref>{{cite web |last=French |first=Philip |author-link=Philip French |date=29 May 2011 |title=L'Age d'Or/ Un Chien Andalou |url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2011/may/29/lage-dor-bunuel-chien-andalou-philip-french |access-date=4 December 2024 |work=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> From 1947 to 1960, he honed his skills as a director in Mexico, making grounded and human [[melodramas]] such as ''[[Gran Casino]]'' (1947), ''[[Los Olvidados]]'' (1950) and ''[[Él (film)|Él]]'' (1953).

Buñuel then transitioned to making artful, surrealistic and [[satirical]] films. He earned the {{lang|fr|[[Palme d'Or]]|italic=no}} at the [[1961 Cannes Film Festival]] for ''[[Viridiana]]'' (1961), which criticized the [[Francoist Spain|Francoist dictatorship]]. He satirized social conditions in ''[[The Exterminating Angel]]'' (1962) and ''[[The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie]]'' (1972), the latter of which won the [[Academy Award for Best International Feature Film|Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film]]. He also directed ''[[Diary of a Chambermaid (1964 film)|Diary of a Chambermaid]]'' (1964) and ''[[Belle de Jour (film)|Belle de Jour]]'' (1967). He earned the [[National Society of Film Critics Award for Best Director]] for his final film, ''[[That Obscure Object of Desire]]'' (1977).<ref name="Ramirez Berg">{{cite web |last=Berg |first=Charles Ramírez |title=Program Notes: THAT OBSCURE OBJECT OF DESIRE |url=http://www.austinfilm.org/essential-cinema/program-notes-that-obscure-object-of-desire |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150610201718/http://www.austinfilm.org/essential-cinema/program-notes-that-obscure-object-of-desire |archive-date=10 June 2015 |access-date=9 October 2017 |publisher=[[Austin Film Society]]}}</ref>

Buñuel earned five [[Cannes Film Festival]] prizes, two [[Berlin International Film Festival]] prizes, a [[BAFTA Award]] and an [[Academy Award]] in 1972. Buñuel received numerous honors including [[National Prize for Arts and Sciences]] for Fine Arts in 1977, the [[11th Moscow International Film Festival|Moscow International Film Festival]] Contribution to Cinema Prize in 1979, and the [[Golden Lion|Career Golden Lion]] in 1982. He was nominated twice for the [[Nobel Prize in Literature]], in [[1968 Nobel Prize in Literature|1968]] and then in [[1972 Nobel Prize in Literature|1972]]. Seven of Buñuel's films are included in ''[[Sight & Sound]]''{{'s}} 2012 critics' poll of the top 250 films of all time.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pendragon |first=The |date=26 April 2018 |title=Sight & Sound 2012 critics top 250 films |url=https://thependragonsociety.com/sight-sound-2012-critics-top-250-films/ |access-date=24 September 2019 |website=The Pendragon Society |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Critics' Top 250 Films |url=http://explore.bfi.org.uk/sightandsoundpolls/2012/critics |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131026034922/http://explore.bfi.org.uk/sightandsoundpolls/2012/critics |archive-date=26 October 2013 |access-date=18 August 2012 |website=Sight and Sound |publisher=British Film Institute}}</ref> Buñuel's obituary in ''[[The New York Times]]'' called him "an [[iconoclast]], moralist, and revolutionary who was a leader of avant-garde surrealism in his youth and a dominant international movie director half a century later".<ref name="NYTObit">{{cite news |last=Flint |first=Peter B. Flint |date=30 July 1983 |title=Luis Buñuel Dies at 83; Filmmaker for 50 Years |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1983/07/30/obituaries/luis-bunuel-dies-at-83-film-maker-for-50-years.html |access-date=6 August 2012 |newspaper=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
[[File:Vista parcial de Calanda. Foto José Antonio Bielsa.JPG|thumb|right|alt=Calanda, Spain|[[Calanda, Spain|Calanda]], Spain, in 2013]]
Buñuel was born on 22 February 1900 in [[Calanda, Spain|Calanda]], a small town in the [[Aragon]] region of Spain.<ref name="Alcala">{{cite book |last=Alcalá |first=Manuel |title=Buñuel (Cine e ideologia) |publisher=Edicusa |year=1973 |isbn=978-84-229-0101-3 |location=Madrid}}</ref>{{rp|pp.16–17}} His father was Leonardo Buñuel, also a native of Calanda, who had left home at age 14 to start a hardware business in [[Havana]], Cuba, ultimately amassing a fortune and returning home to Calanda at the age of 43, in 1898.<ref name="Havana">{{cite web |title=The Havana of Luis Buñuel |url=https://www.arteporexcelencias.com/en/events-500-aniversario/havana-luis-bunuel |access-date=11 June 2020 |website=Arte por Excelencias}}</ref> He married the 18-year-old daughter of the only innkeeper in Calanda, María Portolés Cerezuela.<ref name="gallegos">{{cite web |last1=Salgado |first1=Fernando |date=27 March 2014 |title=Dos gallegos y Buñuel padre |url=https://www.globalgalicia.org/noticia/actualidad/2013/10/13/dos-gallegos-bunuel-padre/0003_201310SM13P20994.htm |access-date=11 June 2020 |website=La Voz de Galicia |publisher=GlobalGalicia}}</ref> The eldest of seven children, Luis had two brothers, Alfonso and Leonardo, and four sisters: Alicia, Concepción, Margarita and María.<ref name="schwarze">{{cite book |last=Schwarze |first=Michael |title=Luis Buñuel |publisher=Plaza & Janes |year=1988 |isbn=978-84-01-45079-2 |location=Barcelona |pages=9}}</ref> He later described his birthplace by saying that in Calanda, "the [[Middle Ages]] lasted until [[World War&nbsp;I]]".<ref name="Luis Buñuel 1983">Luis Buñuel, ''My Last Sigh'', translated by Abigail Israel, New York: Alfred Knopf, 1983.</ref>

When Buñuel was four months old, the family moved to [[Zaragoza]], where they were one of the wealthiest families in town.<ref name=Alcala />{{rp|p.22}} In Zaragoza, Buñuel received a strict [[Society of Jesus|Jesuit]] education at the private Colegio del Salvador,<ref name=Alcala />{{rp|pp.23–36}} starting at the age of seven and continuing for the next seven years.<ref name="Lorca, Buñuel, Dalí">{{cite book |last1=Edwards |first1=Gwynne |title=Lorca, Buñuel, Dalí: Forbidden Pleasures and Connected Lives |date=2009 |publisher=I.B. Tauris |isbn=978-1848850071 |location=London}}</ref>{{rp|p.22}} After being kicked and insulted by the study hall proctor before a final exam, Buñuel refused to return to the school.<ref name="directors guide" /> He told his mother he had been expelled, which was not true; in fact, he had received the highest marks on his world history exam.<ref name="Luis Buñuel 1983"/> Buñuel finished the last two years of his high school education at the local public school,<ref name="directors guide">{{cite web |title=Luis Bunuel |url=http://www.greatestdirectors.com/buneul.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141113163759/http://www.greatestdirectors.com/buneul.html |archive-date=13 November 2014 |access-date=23 July 2012 |website=The Directors Guide |publisher=Website Creations}}</ref> graduating at the age of 16. Even as a child, Buñuel was something of a cinematic showman; friends from that period described productions in which Buñuel projected shadows on a screen using a [[magic lantern]] and a bedsheet.<ref name="A Proposito de Bunuel">{{cite web |last=Gobierno de Aragon |title=A Proposito de Bunuel – Screenplay |url=http://www.american-buddha.com/bunuel.screenplay.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140922133937/http://american-buddha.com/bunuel.screenplay.htm |archive-date=22 September 2014 |access-date=4 August 2012}}</ref> He also excelled at [[boxing]] and playing the [[violin]].<ref name="Encyclopædia Britannica" />
[[File:Benjamín Jarnés, Humberto Pérez de la Ossa, Luis Buñuel. Rafael Barradas y Federico García Lorca. Madrid, 1923.jpg|thumb |245x245px| left | alt= Benjamín Jarnés, Humberto Pérez de la Ossa, Luis Buñuel. Rafael Barradas y Federico García Lorca. Madrid, 1923 |
Luis Buñuel (top row, right), Madrid, 1923]]
In his youth, Buñuel was deeply religious, serving at Mass and taking Communion every day, until, at the age of 16, he grew disgusted with what he perceived as the illogicality of the Church, along with its power and wealth.<ref name="brandon">{{cite book |last=Brandon |first=Ruth |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9_Z0rVDhNGsC&q=bunuel+agronomy&pg=PA291 |title=Surreal Lives: The Surrealists 1917–1945 |publisher=Macmillan |year=1999 |isbn=978-0-8021-3727-2 |location=London}}</ref>{{rp|p.292}}

In 1917, he attended the [[Complutense University of Madrid|University of Madrid]], first studying [[agronomy]] then [[industrial engineering]] and finally switching to [[philosophy]].<ref name="smith celebrities">{{cite book |last=Smith |first=Warren Allen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=x73FqQgvzgQC&q=luis+bunuel+agronomy&pg=PA25 |title=Celebrities in Hell |publisher=Barricade Books |year=2002 |isbn=978-1-56980-214-4 |location=Fort Lee, NJ |pages=25}}</ref> He developed very close relationships with painter [[Salvador Dalí]] and poet [[Federico García Lorca]], among other important Spanish creative artists living in the [[Residencia de Estudiantes]], with the three friends forming the nucleus of the Spanish Surrealist [[avant-garde]],<ref name="delgado">{{cite book |last=Delgado |first=Manuel and Alice J. Poust |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fOJRnesy3x8C |title=Lorca, Buņuel, Dalí: Art and Theory |publisher=Associated University Presses |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-8387-5508-2 |location=Cranbury NJ |pages=passim}}</ref> and becoming known as members of "[[Generation of '27|La Generación del 27]]".<ref name="poets.org">{{cite web |title=La Generacion del 27: Dalí, Buñuel, and Lorca |url=http://www.poets.org/viewmedia.php/prmMID/5944 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130726060027/https://www.poets.org/viewmedia.php/prmMID/5944 |archive-date=26 July 2013 |access-date=24 July 2012 |publisher=Poets.org}}</ref> Buñuel was especially taken with García Lorca, later writing in his autobiography: <blockquote>We liked each other instantly. Although we seemed to have little in common—I was a redneck from Aragon, and he an elegant Andalusian—we spent most of our time together...We used to sit on the grass in the evenings behind the Residencia (at that time, there were vast open spaces reaching to the horizon), and he would read me his poems. He read slowly and beautifully, and through him I began to discover a wholly new world.<ref name="my last sigh">{{cite book |last=Buñuel |first=Luis |url=https://archive.org/details/mylastsigh0000buue |title=My last sigh |publisher=Knopf |year=1983 |isbn=978-0-394-52854-0 |location=New York |url-access=registration}}</ref>{{rp|p.62}}</blockquote> Buñuel's relationship with Dalí was somewhat more troubled, being tinged with jealousy over the growing intimacy between Dalí and Lorca and resentment over Dalí's early success as an artist.<ref name=brandon />{{rp|p.300}}

Buñuel's interest in films was intensified by [[Fritz Lang]]'s ''[[Destiny (1921 film)|Der müde Tod]]'': "I came out of the [[Théâtre du Vieux-Colombier|Vieux Colombier]] [theater] completely transformed. Images could and did become for me the true means of expression. I decided to devote myself to the cinema".<ref name="Buffalo Film Seminars 1">{{cite web |last=Christian |first=Diane | first2= Bruce | last2=Jackson |title=Luis Buñuel That Obscure Object of Desire/ Cet obscur objet du désir 1977 |url=http://csac.buffalo.edu/desire.pdf |access-date=5 August 2012 |website=Buffalo Film Seminars |publisher=Market Arcade Film & Arts Center and State University of New York at Buffalo}}</ref> At the age of 72, Buñuel had not lost his enthusiasm for this film, asking the octogenarian Lang for his autograph.<ref name=brandon />{{rp|p.301}}
{{clear|left}}

==Career==
=== 1925–1930: Early French period ===
[[File:Jean epstein 1920.jpg|thumb|right|upright|150px|[[Jean Epstein]], Buñuel's first film collaborator]]
In 1925 Buñuel moved to Paris, where he began work as a secretary in an organization called the International Society of Intellectual Cooperation.<ref name="bfi vol 3">{{cite book |last=Hammond |first=Paul |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=V96tee1l2q8C&q=bunuel+intellectual+cooperation&pg=PA124 |title="L'Age d'Or" in British Film Institute Film Classics, Volume 3 |publisher=Taylor and Francis |year=2003 |isbn=978-1-57958-328-6 |location=New York}}</ref>{{rp|p.124}} He also became actively involved in cinema and theater, going to the movies as often as three times a day.<ref name="williams">{{cite book |last=Williams |first=Alan Larson |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ESVZOghoi6kC&q=jean+epstein+luis+bunuel&pg=PA152 |title=Republic of Images: A History of French Filmmaking |publisher=Harvard University Press |year=1992 |isbn=978-0-674-76267-1 |location=Cambridge |pages=152}}</ref> Through these interests, he met a number of influential people, including the pianist [[Ricardo Viñes]], who was instrumental in securing Buñuel's selection as artistic director of the Dutch premiere of [[Manuel de Falla]]'s puppet-opera ''[[El retablo de maese Pedro]]'' in 1926.<ref name="talens">{{cite book |last=Taléns |first=Jenaro |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5209-5Ai_ZwC&q=bunuel+abel+gance&pg=PA30 |title=The Branded Eye: Buñuel's Un Chien Andalou |publisher=University of Minnesota Press |year=1993 |isbn=978-0-8166-2046-3 |location=Minneapolis}}</ref>{{rp|p.29}}

He decided to enter the film industry and enrolled in a private film school run by [[Jean Epstein]] and some associates.<ref name=williams /> At that time, Epstein was one of the most celebrated commercial directors working in France, his films being hailed as "the triumph of [[impressionism]] in motion, but also the triumph of the modern spirit".<ref name="sadoul">{{cite book |last=Sadoul |first=Georges |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PvsZikRu-hAC&q=jean+epstein+reputation&pg=PA19 |title=Dictionary of Film Makers |publisher=University of California Press |year=1972 |isbn=978-0-520-02151-8 |location=Berkeley & Los Angeles |pages=77}}</ref> Before long, Buñuel was working for Epstein as an assistant director on ''[[Mauprat (film)|Mauprat]]'' (1926) and ''[[The Fall of the House of Usher (1928 French film)|La chute de la maison Usher]]'' (1928),<ref name="edwards">{{cite book |last=Edwards |first=Gwynne |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=r5_VlQTnbD0C&q=bunuel+baker&pg=PA21 |title=A Companion to Luís Buñuel |publisher=Tamesis |year=2005 |isbn=978-1-85566-108-0 |location=Woodbridge}}</ref> and also for [[Mario Nalpas]] on {{lang|fr|La Sirène des Tropiques}} (''[[Siren of the Tropics]]'') (1927), starring [[Josephine Baker]].<ref name="fandor">{{cite web |title=Siren of the Tropics |url=http://www.fandor.com/films/siren_of_the_tropics |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150130222724/https://www.fandor.com/films/siren_of_the_tropics |archive-date=30 January 2015 |access-date=23 July 2012 |website=fandor |publisher=Our Film Festival, Inc.}}</ref> He appeared on screen in a small part as a smuggler in [[Jacques Feyder]]'s ''[[Carmen (1926 film)|Carmen]]'' (1926).<ref name="brain juice">{{cite web |title=Luis Buñuel |url=http://www.brain-juice.com/cgi-bin/show_bio.cgi?p_id=136 |access-date=23 July 2012 |website=brain-juice |publisher=Brain-Juice.Com, Inc.}}</ref>

When Buñuel derisively rejected Epstein's demand that he assist Epstein's mentor, [[Abel Gance]], who was at the time working on the film ''[[Napoléon (1927 film)|Napoléon]]'', Epstein dismissed him angrily, saying "How can a little asshole like you dare to talk that way about a great director like Gance?"<ref name=talens />{{rp|p.30}} then added "You seem rather surrealist. Beware of surrealists, they are crazy people."<ref name="de la colina">{{cite book |last=De La Colina |first=Jose |title=Objects of Desire: Conversations with Luis Bunuel |publisher=Marsilio Publishers |year=1994 |isbn=978-0-941419-69-7 |pages=80}}</ref>

After parting with Epstein, Buñuel worked as film critic for ''[[La Gaceta Literaria]]'' (1927) and ''[[Cahiers d'Art|Les Cahiers d'Art]]'' (1928).<ref name=talens />{{rp|p.30}} In the periodicals ''{{interlanguage link|L'Amic de les Arts|ca}}'' and ''{{interlanguage link|La gaseta de les Arts|ca|Gaseta de les Arts}}'', he and Dalí carried on a series of "call and response" essays on cinema and theater, debating such technical issues as segmentation, [[Cut-up technique|découpage]], the [[Insert (filmmaking)|insert shot]] and [[Film editing|rhythmic editing]].<ref name="dali collected writings">{{cite book |last=Dalí |first=Salvador |url=http://www.paolocirio.net/work/amazon-noir/amazon-noir-books/AMAZON-NOIR--The_Collected_Writings_of_Salvador_Dal%C3%AD--By--Salvador_Dali_Haim_N_Finkelstein--0521560276.pdf |title=The Collected Writings of Salvador Dalí |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1998 |isbn=978-0-521-56027-6 |location=Cambridge |access-date=24 July 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201028031157/https://www.paolocirio.net/work/amazon-noir/amazon-noir-books/AMAZON-NOIR--The_Collected_Writings_of_Salvador_Dal%C3%AD--By--Salvador_Dali_Haim_N_Finkelstein--0521560276.pdf |archive-date=28 October 2020 |url-status=dead}}</ref> He also collaborated with the celebrated writer [[Ramón Gómez de la Serna]] on the script for what he hoped would be his first film, "a story in six scenes" called ''Los caprichos''.<ref name=talens />{{rp|pp.30–31}} Through his involvement with ''Gaceta Literaria'', he helped establish Madrid's first cine-club and served as its inaugural chairman.<ref name="gomez mesa">{{cite journal |last=Gómez Mesa |first=Luis. |year=1978 |title=La generación cinematográfica del '27 |journal=Cinema 2002 |issue=37 |pages=52–58}}</ref>

====''Un Chien Andalou'' (1929)====
[[File:Salvador Dalí 1939.jpg|thumb|right|upright|[[Salvador Dalí]]]]
After his apprenticeship with Epstein, Buñuel shot and directed a 16-minute short, {{Lang|fr|[[Un Chien Andalou]]}}, with [[Salvador Dalí]]. The film, financed by Buñuel's mother,<ref name="brain juice andalusian dog">{{cite web |title=Un chien Andalou (An Andalusian Dog, 1929) |url=http://www.brain-juice.com/cgi-bin/show_wok.cgi?p_id=136&w_id=391 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061205212607/http://www.brain-juice.com/cgi-bin/show_wok.cgi?p_id=136&w_id=391 |archive-date=5 December 2006 |access-date=23 July 2012 |publisher=Brain-Juice.Com}}</ref> consists of a series of startling images of a [[Freudian]] nature,<ref name="mansfield">{{cite book |last=Mansfield |first=Nick |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qBVh5gVTlC4C |title=Subjectivity: Theories of the Self from Freud to Haraway |publisher=New York University Press |year=2000 |isbn=978-0-8147-5650-8 |location=New York |pages=36}}</ref> starting with a woman's eyeball being sliced open with a razor blade. {{Lang|fr|Un Chien Andalou}} was enthusiastically received by the burgeoning French [[surrealism|surrealist]] movement<ref name="richardson">{{cite book |last=Richardson |first=Michael |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v1C6E_zJi6UC&q=chien+andalou+reception+surrealist&pg=PA29 |title=Surrealism and Cinema |publisher=Berg |year=2006 |isbn=978-1-84520-225-5 |location=Oxford |pages=27}}</ref> and continues to be shown regularly in [[Film society|film societies]].<ref name="mathijs">{{cite book |last=Mathijs |first=Ernest |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uPtuaV7IAt0C&q=chien+andalou+film+societies&pg=PT194 |title=Cult Cinema |publisher=Blackwell |year=2011 |isbn=978-1-4051-7374-2 |location=West Sussex}}</ref> The script was written in six days at Dalí's home in [[Cadaqués]]. In a letter to a friend written in February 1929, Buñuel described the writing process:

<blockquote>We had to look for the plot line. Dalí said to me, 'I dreamed last night of ants swarming around in my hands', and I said, 'Good Lord, and I dreamed that I had sliced somebody or other's eye. There's the film, let's go and make it.'<ref name="etherington-smith">{{cite book |last=Etherington-Smith |first=Meredith |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=soncxLrkYX0C&q=We+had+to+look+for+the+plot+line.+Dal%C3%AD+said+to+me%2C+%22I+dreamed+last+night+of+ants+swarming+around+in+my+hands%27%2C+and+I+said%2C+%22Good+Lord%2C+and+I+dreamed+that+I+had+sliced+somebody+or+other%27s+eye.+There%27s+the+film%2C+let%27s+go+and+make+it.&pg=PA94 |title=The Persistence of Memory: A Biography of Dalí |publisher=Da Capo Press |year=1995 |isbn=978-0-306-80662-9 |location=New York |pages=94 |authorlink=Meredith Etherington-Smith}}{{Dead link|date=August 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref></blockquote>

[[File:Un Chien Andalou (1929).webm|thumb|left|thumbtime=5|''[[Un Chien Andalou]]'' (1929)]]
In deliberate contrast to the approach taken by Jean Epstein and his peers, which was to never leave anything in their work to chance, with every aesthetic decision having a rational explanation and fitting clearly into the whole,<ref name="o'donoghue">{{cite magazine |last=O'Donoghue |first=Darragh |date=12 February 2004 |title=On Some Motifs in Poe: Jean Epstein's La Chute de la maison Usher |url=http://sensesofcinema.com/2004/feature-articles/la_chute_de_la_maison_usher/#b4 |access-date=27 July 2012 |magazine=Senses of Cinema}}</ref> Buñuel and Dalí made a cardinal point of eliminating all logical associations.<ref name="Adamowicz">{{cite book |last=Adamowicz |first=Elza |url=http://www.ibtauris.com/Books/The%20arts/Film%20TV%20%20radio/Films%20cinema/Film%20guides%20%20reviews/~/media/Files/Extracts/Visual%20Culture/9781848850569.ashx |title=Un Chien Andalou: (Luis Buñuel and Salvador Dalí, 1929) |publisher=I.B.Tauris |year=2010 |isbn=978-1-84885-056-9 |location=London |pages=8}}</ref> In Buñuel's words: "Our only rule was very simple: no idea or image that might lend itself to a rational explanation of any kind would be accepted. We had to open all doors to the irrational and keep only those images that surprised us, without trying to explain why".<ref name="my last sigh" />{{rp|p.104}}

It was Buñuel's intention to outrage the self-proclaimed artistic vanguard of his youth, later saying: "Historically the film represents a violent reaction against what in those days was called 'avant-garde,' which was aimed exclusively at artistic sensibility and the audience's reason."<ref name="art in cinema">{{cite book |last=Buñuel |first=Luis |url=https://www.scribd.com/doc/32547313/Art-in-Cinema |title="Notes on the Making of Un Chien Andalou", in Art in Cinema : documents toward a history of the film society |publisher=Temple University Press |year=2006 |isbn=978-1-59213-425-0 |location=Philadelphia |pages=101–102 |access-date=9 September 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305164412/https://www.scribd.com/doc/32547313/Art-in-Cinema |archive-date=5 March 2016 |url-status=dead}}</ref> Against his hopes and expectations, the film was a popular success with the very audience he had wanted to insult.<ref name="koller">{{cite web |last=Koller |first=Michael |date=9 June 2011 |title=Un Chien Andalou |url=http://sensesofcinema.com/2001/cteq/chien/ |access-date=23 July 2012 |website=Senses of Cinema |publisher=Film Victoria}}</ref>[[Roger Ebert]] called it one of the most famous short films of the century.<ref name="ebert viridiana"/> Buñuel exclaim in exasperation: "What can I do about the people who adore all that is new, even when it goes against their deepest convictions, or about the insincere, corrupt press, and the inane herd that saw beauty or poetry in something which was basically no more than a desperate impassioned call for murder?"<ref>{{cite journal |last=Buñuel |first=Luis |date=12 December 1929 |title=Preface to the script for Un Chien Andalou |journal=La Révolution Surréaliste |number=12}}</ref>

Although {{Lang|fr|Un Chien Andalou}} is a [[silent film]], during the original screening (attended by the elite of the Parisian art world), Buñuel played a sequence of phonograph records which he switched manually while keeping his pockets full of stones with which to pelt anticipated hecklers.<ref name="maverick arts">{{cite web |title=Un Chien Andalou |url=http://www.maverick-arts.com/cgi-bin/MAVERICK?&issue=340 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181105160434/http://www.maverick-arts.com/cgi-bin/MAVERICK?&issue=340 |archive-date=5 November 2018 |access-date=23 July 2012 |work=Maverick Arts Magazine}}</ref> After the premiere, Buñuel and Dalí were granted formal admittance to the tight-knit community of Surrealists, led by poet [[André Breton]].<ref name=hoberman />

====''L'Age d'Or'' (1930)====
[[File:Marie-Laure de Noailles.jpg|thumb|upright|left|[[Marie-Laure de Noailles]] was a prominent patron of avant-garde artists, who received ''[[L'Age d'Or]]'' as a birthday gift from her husband, [[Charles de Noailles|Charles]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Gray |first1=Francine du Plessix |date=17 September 2007 |title=The Surrealists' Muse |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2007/09/24/the-surrealists-muse |access-date=31 May 2020 |website=newyorker.com/}}</ref>]]
Late in 1929, on the strength of {{Lang|fr|Un Chien Andalou}}, Buñuel and Dalí were commissioned to make another short film by [[Marie-Laure de Noailles|Marie-Laurie]] and [[Charles de Noailles]], owners of a private cinema on the [[Place des États-Unis]] and financial supporters of productions by Jacques Manuel, [[Man Ray]] and [[Pierre Chenal]].<ref name="bfi vol 3" />{{rp|p.124}} At first, the intent was that the new film be around the same length as ''Un Chien'', only this time with sound. But by mid-1930, the film had grown segmentally to an hour's duration.<ref name="bfi vol 3" />{{rp|p.116}} Anxious that it was over twice as long as planned and at double the budget, Buñuel offered to trim the film and cease production, but Noailles gave him the go-ahead to continue the project.<ref name="bfi vol 3" />{{rp|p.116}}

The film, ''[[L'Age d'Or]]'', was begun as a second collaboration with Dalí, but, while working on the scenario, the two had a falling out; Buñuel, who at the time had strong leftist sympathies,<ref name="gubern">{{cite book |last=Gubern |first=Román and Paul Hammond |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=elueEkeLL_oC&q=bunuel+espana+1936&pg=PA427 |title=Luis Bunuel: The Red Years, 1929–1939 |publisher=University of Wisconsin Press |year=2012 |isbn=978-0-299-28474-9 |location=Madison}}</ref> desired a deliberate undermining of all bourgeois institutions, while Dalí, who eventually supported the Spanish fascist [[Francisco Franco]] and various figures of the European aristocracy, wanted merely to cause a scandal through the use of various [[Scatology|scatological]] and anti-Catholic images.<ref name="film reference">{{cite web |title=Marxism – European Cinema Before and After World War II |url=http://www.filmreference.com/encyclopedia/Independent-Film-Road-Movies/Marxism-EUROPEAN-CINEMA-BEFORE-AND-AFTER-WORLD-WAR-II.html |access-date=23 July 2012 |website=film reference |publisher=Advameg, Inc.}}</ref> The friction between them was exacerbated when, at a dinner party in Cadaqués, Buñuel tried to throttle Dalí's girlfriend, [[Gala Dalí|Gala]], the wife of Surrealist poet [[Paul Éluard]].<ref name="thurlow">{{cite book |last=Thurlow |first=Clifford |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HX8XcfTw6KIC |title=Making Short Films: The Complete Guide from Script to Screen, 2nd ed |publisher=Berg |year=2008 |isbn=978-1-84520-803-5 |location=Oxford |pages=3}}</ref> In consequence, Dalí had nothing to do with the actual shooting of the film.<ref name="dali">{{cite book |last=Dalí |first=Salvador |title=The Secret Life of Salvador Dali |publisher=Dial Press |year=1942 |location=New York}}</ref>{{rp|pp.276–277}} During the course of production, Buñuel worked around his technical ignorance by filming mostly in sequence and using nearly every foot of film that he shot. Buñuel invited friends and acquaintances to appear, for nothing, in the film; for example, anyone who owned a tuxedo or a party frock got a part in the salon scene.<ref name="bfi vol 3" />{{rp|p.116}}

{{quote box|bgcolor=#CCDDFF|align=right|width=25%|quote=A film called ''L'Age d'or'', whose non-existent artistic quality is an insult to any kind of technical standard, combines, as a public spectacle, the most obscene, disgusting and tasteless incidents. Country, family, and religion are dragged through the mud.<ref>{{cite news |last=Bodin |first=Richard Pierre |date=7 December 1930 |title=Review of "L'age d'Or" |newspaper=Le Figaro}}</ref> |source=Excerpt from Richard Pierre Bodin's review in {{Lang|fr|[[Le Figaro]]}}, 7 December 1930.}} ''L'Age d'Or'' was publicly proclaimed by Dalí as a deliberate attack on Catholicism, and this precipitated a much larger scandal than {{Lang|fr|Un Chien Andalou}}.<ref name="fanes">{{cite book |last=Fanés |first=Fèlix |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bDpziok_K7gC&q=l%27age+d%27or+dali+dispute+bunuel&pg=PA171 |title=Salvador Dali: The Construction of the Image |publisher=Yale University Press |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-300-09179-3 |location=New Haven |pages=171}}</ref> One early screening was taken over by members of the fascist [[Ligue des Patriotes|League of Patriots]] and the Anti-Jewish Youth Group, who hurled purple ink at the screen<ref name="ado kyrou">{{cite book |last=Kyrou |first=Ado |title=Luis Buñuel: an introduction |publisher=Simon and Schuster |year=1963 |location=New York |pages=30}}</ref> and then vandalised the adjacent art gallery, destroying a number of valuable surrealist paintings.<ref name="moria">{{cite web |last=Scheib |first=Richard |date=15 December 2005 |title=L'Age d'Or |url=http://www.moria.co.nz/fantasy/lagedor.htm |access-date=23 July 2012 |publisher=Moria – The Science Fiction, Horror and Fantasy Film Review}}</ref> The film was banned by the Parisian police "in the name of public order".<ref name="Instituto Cervantes">{{cite book |last=Instituto Cervantes |title=Buñuel, 100 año: es peligroso asomarse al Interior/ Buñuel, 100 Years: It' s Dangerous to Look Inside |publisher=Museum of Modern Art |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-8109-6219-4 |location=New York |pages=62}}</ref> The de Noailles, both Catholics, were threatened with [[Excommunication#Catholic Church|excommunication]] by [[Holy See|The Vatican]] because of the film's blasphemous final scene (which visually links [[Jesus Christ]] with the writings of the [[Marquis de Sade]]), so they made the decision in 1934 to withdraw all prints from circulation, and ''L'Age d'Or'' was not seen again until 1981, after their deaths,<ref name="laufer">{{cite web |last=Laufer |first=Laura |title=L'Âge d'or" de Luis Bunuel |url=http://adagio.over-blog.fr/article-25951854.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130615233326/http://adagio.over-blog.fr/article-25951854.html |archive-date=15 June 2013 |access-date=23 July 2012 |publisher=Le Centre Georges-Pompidou}}</ref> although a print was smuggled to England for private viewing.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Lim |first1=Dennis |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yHcIp0sa6MkC&q=l%27age+d%27or+banned&pg=PA7 |title=The Village Voice Film Guide: 50 Years of Movies from Classics to Cult Hits |date=2006 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=978-0471787815 |location=New York |page=7 |access-date=8 October 2014}}</ref> The furor was so great that the premiere of another film financed by the de Noailles, [[Jean Cocteau]]'s ''[[The Blood of a Poet]]'', had to be delayed for over two years until outrage over ''L'Age d'Or'' had died down.<ref name="burke">{{cite book |last=Burke |first=Carolyn |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PVmJOWev0p8C&q=Noailles+excommunication&pg=PA113 |title=Lee Miller: A Life |publisher=Knopf |year=2005 |isbn=978-0-375-40147-3 |location=New York |pages=114}}</ref> To make matters worse, Charles de Noailles was forced to withdraw his membership from the [[Jockey-Club de Paris|Jockey Club]].<ref name="teitelbaum">{{cite book |last=Teitelbaum |first=Mo Amelia |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CuT3JqcH8hcC&q=charles+de+noailles+jockey+club&pg=PA102 |title=The Stylemakers: Minimalism and Classic-Modernism 1915–45 |publisher=Philip Willson |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-85667-703-8 |location=London |pages=102}}</ref>

Concurrent with the ''[[succès de scandale]]'', both Buñuel and the film's leading lady, [[Lya Lys]], received offers of interest from [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer]] and traveled to Hollywood at the studio's expense.<ref name="durgnat">{{cite book |last=Durgnat |first=Raymond |title=Luis Buñuel |publisher=University of California Press |year=1968 |location=Berkeley}}</ref> While in the United States, Buñuel associated with other celebrity expatriates including [[Sergei Eisenstein]], [[Josef von Sternberg]], [[Jacques Feyder]], [[Charles Chaplin]] and [[Bertolt Brecht]].<ref name="brain juice" /> All that was required of Buñuel by his loose-ended contract with MGM was that he "learn some good American technical skills",<ref name="walters">{{cite book |last=Walters |first=Rob |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ciuJ0UTCnmQC&q=luis+bunuel+MGM&pg=PA65 |title=Spread Spectrum: Hedy Lamarr And the Mobile Phone |publisher=BookSurge Publishing |year=2006 |isbn=978-1-4196-2129-1 |location=Great Britain |pages=65}}</ref> but, after being ushered off the first set he visited because the star, [[Greta Garbo]], did not welcome intruders, he decided to stay at home most of the time and only show up to collect his paycheck.<ref name="Doniol-Valcroze">{{cite journal |last1=Doniol-Valcroze |first1=Jacques |last2=Bazin |first2=André |date=July 1954 |title=Entretien avec Luis Buñuel |journal=Cahiers du Cinéma |issue=37 |pages=44–48}}</ref> His only enduring contribution to MGM came when he served as an extra in ''La Fruta Amarga'', a Spanish-language remake of ''[[Min and Bill]]''.<ref name="jarvinen">{{cite book |last=Jarvinen |first=Lisa |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=W10o8udrUakC |title=The Rise of Spanish-Language Filmmaking: Out from Hollywood's Shadow, 1929–1939 |publisher=Rutgers University Press |year=2012 |isbn=978-0-8135-5328-3 |location=Piscataway NJ |pages=58}}</ref> When, after a few months at the studio, he was asked to watch [[Dailies|rushes]] of [[Lili Damita]] to gauge her Spanish accent, he refused and sent a message to studio boss [[Irving Thalberg]] stating that he was there as a Frenchman, not a Spaniard, and he "didn't have time to waste listening to one of the whores".<ref name="bazin">{{cite book |last=Bazin |first=Andre |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=S4mCa7JzhI8C&q=luis+bunuel+damita&pg=PA18 |title=Buņuel, Dreyer, Welles |publisher=Editorial Fundamentos |year=1991 |isbn=978-84-245-0521-9 |location=Madrid}}</ref>{{rp|p.18}} He was back in Spain shortly thereafter.<ref name=durgnat />

=== 1931–1937: Spain ===
<!-- Deleted image removed: [[File:Screen capture of classroom scene from Las Hurdas, Tierra Sin Pan.jpeg|299px|thumb|The classroom scene from ''Las Hurdes: Tierra Sin Pan'' is an ironic statement of Buñuel's Marxist sympathies.<ref name=durgnat />{{rp|p.59}}]]  -->
Spain in the early 1930s was a time of political and social turbulence.<ref name="blinkhorn">{{cite book |last=Blinkhorn |first=Martin |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CnJawWYdjNUC&q=spain+1931+upheaval |title=Democracy And Civil War in Spain 1931–1939 |publisher=Routledge |year=1988 |isbn=978-0-415-00699-6 |location=London |pages=3–31}}</ref> Due to both a surge in anti-clerical sentiment and a longrunning desire for retribution for the corruption and malfeasance of the extreme right and their supporters in the church, Anarchists and [[Radical Socialist Republican Party|Radical Socialists]] sacked [[Monarchism|monarchist]] headquarters in [[Madrid]] and proceeded to burn down or otherwise wreck more than a dozen churches in the capital. Similar revolutionary acts occurred in many other cities in southern and eastern Spain, in most cases with the acquiescence and occasionally with the assistance of the official Republican authorities.<ref name="payne">{{cite book |last=Payne |first=Stanley G. |url=http://libro.uca.edu/payne2/payne25.htm |title=A History of Spain and Portugal, V. 2 |publisher=University of Wisconsin Press |year=1976 |isbn=978-0-299-06284-2 |location=Madison |pages=630}}</ref>

Buñuel's future wife, Jeanne Rucar, recalled that during that period, "he got very excited about politics and the ideas that were everywhere in pre-Civil War Spain".<ref name="rucar de bunuel espanol">{{cite book |last=Rucar de Buñuel |first=Jeanne |author-link=Jeanne Rucar |title=Memorias de un mujer sin piano |publisher=Alianza Editorial |year=1990 |isbn=978-9683903907 |location=Madrid |pages=58}}</ref> In the first flush of his enthusiasm, Buñuel joined the [[Communist Party of Spain]] (PCE) in 1931,<ref name=gubern />{{rp|pp.85–114}} though later in life he denied becoming a Communist.<ref name="aub">{{cite book |last=Aub |first=Max |title=Conversaciones con Buñuel: Seguidas de 45 entrevistas con familiares, amigos y colaboradores del cineasta aragonés |publisher=Aguilar |year=1985 |isbn=978-84-03-09195-5 |location=Madrid}}</ref>{{rp|p.72}}

[[File:Grupo de jurdanos ante la cámara fotográfica, de Venancio Gombau.jpg|thumb|left|Group of Hurdanos early in the 20th century]] 
In 1932, Buñuel was invited to serve as film documentarian for the celebrated ''Mission Dakar-Djibouti'', the first large-scale French anthropological field expedition, which, led by [[Marcel Griaule]], unearthed some 3,500 African artifacts for the new [[Musée de l'Homme]].<ref name="ruoff-45">{{cite journal |last=Ruoff |first=Jeffrey |date=Spring–Summer 1998 |title=An Ethnographic Surrealist Film: Luis Buñuel's Land Without Bread |url=https://www.dartmouth.edu/~jruoff/Articles/EthnographicSurrealist.htm |url-status=dead |journal=Visual Anthropology Review |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=45–57 |doi=10.1525/var.1998.14.1.45 |url-access=subscription |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150521022811/http://www.dartmouth.edu/~jruoff/Articles/EthnographicSurrealist.htm |archive-date=21 May 2015 |access-date=10 January 2016}}</ref> Although he declined, the project piqued his interest in [[ethnography]]. After reading the academic study, ''Las Jurdes: étude de géographie humaine'' (1927) by {{ill|Maurice Legendre|es|Maurice Legendre|fr|Maurice Legendre (historien)|pt|Maurice Legendre}}, he decided to make a film focused on [[peasant]] life in [[Las Hurdes]], perhaps the poorest [[comarca]] in [[Extremadura]], one of Spain's poorest regions.<ref name="margulies">{{cite book |last=Margulies |first=Ivone |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UP3Gf8KfsXwC |title=Rites of Realism: Essays on Corporeal Cinema |publisher=Duke University Press |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-8223-3078-3 |location=Durham, NC |pages=14}}</ref> The film, called ''[[Las Hurdes: Tierra Sin Pan]]'' (1933), was financed on a budget of 20,000 pesetas donated by a working-class [[anarchist]] friend named [[Ramón Acín]], who had won the money in a lottery.<ref name="weir">{{cite book |last=Weir |first=David |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fRR8eWzRhbYC&q=las+hurdes+acin&pg=PA253 |title=Anarchy & Culture: The Aesthetic Politics of Modernism |publisher=University of Massachusetts Press |year=1997 |isbn=978-1-55849-083-3 |location=Amherst |pages=253}}</ref> In the film, Buñuel matches scenes of deplorable social conditions with narration that resembles travelogue commentary delivered by a detached-sounding announcer,<ref name="Harvard Film Archive">{{cite web |title=Buñuel: The Beginning and the End |url=http://hcl.harvard.edu/hfa/films/2011aprjun/bunuel.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150530154225/http://hcl.harvard.edu/hfa/films/2011aprjun/bunuel.html |archive-date=30 May 2015 |access-date=31 July 2012 |publisher=Harvard Film Archive}}</ref> while the soundtrack thunders inappropriate music by [[Johannes Brahms|Brahms]].<ref name="Sloniowski">{{cite journal |last1=Sloniowski |first1=Jeannette |date=Fall 1998 |title="Las Hurdes" and the political efficacy of the grotesque |journal=Canadian Journal of Film Studies |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=30–48 |doi=10.3138/cjfs.7.2.30 |jstor=24402254 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

{{quote box|bgcolor=#CCDDFF|align=right|width=25%|quote=Though the material is organized with masterly skill, the very conception of "art" here seems irrelevant. It is the most profoundly disturbing film I have ever seen.<ref name="tony richardson">{{cite book |last=Richardson |first=Tony |url=https://archive.org/details/worldofluisbunue00luis/page/129 |title="The Films of Luis Buñuel," in The World of Luis Buñuel, ed. Joan Mellen |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=1978 |isbn=978-0-19-502398-5 |location=New York |pages=[https://archive.org/details/worldofluisbunue00luis/page/129 129]}}</ref>  |source=Award-winning film director [[Tony Richardson]] on ''Las Hurdes: Tierra Sin Pan''}}

''Las Hurdes'' was banned by the [[Second Spanish Republic]] and then by the [[Francoist Spain|Francoist dictatorship]].<ref name="Russell">{{cite web |last=Russell |first=Dominique |date=15 April 2005 |title=Luis Buñuel |url=http://sensesofcinema.com/2005/great-directors/bunuel/ |access-date=31 July 2012 |work=Senses of Cinema}}</ref> It is a film which continues to perplex viewers and resists easy categorization by film historians.<ref name="juhasz">{{cite book |last=Juhasz |first=Alexandra |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TXaFokB-qx4C&q=bunuel+las+hurdes+reading+ethnographic |title=F Is For Phony: Fake Documentary And Truth's Undoing |publisher=U of Minnesota Press |year=2006 |isbn=978-0-8166-4251-9 |location=Minneapolis |pages=101}}</ref> ''Las Hurdes'' has been called one of the first examples of [[mockumentary]],<ref name="mockumentary">{{cite web |title=Week 16: Mockumentary |url=http://www.documentarysite.com/?p=101 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130121172356/http://www.documentarysite.com/?p=101 |archive-date=21 January 2013 |access-date=31 July 2012 |website=Documentary film and video course syllabus. |publisher=Documentary Site}}</ref> and has been labeled a "surrealist documentary", a term defined by critic {{interlanguage link|Mercè Ibarz|ca|Mercè Ibarz Ibarz|es||eu||fr}} as "A multi-layered and unnerving use of sound, the juxtaposition of narrative forms already learnt from the written press, travelogues and new pedagogic methods, as well as a subversive use of photographed and filmed documents understood as a basis for contemporary propaganda for the masses".<ref name="ibarz">{{cite book |last=Ibarz |first=Mercè |url=https://archive.org/details/luisbunuelnewrea0000unse/page/28 |title="A Serious Experiment: Land Without Bread, 1933", in Luis Buñuel: New Readings. ed. Isabel Santaolalla and Peter William Evans |publisher=British Film Institute |year=2004 |isbn=978-1-84457-003-4 |location=London |pages=[https://archive.org/details/luisbunuelnewrea0000unse/page/28 28]}}</ref> Catherine Russell has stated that in ''Las Hurdes'', Buñuel was able to reconcile his political philosophy with his surrealist aesthetic, with surrealism becoming "a means of awakening a marxist materialism in danger of becoming a stale orthodoxy".<ref>{{cite book |last=Russell |first=Catherine |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TXaFokB-qx4C |title="Surrealist Ethnography: Las Hurdes and the Documentary Unconscious", in F Is for Phony: Fake Documentary And Truth's Undoing, edited by Alexandra Juhasz and Jesse Lerner |publisher=U of Minnesota Press |year=2006 |isbn=978-0-8166-4251-9 |location=Minneapolis |page=112}}</ref>

After ''Las Hurdes'' in 1933, Buñuel worked in Paris in the [[Dubbing (filmmaking)|dubbing]] department of [[Paramount Pictures]], but following his marriage in 1934, he switched to [[Warner Brothers]] because they operated dubbing studios in Madrid.<ref name="acevedo-munoz">{{cite book |last=Acevedo-Muñoz |first=Ernesto R. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=M-Q1iOxo00wC&q=bunuel+filmofono |title=Buñuel and Mexico: The Crisis of National Cinema |publisher=University of California Press |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-520-23952-4 |location=Berkeley and Los Angeles}}</ref>{{rp|p.39}} A friend, {{interlanguage link|Ricardo Urgoiti|ca||es||eu}}, who owned the commercial film company {{ill|Filmófono|es|Filmófono|eu}}, invited Buñuel to [[Film producer|produce]] films for a mass audience. He accepted the offer, viewing it as an "experiment" as he knew the film industry in Spain was still far behind the technical level of Hollywood or Paris.<ref name="higginbotham">{{cite book |last=Higginbotham |first=Virginia |title=Luis Buñuel |publisher=Twayne Publishers |year=1979 |isbn=978-0-8057-9261-4 |location=New York}}</ref>{{rp|p.56}} According to film historian [[Manuel Rotellar]]'s interviews with members of the cast and crew of the Filmófono studios, Buñuel's only condition was that his involvement with these pictures be completely anonymous, apparently for fear of damaging his reputation as a surrealist.<ref name="rotellar">{{cite journal |last=Rotellar |first=Manuel |year=1978 |title=Luis Buñuel en Filmófono |journal=Cinema 2002 |issue=37 |pages=36–40}}</ref> Rotellar insists, however, "the truth is that it was Luis Buñuel who directed the Filmófono productions".<ref name=rotellar />{{rp|p.37}} [[José Luis Sáenz de Heredia]], the titular director of two of the films created during Buñuel's years as "executive producer" at Filmófono, recounted that it was Buñuel who "explained to me every morning what he wanted...We looked at the takes together and it was Buñuel who chose the shots, and in editing, I wasn't even allowed to be present."<ref name=rotellar />{{rp|p.39}} Of the 18 films produced by Buñuel during his years at Filmófono, the four that are believed by critical consensus to have been directed by him<ref name="mortimore">{{cite journal |last=Mortimore |first=Roger |date=Summer 1975 |title=Buñuel, Sáenz de Heredia, and Filmófono |journal=Sight and Sound |volume=44 |pages=180–182}}</ref> are:
<blockquote>
* ''Don Quintín el amargao'' (Don Quintin the Sourpuss), 1935 – a musical based on [[:es:Don Quintín, el amargao|a play]] by [[Carlos Arniches]],<ref name="fuentes, victor">{{cite book |last=Fuentes |first=Victor |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Mdz1N3xs24IC&q=Don+Quint%C3%ADn+el+amargao+arniches+bunuel&pg=PA57 |title=Los mundos de Buñuel |publisher=[[Ediciones Akal]] |year=2000 |isbn=978-84-460-1450-8 |location=Madrid}}</ref> the first ''[[zarzuela]]'' (a type of Spanish opera) filmed in sound.<ref>{{cite web |title=Don Quintín el Amargao on AllMovie Don Quintín el Amargao (1935) |url=https://www.allmovie.com/movie/don-quint%C3%ADn-el-amargao-v235543 |access-date=2 November 2013 |website=allmovie.com |publisher=AllMovie, a division of All Media Network}}</ref> 
* ''[[Juan Simón's Daughter (1935 film)|La hija de Juan Simón]]'' (Juan Simón's Daughter), 1935 – another musical and a major commercial success<ref name="bentley">{{cite book |last=Bentley |first=Bernard P. E. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=M6kRqqwNMm0C&pg=PA61 |title=A Companion to Spanish Cinema |publisher=Tamesis |year=2008 |isbn=978-1-85566-176-9 |location=Woodbridge, Suffolk |pages=61}}</ref>
* {{ill|¿Quién me quiere a mí?|es|lt=''¿Quién me quiere a mí?''}} (Who Loves Me?), 1936 – a sentimental comedy that Buñuel called "my only commercial failure, and a pretty dismal one at that".<ref name="my last sigh" />{{rp|p.144}}
* ''[[¡Centinela, alerta!]]'', (Sentry, Keep Watch!), 1937 – a comedy and Filmófono's biggest box-office hit.<ref name=bentley />
</blockquote>

During the [[Spanish Civil War]] (1936–1939), Buñuel placed himself at the disposal of the Republican government.<ref name="an unspeakable betrayal">{{cite book |last=Buñuel |first=Luis |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tK3KPgv34U8C |title=An Unspeakable Betrayal: Selected Writings of Luis Buñuel |publisher=University of California Press |year=2002 |isbn=978-0-520-23423-9 |location=Berkeley and Los Angeles}}</ref>{{rp|p.255}} The minister for foreign affairs sent him first to [[Geneva]] (September 1936) and then to Paris<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Gubern |first1=Román |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=elueEkeLL_oC&q=luis+bunuel+in+geneva&pg=PA260 |title=Luis Buñuel: The Red Years, 1929–1939, p.260 |last2=Hammond |first2=Paul |date=4 January 2012 |publisher=University of Wisconsin Pres |isbn=9780299284732 |language=en}}</ref> for two years (1936–38), with official responsibility for cataloging Republican propaganda films.<ref name=edwards />{{rp|p.6}} Besides the cataloguing, Buñuel took left-wing tracts to Spain, did some occasional spying, acted as a bodyguard, and supervised the making of a documentary, entitled ''[[España 1936]]'' in France and {{ill|Espagne 1937|es|lt=''España leal, ¡en armas!''}} in Spain, that covered the elections, the parades, the riots, and the war.<ref name="del olmo">{{cite journal |last=del Olmo |first=F. Javier Ruiz |year=2010 |title=Language and Collective Identity in Buñuel. Propaganda in the Film "España 1936" |journal=Comunicar |volume=XVIII |issue=35 |pages=69–76 |doi=10.3916/C35-2010-02-07 |hdl=10630/4849 |doi-access=free |hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Espana leal, en armas |url=http://explore.bfi.org.uk/4ce2b712e8a58 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140506112908/http://explore.bfi.org.uk/4ce2b712e8a58 |archive-date=6 May 2014 |access-date=6 August 2012 |website=BFI Film Forever |publisher=British Film Institute}}</ref> In August 1936, [[Federico García Lorca]] was shot and killed by Nationalist militia.<ref name="beevor">{{cite book |last=Beevor |first=Antony |url=https://archive.org/details/battleforspainsp00anto/page/100 |title=The Battle for Spain. The Spanish Civil War 1936–1939 |publisher=Penguin Books |year=2006 |isbn=978-0-14-303765-1 |location=London |pages=[https://archive.org/details/battleforspainsp00anto/page/100 100]}}</ref> According to his son, [[Juan Luis Buñuel|Juan Luis]], Buñuel rarely talked about Lorca but mourned the poet's untimely death throughout his life.<ref name="ehrlich">{{cite magazine |last=Ehrlich |first=Linda C. |date=9 July 2009 |title=A Buñuel Scrapbook: The Last Script: Remembering Luis Buñuel (1) and Calanda: 40 Years Later |url=http://sensesofcinema.com/2009/feature-articles/last-script-bunuel-calanda/ |access-date=3 August 2012 |magazine=Senses of Cinema}}</ref>

Buñuel essentially functioned as the coordinator of film propaganda for the Republic, which meant that he was in a position to examine all film shot in the country and decide what sequences could be developed and distributed abroad.<ref name="faber">{{cite web |last=Faber |first=Sebastiaan |date=4 December 2011 |title=Luis Buñuel, chameleon: Revelations from the "Red Decade" |url=http://www.albavolunteer.org/2011/12/luis-bunuel-chameleon-revelations-from-the-%E2%80%9Cred-decade%E2%80%9D/ |access-date=3 August 2012 |website=The Volunteer |publisher=Abraham Lincoln Brigade Archives (ALBA)}}</ref> The Spanish Ambassador suggested that Buñuel revisit Hollywood where he could give technical advice on films being made there about the Spanish Civil War,<ref name=edwards />{{rp|p.6}} so in 1938, he and his family traveled to the United States using funds obtained from his old patrons, the Noailles.<ref name="hoberman">{{cite journal |last=Hoberman |first=J. |date=14 May 2012 |title=A Charismatic Chameleon: On Luis Buñuel |url=http://www.thenation.com/article/167559/charismatic-chameleon-luis-bunuel# |journal=The Nation |access-date=3 August 2012}}</ref> Almost immediately upon his arrival in America, however, the war ended and the [[Motion Picture Association of America|Motion Picture Producers and Distributors Association of America]] discontinued making films on the Spanish conflict.<ref name="robert cole">{{cite book |last=Cole |first=Robert |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Wu_bOQiXGs4C |title=Propaganda, Censorship And Irish Neutrality in the Second World War |publisher=Edinburgh University Press |year=2006 |isbn=978-0-7486-2277-1 |location=Edinburgh |pages=28}}</ref> According to Buñuel's wife, returning to Spain was impossible since the Fascists had seized power,<ref name="rucar de bunuel espanol" />{{rp|p.63–64}} so Buñuel decided to stay in the U.S. indefinitely, stating that he was "immensely attracted by the American naturalness and sociability".<ref name="an unspeakable betrayal" />{{rp|p.255}}

=== 1938–1945: United States ===
[[File:Museum of modern art airways to peace exhibition 1943.jpg|295px|thumb|Museum of Modern Art, 1943. Buñuel was employed at MOMA during WWII, supervising and editing documentaries for Latin
American countries, commissioned by the Committee on Inter-American Affairs headed by [[Nelson Rockefeller]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Bailey |first1=John |title=The Lifelong Sigh of Don Luis Buñuel |url=https://ascmag.com/blog/johns-bailiwick/the-lifelong-sigh-of-don-luis-bunuel |access-date=30 May 2020 |website=American Cinematographer |publisher=American Society of Cinematographers}}</ref>]]
Returning to Hollywood in 1938, he was befriended by [[Frank Davis (producer)|Frank Davis]], an MGM producer and member of the [[Communist Party USA]],<ref name=gubern />{{rp|p.349}} who placed Buñuel on the payroll of ''Cargo of Innocence'', a film about Spanish refugee mothers and children fleeing from [[Bilbao]] to the USSR.<ref name="edwards - lorca etc.">{{cite book |last=Edwards |first=Gwynne |title=Lorca, Buñuel, Dalí: forbidden pleasures and connected lives |publisher=I. B. Tauris |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-84885-007-1 |location=London |pages=194}}</ref> The project was shelved precipitately when another Hollywood film about the Spanish Civil War, ''[[Blockade (1938 film)|Blockade]]'', was met with disfavor by the [[National Legion of Decency|Catholic League of Decency]].<ref name="manchel">{{cite book |last=Manchel |first=Frank |url=https://archive.org/details/filmstudyanalyti0000manc/page/219 |title=Film Study: An Analytical Bibliography, Volume 1 |publisher=Associated University Presses |year=1990 |isbn=978-0-8386-3186-7 |location=Cranbury NJ |pages=[https://archive.org/details/filmstudyanalyti0000manc/page/219 219–220]}}</ref> In the words of biographer Ruth Brandon, Buñuel and his family "lived from one unsatisfactory crumb of work to another" because he "had none of the arrogance and pushiness essential for survival in Hollywood".<ref name=brandon />{{rp|p.358}} He just was not flamboyant enough to capture the attention of Hollywood decision makers, in the opinion of film composer [[George Antheil]]: "Inasmuch as [Buñuel], his wife and his little boy seemed to be such absolutely normal, solid persons, as totally un-Surrealist in the Dalí tradition as one could possibly imagine."<ref name="baxter">{{cite book |last=Baxter |first=John |title=Buñuel |publisher=Carroll & Graf |year=1994 |isbn=978-0-7867-0619-8 |location=New York}}</ref>{{rp|p.172}} For the most part, he was snubbed by many of the people in the film community whom he met during his first trip to America,<ref>{{cite news |date=13 July 2012 |title=A documentary shows the most bitter of Buñuel and intimate portrait |url=http://www.deltaworld.org/cinema/A-documentary-shows-the-most-bitter-of-Bu-uel-and-intimate-portrait/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130414232442/http://www.deltaworld.org/cinema/A-documentary-shows-the-most-bitter-of-Bu-uel-and-intimate-portrait/ |archive-date=14 April 2013 |access-date=8 August 2012 |newspaper=The Delta World.}}</ref> although he was able to sell some gags to Chaplin for ''[[The Great Dictator]]'' (1940).<ref name=taylor />{{rp|p.213}}

In desperation, to market himself to independent producers, he composed a 21-page autobiography, a section of which, headed "My Present Plans", outlined proposals for two documentary films:
* "The Primitive Man", which would depict "the terrible struggle of primitive man against a hostile universe, how the world appeared, ''how they saw it'', what ideas they had on love, on death, on fraternity, how and why religion is born", [italics in original]
* "Psycho-Pathology", which would "expose the origin and development of different psychopathic diseases...Such a documental film, apart from its great scientific interest, could depict on screen a ''New Form of Terror'' or its synonym ''Humour''." [italics in original]<ref name="an unspeakable betrayal" />{{rp|p.257}}

Nobody showed any interest and Buñuel realized that staying in Los Angeles was futile, so he traveled to New York City to see if he could change his fortunes.<ref name=baxter />{{rp|p.174}}

{{quote box|bgcolor=#CCDDFF|align=left|width=25%|quote=Luis Buñuel was there, with his thyroid eyes, the moles on his chin which I remember from so long ago when we first saw the surrealist films in the [[Cinémathèque Française|Cinémathèque]]{{nbsp}}... and as he talked I remember thinking that his paleness was most appropriate for someone who spent his life in dark projection rooms{{nbsp}}... He has a sharp humor, a bitter sarcasm, and at the same time towards women a gentle, special smile.<ref name="Nin">{{cite book |last=Nin |first=Anais |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=igytZ9t8jsAC |title=Diary of Anaïs Nin Volume 3 1939–1944: Vol. 3 (1939–1944) |publisher=Houghton Mifflin Harcourt |year=1969 |isbn=978-0-15-626027-5 |location=New York |pages=109}}</ref> |source=[[Anaïs Nin]], in her diary entry on encountering Buñuel when he was working at MoMA}}
In New York City, Antheil introduced Buñuel to [[Iris Barry]], chief curator of film at the [[Museum of Modern Art]] (MoMA).<ref name=brandon />{{rp|p.360}} Barry talked Buñuel into joining a committee formed to help educate those within the U.S. government who might not have appreciated fully the effectiveness of film as a medium of propaganda. Buñuel was hired to produce a shortened version of [[Leni Riefenstahl]]'s ''[[Triumph of the Will]]'' (1935) as a demonstration project.<ref name="trimborn">{{cite book |last=Trimborn |first=Jürgen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4IFvjEArNg8C |title=Leni Riefenstahl: A Life |publisher=Farrar, Straus and Giroux |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-374-18493-3 |location=New York |pages=123–124}}</ref> The finished product was a compilation of scenes from Riefenstahl's [[Nazism|Nazi]] epic with [[Hans Bertram]]'s ''Feuertaufe''.<ref name=higginbotham />{{rp|p.58}} Buñuel stayed at MoMA to work for the [[Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs]] (OCIAA) as part of a production team that gathered, reviewed and edited films intended as anti-fascist propaganda to be distributed in [[Latin America]] by American embassies.<ref name="schreiber">{{cite book |last=Schreiber |first=Rebecca M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4O1AElNqAZYC&q=bunuel+museum+of+modern+art&pg=PA72 |title=Cold War Exiles in Mexico: U.S. Dissidents and the Culture of Critical Resistance |publisher=Univ of Minnesota Press |year=2008 |isbn=978-0-8166-4308-0 |location=Minneapolis}}</ref>{{rp|p.72}} While being vetted for the job at the OCIAA, upon being asked if he was a Communist, he replied: "I am a Republican," and, apparently, the interviewer did not realize that Buñuel was referring to the Spanish socialist coalition government, not the American political party.<ref name=baxter />{{rp|p.180}} Describing Buñuel's work at MoMA, his friend, composer Gustavo Pittaluga, stated: "Luis created maybe 2,000 remarkable works. We were sent anodyne documentaries, often extremely feeble primary materials, which the Museum team turned into marvellous films. And not just Spanish versions, but also Portuguese, French and English...He would create a good documentary through editing." [italics in original]<ref name="aranda">{{cite book |last=Aranda |first=Francisco |url=https://archive.org/details/luisbunuelcritic0000aran |title=Luis Buñuel: A Critical Biography |publisher=Da Capo Press |year=1976 |isbn=978-0-306-70754-4 |location=New York |url-access=registration}}</ref>{{rp|p.124}}

In 1942, Buñuel applied for American citizenship because he anticipated that MoMA would be put under federal control.<ref name=baxter />{{rp|p.183}} This same year, Dalí published ''[[The Secret Life of Salvador Dalí]]'', in which he made it clear that he had split with Buñuel because the latter was a Communist and an [[atheist]].<ref name="navarro">{{cite book |last=Navarro |first=Vicente |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ShbksjUcH5YC |title="The Jackboot of Dada", in Serpents in the Garden: Liaisons with Culture & Sex, ed. Alexander Cockburn and Jeffery St. Clair |publisher=AK Press |year=2004 |isbn=978-1-902593-94-4 |location=Oakland, CA |pages=148–149}}</ref> News of this reached [[Francis Spellman|Archbishop Spellman]], who angrily confronted Barry with the question: "Are you aware that you are harbouring in this Museum the Antichrist, the man who made a blasphemous film ''L'Age d'Or''?"<ref name="taylor">{{cite book |last=Taylor |first=John Russell |url=https://archive.org/details/strangersinparad00tayl |title=Strangers in paradise: the Hollywood émigrés, 1933–1950 |publisher=Holt, Rinehart & Winston |year=1983 |isbn=978-0-03-061944-1 |location=New York}}</ref>{{rp|p.214}} At the same time, a campaign on the part of Hollywood, through its industry trade paper, the ''[[Motion Picture Herald]]'', to undermine the MoMA film unit resulted in a 66% reduction in the department's budget and Buñuel felt himself compelled to resign.<ref name="robert sitton">{{cite book |last1=Sitton |first1=Robert |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fyMZBQAAQBAJ |title=Lady in the Dark: Iris Barry and the Art of Film |date=2014 |publisher=Columbia University Press |isbn=978-0231165785 |location=New York |page=317 |access-date=16 January 2015}}</ref> In 1944, he returned to Hollywood for the third time, this time as Spanish Dubbing Producer for [[Warner Brothers]].<ref name=baxter />{{rp|p.190}} Before leaving New York City, he confronted Dalí at his hotel, the [[Sherry Netherland Hotel|Sherry Netherland]], to tell the painter about the damage his book had done and then shoot him in the knee.<ref>{{cite web |last1=McRandle |first1=Paul |date=22 February 2013 |title=Buñuel in Yorkville |url=https://surrealistnyc.tumblr.com/post/43719760054/bu%C3%B1uel-in-yorkville |access-date=23 May 2020 |website=Surrealist NYC}}</ref> Buñuel did not carry out the violent part of his plan. Dalí explained himself by saying: "I did not write my book to put YOU on a pedestal. I wrote it to put ME on a pedestal".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Rojas |first1=Carlos |title=El mundo mítico y mágico de Salvador Dalí |date=1985 |publisher=Plaza & Janes |isbn=9788401351259 |location=Barcelona |page=41}}</ref>

[[File:Man Ray 1934.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Man Ray – a friend from Buñuel's surrealist period and collaborator on unrealized Hollywood projects]]
Buñuel's first dubbing assignment on returning to Hollywood was ''[[My Reputation]]'', a [[Barbara Stanwyck]] picture which became ''El Que Diran'' in Buñuel's hands.<ref name=baxter />{{rp|p.190}} In addition to his dubbing work, Buñuel attempted to develop a number of independent projects:
