* In collaboration with an old friend from his Surrealist days, [[Man Ray]], he worked on a scenario called ''The Sewers of Los Angeles'', which took place on a mountain of excrement close to a highway and a dust basin.<ref name=aranda />{{rp|p.129}}
* With his friend, [[José Rubia Barcia]], he co-wrote a screenplay called ''La novia de medianoche'' (The Midnight Bride), a gothic thriller, which lay dormant until it was filmed by Antonio Simón in 1997.<ref>{{cite book |last=Barcia |first=José Rubia |title=Con Luis Buñuel en Hollywood y después |publisher=Ediciós do Castro |year=1992 |isbn=978-84-7492-582-1 |location=Sada, A Coruña |pages=105–160}}</ref>
* He continued working on a screenplay called "Goya and the Duchess of Alba", a treatment he had started as early as 1927, with the actor/producer [[Florián Rey]] and cameraman [[José María Beltrán]], and then resuscitated in 1937 as a project for Paramount.<ref>{{cite book |last=Sánchez Vidal |first=Agustín |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cQbpAAAAIAAJ |title=Góngora, Buñuel, Spanish Avant-Garde and Centenary of Goya's Death, in The Spanish Avant-Garde, ed. Derek Harris |publisher=Manchester University Press |year=1995 |isbn=978-0-7190-4342-0 |location=Manchester |pages=117}}</ref>
* In his autobiography ''Mon Dernier soupir'' (1982, translated in the U.S. as ''My Last Sigh'', 1983, and in the UK as ''My Last Breath'', 1984), Buñuel wrote that, at the request of director [[Robert Florey]], he submitted a treatment of a scene about a disembodied hand, which was later included in the movie ''[[The Beast with Five Fingers]]'' (1946), starring [[Peter Lorre]], without acknowledgement of Buñuel's contribution or payment of any compensation.<ref name="my last sigh" />{{rp|p.189}} However, Brian Taves, film scholar and archivist with the [[Library of Congress]], has challenged the truth of this claim.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Taves |first=Brian |date=Summer 1987 |title=Whose Hand? Correcting a Buñuel myth |journal=Sight and Sound |volume=56 |issue=3 |pages=210–211}}</ref>

In 1945, Buñuel's contract with Warner Brothers expired, and he decided not to renew it in order, as he put it: "to realize my life's ambition for a year: to do nothing".<ref name="bazin cinema of cruelty">{{cite book |last=Bazin |first=André |title=The cinema of cruelty: from Buñuel to Hitchcock |publisher=Seaver Books |year=1982 |isbn=978-0-86579-018-6 |location=New York |pages=89}}</ref> While his family enjoyed themselves at the beach, Buñuel spent much of his time in [[Antelope Valley]] with new acquaintances writer [[Aldous Huxley]] and sculptor [[Alexander Calder]], from whom he rented a house.<ref name=aranda />{{rp|p.130}}

In his autobiography, in a chapter about his second spell in America, Buñuel states that "[o]n several occasions, both American and European producers have suggested that I tackle a film version of [[Malcolm Lowry]]'s ''[[Under the Volcano]]''", but that after reading the book many times as well as eight different screenplays he was unable to come up with a solution for the cinema.<ref name="my last sigh" />{{rp|p.194}} [[Under the Volcano (1984 film)|The movie]] was eventually made in 1984 by [[John Huston]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Maslin |first1=Janet |date=13 June 1984 |title=Under the Volcano |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1984/06/13/movies/film-huston-s-under-the-volcano.html |access-date=22 November 2019 |website=The New York Times}}</ref>

=== 1946–1953: Mexico ===

In 1946, an old friend, producer [[Denise Batcheff|Denise Tual]], the widow of [[Pierre Batcheff]],<ref>{{cite book |last=Pallister |first=Janis L. |url=https://archive.org/details/frenchspeakingwo0000pall/page/93 |title=French-Speaking Women Film Directors: A Guide |publisher=Fairleigh Dickinson Univ Press |year=1997 |isbn=978-0-8386-3736-4 |location=Madison NJ |pages=[https://archive.org/details/frenchspeakingwo0000pall/page/93 93]}}</ref> the [[leading man]] in {{Lang|fr|Un Chien Andalou}}, proposed that she and Buñuel adapt Lorca's play ''[[The House of Bernarda Alba|La casa de Bernarda Alba]]'' for production in Paris.<ref name="camacho">{{cite book |editor-last=Camacho |editor-first=Enrique | others=Essays by Javier Pérez Bazo, Manuel Rodríguez Blanco and Enrique Camacho |title=Buñuel, 100 años : es peligroso asomarse al interior = Buñuel, 100 years : it's dangerous to look inside |publisher=Instituto Cervantes / The Museum of Modern Art |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-8109-6219-4 |location=New York |pages=83}}</ref> As it turned out, though, before they could both make their way to Europe, they encountered problems in securing the rights from Lorca's family.<ref name=bazin />{{rp|p.21}} While in Mexico City, on a stopover, they had asked Óscar Dancigers, a Russian émigré producer active in Mexico, for financing.<ref name=camacho /> Dancigers ran an independent production company that specialized in assisting U.S. film studios with on-location shooting in Mexico, but following World War&nbsp;II, he had lost his connection with Hollywood due to his being [[Hollywood blacklist|blacklisted]] as a Communist.<ref name=schreiber />{{rp|p.73}} Although Dancigers was not enthusiastic about the Lorca project, he did want to work with Buñuel and persuaded the Spanish director to undertake a totally different project.<ref name="my last sigh" />{{rp|p.197}}

[[File:Libertad Lamarque.jpg|thumb|right|135px|Libertad Lamarque, star of Buñuel's first Mexican film. Buñuel was said to have held a long-time grudge against Lamarque because the actress was able to bring him to tears when he viewed a "corny melodrama" which she had made in Argentina: "How could I let myself cry over such an absurd, grotesque, ridiculous scene?"<ref name="bill krohn">{{cite book |last1=Krohn |first1=Bill and Paul Duncan |title=Luis Buñuel: Cinema 1900–1983 |date=2005 |publisher=Taschen |isbn=978-3822833759 |location=Cologne}}</ref>{{rp|p.147}}]]
The [[Golden Age of Mexican cinema]] was peaking in the mid-to-late 1940s, at just the time Buñuel was connecting with Dancigers.<ref name="fein">{{cite journal |last=Fein |first=Seth |year=1994 |title=Hollywood, U.S.-Mexican Relations, and the Devolution of the "Golden Age" of Mexican Cinema |url=http://161.116.18.149/bibliotecaDigital/cinema/filmhistoria/Art.Fein.pdf |url-status=dead |journal=Film-Historia |volume=IV |issue=2 |pages=103–135 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121103004053/http://161.116.18.149/bibliotecaDigital/cinema/filmhistoria/Art.Fein.pdf |archive-date=3 November 2012 |access-date=13 August 2012}}</ref> Movies represented Mexico's third largest industry by 1947, employing 32,000 workers, with 72 film producers who invested 66 million pesos (approximately U.S. $13 million) per year, four active studios with 40 million pesos of invested capital, and approximately 1,500 theaters throughout the nation, with about 200 in Mexico City alone.<ref name="huer">{{cite book |last=Huer |first=Federico |title=La industria cinematográfica mexicana |publisher=Policromía |year=1964 |location=México. DF |pages=48–69}}</ref> For their first project, the two men selected what seemed like a sure-fire success, ''[[Gran Casino]]'', a musical [[period piece]] set in [[Tampico]] during the boom years of oil exploitation, starring two of the most popular entertainers in Latin America: [[Libertad Lamarque]], an Argentine actress and singer, and [[Jorge Negrete]], a Mexican singer and leading man in [[Charro#In cinema|"charro" films]].<ref name="Mira Nouselles">{{cite book |last=Mira Nouselles |first=Alberto |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iZm8wWNXeioC |title=Historical Dictionary of Spanish Cinema |publisher=Scarecrow Press |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-8108-5957-9 |location=Lanham MD}}</ref>{{rp|p.64}} Buñuel recalled: "I kept them singing all the time—a competition, a championship".<ref name=aranda />{{rp|pp.130–131}}

The film was not successful at the box office, with some even calling it a fiasco.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Estève |first=Michel |year=1963 |title=Luis Buñuel |journal=Études Cinématographiques |issue=20–21 |pages=82}}</ref> Different reasons have been given for its failure with the public; for some, Buñuel was forced to make concessions to the bad taste of his stars, particularly Negrete,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Martínez Herranz |first=Amparo |year=2002 |title=Gran Casino de Luis Buñuel |journal=Artigrama |issue=17 |pages=525}}</ref> others cite Buñuel's rusty technical skills<ref name="fuentes discourse">{{cite journal |last=Fuentes |first=Víctor |date=Winter–Spring 2004 |title=Buñuel's Cinematic Narrative and the Latin American New Novel |journal=Discourse |volume=26 |issue=1 & 2 |pages=92 |doi=10.1353/dis.2005.0013}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=García Riera |first=Emilio |title=Historia documental del cine mexicano. Vol. 3 |publisher=Era |year=1969 |isbn=978-968-895-343-3 |location=Mexico |pages=90}}</ref> and lack of confidence after so many years out of the director's chair,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Charity |first=Tom |date=December 2007 |title=Luis Buñuel: Two-Disc Collector's Edition |journal=Sight and Sound |volume=17 |issue=12 |pages=105}}</ref> while still others speculate that Mexican audiences were tiring of genre movies, called "churros", that were perceived as being cheaply and hastily made.<ref name=acevedo-munoz />{{rp|p.48}}<ref>{{cite journal |last=Mraz |first=John |date=February 1984 |title=Mexican Cinema: Of churros and charros |url=http://www.ejumpcut.org/archive/onlinessays/JC29folder/MexFilmBook.html |journal=Jump Cut |issue=29 |pages=23}}</ref>

The failure of ''Gran Casino'' sidelined Buñuel, and it was over two years before he had the chance to direct another picture.<ref>{{cite book |last=Paranaguá |first=Paulo Antonio |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=U7wuAAAAYAAJ&q=bunuel+gran+casino+failure |title=Mexican Cinema |publisher=British Film Institute |year=1995 |isbn=978-0-85170-516-3 |location=London |pages=202}}</ref> According to Buñuel, he spent this time "scratching my nose, watching flies and living off my mother's money",<ref name="my last sigh" />{{rp|p.199}} but he was actually somewhat more industrious than that may sound. With the husband/wife team of Janet and [[Luis Alcoriza]], he wrote the scenario for ''Si usted no puede, yo sí'', which was filmed in 1950 by [[Julián Soler]].<ref name=baxter />{{rp|p.203}} He also continued developing the idea for a surrealistic film called ''Ilegible, hijo de flauta'', with the poet [[Juan Larrea (poet)|Juan Larrea]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Gurney |first=Robert |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jYOIwLxBLfMC |title="Juan Larrea and the Film Buñuel Did Not Make", in Companion to Spanish Surrealism, ed. Robert Havard |publisher=Tamesis Books |year=2004 |isbn=978-1-85566-104-2 |location=Woodbridge, Suffolk |pages=49}}</ref> Dancigers pointed out to him that there was currently public interest in films about street urchins, so Buñuel scoured the back streets and slums of Mexico City in search of material, interviewing social workers about street gang warfare and murdered children.<ref name=baxter />{{rp|pp.203–204}}

During this period, Dancigers was busy producing films for the actor/director [[Fernando Soler]], one of the most durable of Mexican film personalities, having been referred to as the "national paterfamilias".<ref>{{cite book |last=Stock |first=Ann Marie |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2VFTpFmrV5cC |title=Framing Latin American Cinema: Contemporary Critical Perspectives |publisher=University of Minnesota Press |year=1997 |isbn=978-0-8166-2972-5 |location=Minneapolis |pages=213}}</ref> Although Soler typically preferred to direct his own films, for their next collaboration, ''[[El Gran Calavera]]'', based on a play by Adolfo Torrado, he decided that doing both jobs would be too much trouble, so he asked Dancigers to find someone who could be trusted to handle the technical aspects of the directorial duties.<ref name="cine mexicano">{{cite web |title=El gran calavera (1949) |url=http://cinemexicano.mty.itesm.mx/peliculas/gran_calavera.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120421140309/http://cinemexicano.mty.itesm.mx/peliculas/gran_calavera.html |archive-date=21 April 2012 |access-date=16 August 2012 |website=Más de Cien Años de Cine Mexicano |publisher=Cine Club – Cine Mexicano}}</ref> Buñuel welcomed the opportunity, stating that: "I amused myself with the montage, the constructions, the angles...All of that interested me because I was still an apprentice in so-called 'normal' cinema."<ref name="cine mexicano" /> As a result of his work on this film, he developed a technique for making films cheaply and quickly by limiting them to 125 shots.<ref name=schreiber />{{rp|p.73}} ''El Gran Calavera'' was completed in 16 days at a cost of 400,000 pesos (approximately $46,000 US at 1948 exchange rates).<ref name=acevedo-munoz />{{rp|p.52}} The picture has been described as "a hilarious screwball send-up of the Mexican [[nouveau riche]]...a wild roller coaster of mistaken identity, sham marriages and misfired suicides",<ref name ="Harvard.edu" /> and it was a big hit at the box office in Mexico.<ref>{{cite book |last=Dent |first=David W. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HkiJlXXbAy4C |title=Encyclopedia of Modern Mexico |publisher=Scarecrow Press |year=2002 |isbn=978-0-8108-4291-5 |location=Lanham MD |pages=28}}</ref> In 2013, the picture was re-made by Mexican director Gary Alazraki under the title ''[[The Noble Family]]''.<ref>{{cite web |last1=de las Carreras |first1=María Elena |title=El gran calavera (The Great Madcap, 1949), directed by Luis Buñuel |url=https://www.laconservancy.org/sites/default/files/files/GranCalavera_EssayDeLasCarreras.pdf |access-date=30 September 2014 |publisher=The Los Angeles Conservancy}}</ref> In 1949, Buñuel renounced his Spanish citizenship to become a [[Naturalization|naturalized]] [[Mexican citizenship|Mexican]] however different sources stated that he retained his Spanish citizenship along with the Mexican one although remains largely disputed, since it was kept private from the public eye.<ref>{{cite news |last=Pulver |first=Andrew |date=29 March 2011 |title=A short history of Spanish cinema |url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/filmblog/2011/mar/29/short-history-spanish-cinema |access-date=1 September 2012 |work=newEurope |publisher=Guardian News and Media |location=London}}</ref>

The commercial success of ''El Gran Calavera'' enabled Buñuel to redeem a promise he had extracted from Dancigers, which was that if Buñuel could deliver a money-maker, Dancigers would guarantee "a degree of freedom" on the next film project.<ref name=Doniol-Valcroze /> Knowing that Dancigers was uncomfortable with experimentalism, especially when it might affect the bottom line, Buñuel proposed a commercial project titled ''¡Mi huerfanito jefe!'', about a juvenile street vendor who can't sell his final lottery ticket, which ends up being the winner and making him rich.<ref>{{cite web |title=Los olvidados (1950) |url=http://cinemexicano.mty.itesm.mx/peliculas/olvidados.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120717025021/http://cinemexicano.mty.itesm.mx/peliculas/olvidados.html |archive-date=17 July 2012 |access-date=20 August 2012 |website=Las 100 mejores películas del cine mexicano: 2 |publisher=Cine Club – Cine Mexicano}}</ref> Dancigers was open to the idea, but instead of a "''[[feuilleton]]''", he suggested making "something rather more serious".<ref name="ibanez and palacio">{{cite book |last=Ibañez |first=Juan Carlos and Manuel Palacio |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hx5VfnjrGLUC |title="Los Olvidados/The Young and the Damned", in The Cinema of Latin America, ed. Alberto Elena and Marina Díaz López |publisher=Columbia University Press |year=2003 |isbn=978-1-903364-84-0 |location=New York}}</ref>{{rp|p.60}} During his recent researches through the slums of Mexico City, Buñuel had read a newspaper account of a twelve-year-old boy's body being found on a garbage dump, and this became the inspiration, and final scene, for the film, eventually called ''[[Los Olvidados]]''.<ref name="de la colina" />{{rp|pp.53–54}}

{{quote box|bgcolor=#CCDDFF|align=left|width=25%|quote=The world doesn't work like Hollywood told us it does, and Buñuel knew well that poverty's truths could not be window-dressed in any way. This film continues to provoke reactions for its unapologetic portrayal of life without hope or trust. It stands out among Buñuel's works as the moment when he broke surface and bellowed, before sinking back into the world of the privileged where his surreal view most loved to play.<ref>{{cite news |last=Pierre |first=DBC |date=16 February 2007 |title=The lost boys |url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2007/feb/17/film |access-date=20 August 2012 |work=The Guardian, 16 February 2007 |location=London}}</ref>  |source=[[Booker Prize]] winning author [[DBC Pierre]] on ''Los Olvidados''}}
The film tells the story of a street gang of children who terrorize their impoverished neighborhood, at one point brutalizing a blind man<ref>{{cite thesis | last=Villarreal | first=Rachel Kram | title=Gladiolas for the Children of Sanchez: Ernesto P. Uruchurtu's Mexico City, 1950-1968 | publisher=The University of Arizona | date=2008 | url=https://repository.arizona.edu/handle/10150/195062 | degree=PhD | access-date=2026-02-23}}</ref> and at another assaulting a legless man who moves around on a dolly, which they toss down a hill.<ref name="ed gonzalez">{{cite magazine |last=Gonzalez |first=Ed |title=Los Olvidados **** |url=https://www.slantmagazine.com/film/review/los-olvidados/208 |access-date=20 August 2012 |magazine=Slant Magazine}}</ref> Film historian Carl J. Mora has said of ''Los Olvidados'' that the director "visualized poverty in a radically different way from the traditional forms of Mexican melodrama. Buñuel's street children are not 'ennobled' by their desperate struggle for survival; they are in fact ruthless predators who are not better than their equally unromanticized victims".<ref name="mora">{{cite book |last=Mora |first=Carl J. |url=https://archive.org/details/mexicancinemaref00mora |title=Mexican Cinema: Reflections of a Society |publisher=University of California Press |year=1982 |isbn=978-0-520-04304-6 |location=Berkeley and Los Angeles}}</ref>{{rp|p.91}} The film was made quickly (18 days) and cheaply (450,000 pesos), with Buñuel's fee being the equivalent of $2,000.<ref name=baxter />{{rp|pp.210–211}} During filming, a number of members of the crew resisted the production in a variety of ways: one technician confronted Buñuel and asked why he didn't make a "real" Mexican movie "rather than a miserable picture like this one";<ref name="my last sigh" />{{rp|p.200}} the film's hairdresser quit on the spot over a scene in which the protagonist's mother refuses to give him food ("In Mexico, no mother would say that to her son.");<ref name="mraz nacho lopez">{{cite book |last=Mraz |first=John |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=e4f6kkFbbJQC |title=Nacho Lopez, Mexican Photographer |publisher=University of Minnesota Press |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-8166-4047-8 |location=Minneapolis}}</ref>{{rp|p.99}} another staff member urged Buñuel to abandon shooting on a "garbage heap", noting that there were many "lovely residential neighborhoods like [[Lomas de Chapultepec|Las Lomas]]" that were available;<ref name="mraz nacho lopez" />{{rp|p.99}} while Pedro de Urdimalas, one of the scriptwriters, refused to allow his name in the credits.<ref>{{cite web |title=Pedro de Urdimalas |url=http://www.sacm.org.mx/archivos/biografias.asp?txtSocio=08285&offset=0 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140506103309/http://www.sacm.org.mx/archivos/biografias.asp?txtSocio=08285&offset=0 |archive-date=6 May 2014 |access-date=21 August 2012 |publisher=Sociedad de Autores y Compositores de México (SACM)}}</ref>

[[File:Paz0.jpg|thumb|right|155px|Octavio Paz, ardent champion of ''Los Olvidados'' and close friend during Buñuel's exile in Mexico<ref>{{cite book |last=Caistor |first=Nick |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OkPr_MWp2wMC |title=Octavio Paz |publisher=Reaktion Books |year=2007 |isbn=978-1-86189-303-1 |location=London |page=36}}</ref>]]
This hostility was also felt by those who attended the movie's première in Mexico City on 9 November 1950, when ''Los Olvidados'' was taken by many as an insult to Mexican sensibilities and to the Mexican nation.<ref name=acevedo-munoz />{{rp|p.67}} At one point, the audience shrieked in shock as one of the characters looked straight into the camera and hurled a rotten egg at it, leaving a gelatinous, opaque ooze on the lens for a few moments.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Faber |first=Sebastiaan |year=2012 |title=Buñuel's Impure Modernism |journal=Modernist Cultures |volume=7 |issue=1 |pages=56–76 |doi=10.3366/mod.2012.0028}}</ref> In his memoir, Buñuel recalled that after the initial screening, the painter [[Frida Kahlo]] refused to speak to him, while poet [[León Felipe]]'s wife had to be restrained physically from attacking him.<ref name="my last sigh" />{{rp|pp.200–201}} There were even calls to have Buñuel's Mexican citizenship revoked.<ref name="de la colina" />{{rp|p.61}} Dancigers, panicked by what he feared would be a complete debacle, quickly commissioned an alternate "happy" ending to the film,<ref name="unesco">{{cite web |title=Nomination Form, Memory of the World Register |url=https://media.unesco.org/sites/default/files/webform/mow001/los_olvidados.pdf |access-date=27 February 2025 |publisher=UNESCO}}</ref> and also tacked on a preface showing stock footage of the skylines of New York City, London and Paris with voice-over commentary to the effect that behind the wealth of all the great cities of the world can be found poverty and malnourished children, and that Mexico City "that large modern city, is no exception".<ref>{{cite book |last=Ross |first=John |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=psHQERn0VMcC |title=El Monstruo: Dread and Redemption in Mexico City |publisher=Nation Books |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-56858-424-9 |location=New York |pages=203}}</ref> Regardless, attendance was so poor that Dancigers withdrew the film after only three days in theaters.<ref name="berg los olvidados">{{cite web |last=Berg |first=Charles Ramírez |title=Los Olvidados (1950) |url=http://www.austinfilm.org/page.aspx?pid=1692 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130414101344/http://www.austinfilm.org/page.aspx?pid=1692 |archive-date=14 April 2013 |access-date=30 August 2012 |website=Essential Cinema |publisher=Austin Film Society}}</ref>

Through the efforts of future Nobel Prize for Literature laureate [[Octavio Paz]], who at the time was in Mexico's diplomatic service, ''Los Olvidados'' was chosen to represent Mexico at the [[Cannes Film Festival]] of 1951, and Paz promoted the film assiduously by distributing a supportive manifesto<ref>{{cite news |last=Paz |first=Octavio |date=29 September 1983 |title=Cannes, 1951. Los olvidados |url=http://elpais.com/diario/1983/09/29/opinion/433638005_850215.html |access-date=30 August 2012 |newspaper=El País}}</ref> and parading outside the cinema with a placard.<ref>{{cite book |last=Wilson |first=Jason |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6wk4AAAAIAAJ |title=Octavio Paz, a Study of His Poetics |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1979 |isbn=978-0-521-22306-5 |location=Cambridge |pages=25}}</ref> Opinion in general was enthusiastic, with the Surrealists (Breton and poet [[Jacques Prévert]]) and other artistic intellectuals (painter [[Marc Chagall]] and poet/dramatist/filmmaker [[Jean Cocteau]]) laudatory, but the communist critic Georges Sadoul objected to what he saw as the film's "bourgeois morality" because of its positive depictions of a "bourgeois teacher" and a "bourgeois state" in rehabilitating street children, as well as a scene in which the police demonstrate their utility by stopping a pederast from assaulting a child.<ref>{{cite web |last=Garmendia |first=Arturo |date=27 January 2010 |title=La batalla por 'Los Olvidados' de Buñuel |url=http://www.cineforever.com/2010/01/27/la-batalla-por-los-olvidados-de-bunuel/ |access-date=31 August 2012 |work=Cineforever}}</ref> Buñuel won the Best Director prize that year at Cannes, and also won the [[International Federation of Film Critics|FIPRESCI International Critics' Award]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Steffen |first=James |title=Los Olvidados |url=https://www.tcm.com/this-month/article/93547 |website=Turner Classic Movies Film Article |publisher=Turner Entertainment Networks}}</ref> The film was reissued in Mexico where it ran for two months to much greater acceptance and profit.<ref>{{cite book |last=Faber |first=Sebastiaan |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WAY693mPUWsC |title=Exile and Cultural Hegemony: Spanish Intellectuals in Mexico, 1939–1975 |publisher=Vanderbilt University Press |year=2002 |isbn=978-0-8265-1422-6 |location=Nashville |pages=xiv}}</ref> ''Los Olvidados'' and its triumph at Cannes made Buñuel a celebrity and the most important Spanish-speaking film director in the world.<ref>{{cite book |last=Gazetas |first=Aristides |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CPuZ-2UtVRwC |title=An Introduction to World Cinema |publisher=McFarland |year=2008 |isbn=978-0-7864-3907-2 |location=Jefferson NC |pages=198}}</ref> In 2003, ''Los Olvidados'' was inscribed by [[UNESCO]] in the [[Memory of the World Programme#Memory of the World Register|Memory of the World International Register]], calling it: "the most important document in Spanish about the marginal lives of children in contemporary large cities".<ref>{{cite web |title=Los olvidados |url=https://www.unesco.org/en/memory-world/los-olvidados |access-date=27 February 2025 |publisher=UNESCO Memory of the World}}</ref>

{{quote box|bgcolor=#CCDDFF|align=right|width=25%|quote=Here in Mexico, I have become a professional in the film world. Until I came here I made a film the way a writer makes a book, and on my friends' money at that. I am very grateful and happy to have lived in Mexico, and I have been able to make my films here in a way I could not have in any other country in the world. It is quite true that in the beginning, caught up by necessity, I was forced to make cheap films. But I never made a film which went against my conscience or my convictions. I have never made a superficial, uninteresting film.<ref>{{cite journal |year=1963 |title=Interview with Wilfried Berghahn |journal=Filmkritik |issue=5}}</ref>  |source= – Luis Buñuel on his mid-century career in Mexico. }}
Buñuel remained in Mexico for the rest of his life, although he spent periods of time filming in France and Spain. In Mexico, he filmed 21 films over 18 years. For many critics, although there were occasional widely acknowledged masterpieces like ''Los Olvidados'' and ''[[Él (film)|Él]]'' (1953), the majority of his output consisted of generic fare which was adapted to the norms of the national film industry, frequently adopting melodramatic conventions that appealed to local tastes.<ref name="lim">{{cite news |last1=Lim |first1=Dennis |date=8 February 2009 |title=Mexican-era Luis Buñuel |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2009-feb-08-ca-secondlook8-story.html |access-date=20 September 2014 |work=Los Angeles Times}}</ref> Other commentators, however, have written of the deceptive complexity and intensity of many of these films, arguing that, collectively, they, "bring a philosophical depth and power to his cinema, together offering a sustained meditation on ideas of religion, class inequity, violence and desire".<ref name ="Harvard.edu" /> Although Buñuel usually had little choice regarding the selection of these projects,<ref name="Delmas">{{cite journal |last1=Delmas |first1=Jean |date=February 1966 |title=Buñuel, Citizen of Mexico |journal=Jeune Cinema |issue=12}}</ref> they often deal with themes that were central to his lifelong concerns:<ref name="adler">{{cite news |last1=Adler |first1=Renata |date=21 June 1968 |title=Screen: Bunuel's Relentless 'Nazarin':Film Set in the Mexico of Porfirio Diaz |url=https://www.nytimes.com/movie/review?res=9C02E1D7163AE134BC4951DFB0668383679EDE |access-date=27 September 2014 |work=The New York Times}}</ref> 
* sexual pathology:<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gutierrez-Albill |first1=Julian Daniel |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=E38AAwAAQBAJ |title=Queering Buñuel: Sexual Dissidence and Psychoanalysis in His Mexican and Spanish Cinema |date=2008 |publisher=I.B.Tauris |isbn=9781845116682 |location=London |pages=59–62 |access-date=27 September 2014}}</ref> ''Él'' (1953), ''[[Ensayo de un crimen]]'' (1955), and ''[[Wuthering Heights (1954 film)|Abismos de pasión]]'' (1954)
*the destructive effects of rampant [[machismo]]:<ref>{{cite book |last1=Evans |first1=Peter William |title=The Films of Luis Buñuel. Subjectivity and Desire |date=1995 |publisher=Clarendon Press |isbn=978-0198159063 |location=Oxford |page=143}}</ref> ''[[El Bruto]]'', (1953), ''[[El río y la muerte]]'', (1955); 
*the blurring of fantasy and reality:<ref>{{cite web |title=Luis Buñuel's Cinema of Entrapment in the Age of Cowardice: The Search for a Greater Truth |url=http://users.hal-pc.org/~questers/JAVA/fire/Bunuel.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402034318/http://users.hal-pc.org/~questers/JAVA/fire/Bunuel.html |archive-date=2 April 2015 |access-date=27 September 2014 |publisher=Gregory and Maria Pearse}}</ref> ''[[Subida al cielo]]'' (1952), ''[[La ilusión viaja en tranvía]]'' (1954); 
*the disruptive status of women in a male-dominated culture:<ref>{{cite web |last1=Muñoz |first1=Sara |title=La construcción femenina en el discurso cinematográfico de Buñuel: la femme fatale |url=http://www.hispanetjournal.com/4Surrealfemme-EDITADO.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160812011205/http://www.hispanetjournal.com/4Surrealfemme-EDITADO.pdf |archive-date=12 August 2016 |access-date=27 September 2014 |website=Hispanet Journal 2}}</ref> ''[[Susana (film)|Susana]]'' (1951), ''[[La hija del engaño]]'' (1951—a remake of the Filmófono production ''Don Quintín el amargao'' of 16 years earlier),<ref>{{cite web |title=La hija del engaño (1951) |url=http://cinemexicano.mty.itesm.mx/peliculas/hija_enganio.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171012084702/http://cinemexicano.mty.itesm.mx/peliculas/hija_enganio.html |archive-date=12 October 2017 |access-date=1 October 2014 |website=Más de Cien Años de Cine Mexicano |publisher=Maximiliano Maza}}</ref> ''[[Una mujer sin amor]]'' (1952); and
*the absurdity of the religious life:<ref name=edwards />{{rp|pp.118–19}} ''[[Nazarín]]'' (1959) and ''Simón del desierto'' (1965).

[[Pauline Kael]] says of Buñuel that "at his most indifferent" he is sometimes at his best  and most original, as seen in parts of ''Nazarin.''<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kael| first=Pauline |title=The Age of Movies: Selected Writings of Pauline Kael (paperback) |url=https://www.loa.org/books/348-the-age-of-movies-selected-writings-of-pauline-kael-paperback/ |access-date=7 October 2025 |website=Library of America |page=236 |language=en-US}}</ref>

As busy as he was during the 1950s and early 1960s, there were still many film projects that Buñuel had to abandon due to lack of financing or studio support, including a cherished plan to film Mexican novelist [[Juan Rulfo]]'s ''[[Pedro Páramo]]'', of which he enjoyed "the crossing from the mysterious to the real, almost without transition. I really like this mixture of reality and fantasy, but I don't know how to bring it to the screen."<ref>{{cite book |last=Poniatowska |first=Elena |title=Palabras cruzadas |publisher=Ediciones Era |year=1961 |location=Mexico City |pages=191}}</ref> Other unrealized projects during his lifetime included adaptations of [[André Gide]]'s ''Les caves du Vatican''; [[Benito Pérez Galdós]]'s ''[[Fortunata y Jacinta]]'', ''[[Doña Perfecta]]'' and ''Ángel Guerra''; [[Evelyn Waugh]]'s ''[[The Loved One (book)|The Loved One]]''; [[William Golding]]'s ''[[Lord of the Flies]]''; [[Dalton Trumbo]]'s ''[[Johnny Got His Gun]]''; [[J. K. Huysmans]]'s ''[[Là-bas (novel)|Là-Bas]]''; [[Matthew Lewis (writer)|Matthew Lewis]]'s ''[[The Monk]]''; [[José Donoso]]'s ''[[Hell Has No Limits|Lugar sin límites]]''; a film of four stories based on [[Carlos Fuentes]]'s ''[[Aura (Fuentes)|Aura]]''; and [[Julio Cortázar]]'s ''[[Final del juego|Las ménades]]''.<ref name="fuentes discourse" />{{rp|p.96}}

=== 1954–1965: International work ===
[[File:Michel Piccoli Cannes.jpg|thumb|upright|left|[[Michel Piccoli]]. The popular French film star appeared in six Buñuel films, beginning with ''[[Death in the Garden|La Mort en ce jardin]]'', 1956. ]]
As much as he welcomed steady employment in the Mexican film industry, Buñuel was quick to seize opportunities to re-emerge onto the international film scene and to engage with themes that were not necessarily focused on Mexican preoccupations.<ref name=acevedo-munoz />{{rp|p.144}} His first chance came in 1954, when Dancigers partnered with Henry F. Ehrlich, of [[United Artists]], to co-produce a film version of [[Daniel Defoe]]'s ''[[Robinson Crusoe]]'', using a script developed by the Canadian writer [[Hugo Butler]]. The film was produced by George Pepper, the former executive secretary of the Hollywood Democratic Committee. Both Butler and Pepper were emigres from Hollywood who had run afoul of authorities seeking out communists.<ref name=schreiber />{{rp|p.75}}<ref>{{cite web |last=Travers |first=James |date=27 October 2017 |title=Review of the film The Young One (1960) |url=http://www.filmsdefrance.com/review/the-young-one-1960.html |access-date=27 October 2017}}</ref> The result, ''[[Adventures of Robinson Crusoe]]'', was Buñuel's first color film.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Gonzalez |first1=Ed |date=16 July 2002 |title=The Adventures of Robinson Crusoe |url=https://www.slantmagazine.com/film/review/the-adventures-of-robinson-crusoe |access-date=28 September 2014 |website=Slant Magazine}}</ref> Buñuel was given much more time than usual for the filming (three months), which was accomplished on location in Manzanillo, a Pacific seaport with a lush jungle interior, and was shot simultaneously in English and Spanish.<ref name="axmaker robinson crusoe">{{cite web |last1=Axmaker |first1=Sean |title=Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1954) |url=https://www.tcm.com/tcmdb/title/66823/adventures-of-robinson-crusoe#articles-reviews |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130310120515/http://www.tcm.com/tcmdb/title/66823/Adventures-of-Robinson-Crusoe/#articles-reviews |url-status=dead |archive-date=10 March 2013 |access-date=28 September 2014 |website=Turner Classic Movies |publisher=Turner Entertainment Networks}}</ref> When the film was released in the United States, its young star [[Dan O'Herlihy]] used his own money to fund a Los Angeles run for the film and gave free admission to all members of the [[Screen Actors Guild]], who in turn rewarded the little-known actor with his only [[Oscar award|Oscar]] nomination.<ref name="axmaker robinson crusoe" />

In the mid-1950s, Buñuel got the chance to work again in France on international co-productions. The result was what critic [[Raymond Durgnat]] has called the director's "revolutionary triptych", in that each of the three films is "openly, or by implication, a study in the morality and tactics of armed revolution against a right-wing dictatorship".<ref name=durgnat />{{rp|p.100}} The first, ''[[Cela s'appelle l'aurore]]'' (Franco-Italian, 1956) required Buñuel and the "[['Pataphysics|pataphysical]]" writer [[Jean Ferry]] to adapt a novel by [[Emmanuel Roblès]] after the celebrated writer [[Jean Genet]] failed to deliver a script after having been paid in full.<ref name=aranda />{{rp|p.100}} The second film was ''[[Death in the Garden|La Mort en ce jardin]]'' (Franco-Mexican, 1956), which was adapted by Buñuel and his frequent collaborator [[Luis Alcoriza]] from a novel by the Belgian writer [[José-André Lacour]]. The final part of the "triptych" was ''[[La Fièvre Monte à El Pao]]'' (Franco-Mexican, 1959), the last film of the popular French star [[Gérard Philipe]], who died in the final stages of the production.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Canby |first1=Vincent |date=12 February 1988 |title=Film: From Bunuel, 'Los Ambiciosos,' at the Public |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1988/02/12/movies/film-from-bunuel-los-ambiciosos-at-the-public.html |access-date=30 September 2014 |work=The New York Times}}</ref> At one point during the filming, Buñuel asked Philipe, who was visibly dying of cancer, why the actor was making this film, and Philipe responded by asking the director the same question, to which both said they did not know.<ref name="hagopian">{{cite web |last1=Hagopian |first1=Kevin |title=Fever Mounts in El Pao |url=http://www.albany.edu/writers-inst/webpages4/filmnotes/fnf02n11.html |access-date=30 September 2014 |website=New York State Writers Institute |publisher=Writers Institute}}</ref> Buñuel was later to explain that he was so strapped for cash that he, "took everything that was offered to me, as long as it wasn't humiliating".<ref name=hagopian />

In 1960, Buñuel re-teamed with scenarist Hugo Butler and organizer George Pepper, allegedly his favorite producer, to make his second English-language film, a US/Mexico co-production called ''[[The Young One]]'', based on a short story by writer and former CIA-agent [[Peter Matthiessen]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Bunuel |first1=Luis |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hZuzxKQfhYUC&q=pepper&pg=PA191 |title=My Last Sigh: The Autobiography of Luis Bunuel |date=26 March 2013 |publisher=Knopf Doubleday Publishing |isbn=9780345803719}}</ref> This film has been called "a surprisingly uncompromising study of racism and sexual desire, set on a remote island in the Deep South"<ref name ="Harvard.edu" /> and has been described by critic Ed Gonzalez as "salacious enough to make [[Elia Kazan]]'s ''[[Baby Doll]]'' and [[Louis Malle|Luis Malle]]'s ''[[Pretty Baby (1978 film)|Pretty Baby]]'' blush".<ref name="The Young One 4 out of 4">{{cite web |last1=Gonzalez |first1=Ed |date=8 November 2005 |title=The Young One 4 out of 4 |url=https://www.slantmagazine.com/film/review/the-young-one |access-date=30 September 2014 |website=Slant Magazine}}</ref> Although the film won a special award at the Cannes Film Festival for its treatment of racial discrimination,<ref name=bentley />{{rp|p.151}} the US critics were so hostile upon its release that Buñuel was later to say that "a Harlem newspaper even wrote that I should be hung upside down from a lamppost on Fifth Avenue...I made this film with love, but it never had a chance."<ref>{{cite web |last=Rosenbaum |first=Jonathan | author-link=Jonathan Rosenbaum | title=The Young One: Buñuel's Neglected Masterpiece |url=http://www.jonathanrosenbaum.net/2009/07/22909/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141006084401/http://www.jonathanrosenbaum.net/2009/07/22909/ |archive-date=6 October 2014 |access-date=30 September 2014 |website=jonathanrosenbaum.net}}</ref>

At the 1960 Cannes Festival, Buñuel was approached by the young director [[Carlos Saura]], whose film ''[[The Delinquents (1960 film)|Los Golfos]]'' had been entered officially to represent Spain.<ref>{{cite web |title=Los Golfos |url=http://www.festival-cannes.com/en/archives/ficheFilm/id/3299/year/1960.html |access-date=4 October 2014 |work=Festival de Cannes}}</ref> Two years earlier, Saura had partnered with [[Juan Antonio Bardem]] and [[Luis García Berlanga]] to form a production company called UNINCI,<ref name="andrew whittaker">{{cite book |last1=Whittaker |first1=Andrew |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2rZS8SWMroUC |title=Speak the Culture: Spain: Be Fluent in Spanish Life and Culture |date=2008 |publisher=Thorogood Publishing |isbn=978-1854186058 |location=London |page=225 |access-date=4 October 2014}}</ref> and the group was keen to get Buñuel to make a new film in his native country as part of their overall goal of creating a uniquely Spanish brand of cinema.<ref name=aranda />{{rp|p.190–91}} At the same time, Mexican actress [[Silvia Pinal]] was eager to work with Buñuel and talked her producer-husband [[Gustavo Alatriste]] into providing additional funding for the project with the understanding that the director, who Pinal described as "a man worshiped and idolized", would be given "absolute freedom" in carrying out the work.<ref name="agustin de gracia">{{cite news |last1=de Gracia |first1=Agustín |date=31 July 2013 |title=Recuerdan a Luis Buñuel a 30 años de su fallecimiento |url=http://www.laopinion.com/entretenimientocine/article/20130731/Recuerdan-a-Luis-Bunuel-a-30-anos-de-su-fallecimiento&template=print |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141006094142/http://www.laopinion.com/entretenimientocine/article/20130731/Recuerdan-a-Luis-Bunuel-a-30-anos-de-su-fallecimiento%26template%3Dprint |archive-date=6 October 2014 |access-date=4 October 2014 |work=laopinion.com}}</ref> Finally, Buñuel agreed to work again in Spain when further support was provided by producer [[Pere Portabella]]'s company ''Film 59''.<ref name="pere portabella">{{cite web |title=Pere Portabella |url=http://www.moma.org/visit/calendar/films/556 |access-date=4 October 2014 |website=Film Exhibitions |publisher=Museum of Modern Art}}</ref>

Buñuel and his co-scenarist [[Julio Alejandro]] drafted a preliminary screenplay for ''[[Viridiana]]'', which critic [[Andrew Sarris]] has described as incorporating "a plot which is almost too lurid to synopsize even in these enlightened times",<ref name="sarris viridiana">{{cite web |last=Sarris |first=Andrew |author-link=Andrew Sarris |title=The Devil and the Nun |url=http://www2.warwick.ac.uk/fac/arts/film/movie/contents/the_devil_and_the_nun_sarris.pdf |access-date=5 October 2014 |publisher=University of Warwick}}</ref> dealing with rape, incest, hints of necrophilia, animal cruelty and sacrilege, and submitted it to the Spanish censor, who, to the surprise of nearly everyone, approved it after requesting only minor modifications and one significant change to the ending.<ref name="d'lugo films of carlos saura">{{cite book |last1=D'Lugo |first1=Marvin |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RUAks4YGLWAC |title=The Films of Carlos Saura: The Practice of Seeing |date=1991 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-0-691-03142-2 |location=Princeton, NJ |pages=42–43 |access-date=5 October 2014}}</ref> Although Buñuel accommodated the censor's demands, he came up with a final scene that was even more provocative than the scene it replaced: "even more immoral", as Buñuel was later to observe.<ref name="ebert viridiana"/> Since Buñuel had more than adequate resources, top-flight technical and artistic crews, and experienced actors, filming of ''Viridiana'' (which took place on location and at Bardem's studios in Madrid) went smoothly and quickly.<ref name="Pavlovi">{{cite book |last=Pavlović |first=Tatjana |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PtFXpxyWMi4C |title=100 Years of Spanish Cinema |publisher=Wiley |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-4051-8419-9 |location=New York |display-authors=etal}}</ref>{{rp|p. 98}}

Buñuel submitted a cutting copy to the censors and then arranged for his son, Juan Luis, to smuggle the negatives to Paris for the final editing and mixing,<ref>{{cite web |title=Viridiana.50 |url=http://www.viridiana50.com/uninci.php |access-date=5 October 2014 |website=viridiana50.com |publisher=Ministerio de Cultura de España}}</ref> ensuring that the authorities would not have an opportunity to view the finished product before its planned submission as Spain's official entry to the 1961 Cannes Festival.<ref name="buache">{{cite book |last1=Buache |first1=Freddy |title=The Cinema of Luis Buñuel |date=1973 |publisher=Tantivy Press |isbn=978-0-498-01302-7 |location=London |pages=117–20}}</ref> Spain's director general of cinematography José Muñoz-Fontán presented the film on the last day of the festival and then, on the urging of Portabella and Bardem, appeared in person to accept the top prize, the {{lang|fr|[[Palme d'Or]]|italic=no}}, which the film shared with the French entry ''[[Une aussi longue absence]]'', directed by [[Henri Colpi]].<ref name="buache french edition">{{cite book |last1=Buache |first1=Freddy |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tuo1JTpoxQAC |title=Buñuel |date=1975 |publisher=L'Age d'Homme |isbn=9782825133415 |location=Lausanne |page=119 |access-date=5 October 2014}}</ref> Within days, ''[[l'Osservatore Romano]]'', the Vatican's official organ, denounced the film as an insult not only to Catholicism but to Christianity.<ref name="malcolm">{{cite news |last1=Malcolm |first1=Derek |date=1 April 1999 |title=Luis Buñuel: Viridiana |url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/1999/apr/01/derekmalcolmscenturyoffilm.derekmalcolm |access-date=5 October 2014 |work=The Guardian}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Luis Bunuel's Case Study on Bourgeoisie Plight and its Underlining Causes |url=http://www.apotpourriofvestiges.com/2012/02/viridiana-1961-luis-bunuels-case-study.html |access-date=21 September 2019 |website=apotpourriofvestiges.com |publisher=A Potpourri of Vestiges}}</ref> Muñoz-Fontán was dismissed from his government post,<ref name="buache french edition" /> the film was banned in Spain for the next 17 years, all mention of it in the press was prohibited, and the two Spanish production companies UNINCI and ''Film 59'' were disbanded.<ref name="d'lugo films of carlos saura" />

[[File:Jean-Claude Carrière à la BNF.jpg|thumb|right|270px|"When today I amuse myself by making useless calculations, I realize that Buñuel and I shared more than two thousand meals together and that on more than fifteen hundred occasions he knocked on my door, notes in hand, ready to begin work. I'm not even counting the walks, the drinks, the films we watched together, the film festivals."<ref name="carriere flickhead">{{cite web |title=Luis Buñuel Remembered by Jean-Claude Carrière |url=http://home.comcast.net/~flickhead/Luis-Bunuel.html |access-date=15 October 2014 |website=Flickhead |publisher=Jean-Claude Carrière}}</ref> – Jean-Claude Carrière on his long-term collaboration with Buñuel.]]
Buñuel went on to make two more films in Mexico with Pinal and Alatriste, ''[[El ángel exterminador]]'' (1962) and ''[[Simón del desierto]]'' (1965) and was later to say that Alatriste had been the one producer who gave him the most freedom in creative expression.<ref name="Rowman & Littlefield">{{cite book |last1=Alfaro |first1=Eduardo de la Vega |url=https://archive.org/details/mexicoscinema00davi/page/189 |title="The Decline of the Golden Age and the Making of the Crisis," in Mexico's Cinema: A Century of Film and Filmmakers, edited by Joanne Hershfield and David R. Maciel |date=1999 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |isbn=978-0842026826 |location=Lanham MD |page=[https://archive.org/details/mexicoscinema00davi/page/189 189]}}</ref>

In 1963, actor [[Fernando Rey]], one of the stars of ''Viridiana'', introduced Buñuel to producer [[Serge Silberman]], a Polish entrepreneur who had fled to Paris when his family died in the Holocaust<ref>{{cite news |date=25 July 2003 |title=Serge Silberman, productor de Luis Buñuel y de Akira Kurosawa |url=http://elpais.com/diario/2003/07/25/agenda/1059084008_850215.html |access-date=13 October 2014 |work=El Pais}}</ref> and had worked with several renowned French directors, including [[Jean-Pierre Melville]], [[Jacques Becker]], [[Marcel Camus]] and [[Christian-Jaque]].<ref name="ronald bergan">{{cite news |last1=Bergan |first1=Ronald |date=27 July 2003 |title=Serge Silberman: Flamboyant film producer prepared to go out on a limb |url=https://www.theguardian.com/news/2003/jul/28/guardianobituaries.filmnews |access-date=13 October 2014 |work=The Guardian |agency=Guardian News and Media Limited}}</ref> Silberman proposed that the two make an adaptation of [[Octave Mirbeau]]'s ''[[The Diary of a Chambermaid (novel)|The Diary of a Chambermaid]]'', which Buñuel had read several times.<ref name="gonzalez chambermaid">{{cite web |last1=Gonzalez |first1=Ed |date=8 September 2003 |title=The Diary of a Chambermaid |url=https://www.slantmagazine.com/film/review/the-diary-of-a-chambermaid |access-date=15 October 2014 |website=Slant Magazine.}}</ref> Buñuel wanted to do the filming in Mexico with Pinal, but Silberman insisted it be done in France.<ref name="gonzalez chambermaid" />

Pinal was so determined to work again with Buñuel that she was ready to move to France, learn the language and even work for nothing in order to get the part of [[Célestine (Mirbeau)|Célestine]], the title character.<ref name="rivera pinal">{{cite journal |last1=Rivera J. |first1=Héctor |date=13 July 1997 |title=Las experiencias de Silvia Pinal con Buñuel y Gustavo Alatriste |journal=Proceso |issue=n1080 |page=62}}</ref> Silberman, however, wanted French actress [[Jeanne Moreau]] to play the role, so he put Pinal off by telling her that Moreau, too, was willing to act with no fee. Ultimately, Silberman got his way, leaving Pinal so disappointed that she was later to claim that Alatriste's failure to help her secure this part led to the breakup of their marriage.<ref name="rivera pinal" /> When Buñuel requested a French-speaking writer with whom to work on the screenplay, Silberman suggested the 32-year-old [[Jean-Claude Carrière]], an actor whose previous screenwriting credits included only a few films for the comic star/director [[Pierre Étaix]], but once Buñuel learned that Carrière was the heir to a wine-growing family, the newcomer was hired on the spot.<ref name="ronald bergan" /> At first, Carrière found it difficult to work with Buñuel, because the young man was so deferential that he never challenged any of Buñuel's ideas, until, at Buñuel's covert insistence, Silberman told Carrière to stand up to Buñuel now and then; as Carrière was later to say: "In a way, Buñuel needed an opponent. He didn't need a secretary – he needed someone to contradict him and oppose him and to make suggestions."<ref name="tim grierson FilmCraft: Screenwriting">{{cite book |last1=Grierson |first1=Tim |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PHtiAgAAQBAJ |title=FilmCraft: Screenwriting |date=2013 |publisher=Focal Press |isbn=978-0240824864 |location=Burlington MA |page=62 |access-date=15 October 2014}}</ref> The finished 1964 film, ''[[Diary of a Chambermaid (1964 film)|Diary of a Chambermaid]]'', became the first of several to be made by the team of Buñuel, Carrière and Silberman. Carrière later said "Without me and without Serge Silberman, the producer, perhaps Buñuel would not have made so many films after he was 65. We really encouraged him to work. That's for sure."<ref name="Colville-Andersen">{{cite web |last1=Colville-Andersen |first1=Mikael |title=The Storytellers – Interview with Jean-Claude Carriéré |url=http://zakka.dk/euroscreenwriters/screenwriters/jean-claude_carriere.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140331223043/http://zakka.dk/euroscreenwriters/screenwriters/jean-claude_carriere.htm |archive-date=31 March 2014 |access-date=15 October 2014 |website=Zakkatography |publisher=Colville-Andersen.}}</ref> 
This was the second filmed version of Mirbeau's novel, the first being [[The Diary of a Chambermaid (1946 film)|a 1946 Hollywood production]] directed by [[Jean Renoir]], which Buñuel refused to view for fear of being influenced by the famous French director, whom he venerated.<ref name="david kalat">{{cite web |last1=Kalat |first1=David |title=Diary of a Chambermaid |url=https://www.tcm.com/this-month/article/474228 |access-date=15 October 2014 |website=Turner Classic Movies |publisher=Turner Entertainment Networks}}</ref> Buñuel's version, while admired by many, has often been compared unfavorably to Renoir's, with a number of critics claiming that Renoir's ''Diary'' fits better in Renoir's overall ''oeuvre'', while Buñuel's ''Diary'' is not sufficiently "Buñuelian".<ref name="Geoffrey T. Harris">{{cite book |last1=Harris |first1=Geoffrey T. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wUbGJ8kozAoC |title=On Translating French Literature and Film, Volume 1 |date=1996 |publisher=Rodopi |isbn=978-90-5183-933-3 |location=Amsterdam |page=92}}</ref>

After the 1964 release of ''Diary'', Buñuel again tried to make a film of Matthew Lewis's ''[[The Monk]]'', a project on which he had worked, on and off, since 1938, according to producer [[Pierre Braunberger]].<ref name=gubern />{{rp|p.137}} He and Carrière wrote a screenplay, but were unable to obtain funding, which was realized in 1973 under the direction of Buñuel devotee [[Adonis A. Kyrou|Ado Kyrou]], with considerable assistance from both Buñuel and Carrière.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Aspley |first1=Keith |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3KK7JHqNrRsC&q=bunuel+the+monk+lewis+carriere&pg=PA284 |title=Historical Dictionary of Surrealism |date=2010 |publisher=Scarecrow Press |isbn=978-0810858473 |location=Lanham MD |page=284 |access-date=24 October 2014}}</ref>

In 1965, Buñuel managed to work again with Silvia Pinal in what was his last Mexican feature, co-starring Claudio Brook, ''[[Simón del desierto]]''.<ref name="Rowman & Littlefield"/> Pinal was keenly interested in continuing to work with Buñuel, trusting him completely and frequently stating that he brought out the best in her; however, this was their last collaboration.<ref name="La Jornada">{{cite news |date=29 July 2013 |title=No he conocido a alguien que supere a Luis Buñuel: Silvia Pinal |url=http://www.jornada.unam.mx/2013/07/29/espectaculos/a12n1esp |access-date=13 October 2014 |work=La Jornada |agency=DEMOS, Desarrollo de Medios}}</ref>

=== 1966–1983: Acclaim and final films ===
[[File:Catherine Deneuve 1969-2.jpg|thumb|195px|left|Speaking of Buñuel's deafness, actress Catherine Deneuve, star of ''[[Belle de Jour (film)|Belle de Jour]]'' (1967) and ''[[Tristana (film)|Tristana]]'' (1970), said: "Well, I think it was difficult for him, coping with his deafness. Some people said he was not that deaf, but I think, when you don't hear very well and when you're tired, everything sinks into a buzz, and it is very hard. French is not his language, so on ''Belle de Jour'', I'm sure that it was much more of an effort for him to have to explain."<ref name=zohn />]]

In 1966, Buñuel was contacted by [[Robert and Raymond Hakim]], Egyptian-French producers who specialized in sexy films directed by star filmmakers,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bernard |first1=Jami |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pWH97tY1KfMC |title=The X-List: The National Society of Film Critics' Guide to the Movies that Turn Us On |date=2005 |publisher=Da Capo Press |isbn=978-0306814457 |location=Cambridge MA |page=40 |access-date=29 October 2014}}</ref> who offered him the opportunity to direct a film version of [[Joseph Kessel]]'s [[Belle de Jour (novel)|novel]], about an affluent young woman who leads a double life as a prostitute, and that had caused a scandal upon its publication in 1928.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Boucharenc |first1=Myriam |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2GShcPJaDg4C |title=L'écrivain-reporter au cœur des années trente |date=2004 |publisher=Presses Univ. Septentrion |isbn=978-2-85939-842-2 |location=Lille |page=184 |access-date=29 October 2014}}</ref> Buñuel did not like Kessel's novel, considering it "a bit of a soap opera",<ref name="Europe of Cultures">{{cite web |last1=Durieux |first1=Christian |title=Conversation with Luis Buñuel on Belle de jour |url=http://fresques.ina.fr/europe-des-cultures-en/fiche-media/Europe00048/conversation-with-luis-bunuel-on-belle-de-jour.html |access-date=29 October 2014 |website=Europe of Cultures |publisher=INA Institute}}</ref> but he took on the challenge because: "I found it interesting to try to turn something I didn't like into something I did."<ref name="levy belle de jour">{{cite web |last1=Levy |first1=Emanuel |date=16 September 2014 |title=Belle de Jour (1967): Bunuel's Masterpiece Starring Catherine Deneuve |url=http://emanuellevy.com/pick-of-the-week/belle-de-jour-1967-bunuels-masterpiece-starring-catherine-deneuve/ |access-date=29 October 2014 |website=Cinema 24/7}}</ref> So he and Carrière set out enthusiastically to interview women in the brothels of Madrid to learn about their sexual fantasies.<ref name="belle de jour tcm">{{cite web |last=Landazuri |first=Margarita |title=Belle de jour |url=https://www.tcm.com/this-month/article/636738 |access-date=24 October 2014 |website=TCM Classic Movies |publisher=Turner Entertainment Networks}}</ref> Buñuel also was not happy about the choice of the 22-year-old [[Catherine Deneuve]] for the title role, feeling that she had been foisted upon him by the Hakim brothers and Deneuve's lover at the time, director [[François Truffaut]].<ref name="moma belle de jour">{{cite web |last1=Silver |first1=Charles |title=Luis Buñuel's Belle de Jour |url=http://www.moma.org/explore/inside_out/2014/04/22/luis-bunuels-belle-de-jour/ |access-date=29 October 2014 |website=Inside/Out |publisher=Museum of Modern Art}}</ref> As a result, both actress and director found working together difficult, with Deneuve claiming, "I felt they showed more of me than they'd said they were going to. There were moments when I felt totally used. I was very unhappy,"<ref name="anderson belle">{{cite web |last1=Anderson |first1=Melissa |title=Belle de jour: Tough Love |url=https://www.criterion.com/current/posts/2121-belle-de-jour-tough-love |access-date=29 October 2014 |website=Criterion Collection}}</ref> and Buñuel deriding her prudery on the set.<ref name="zohn">{{cite web |last1=Zohn |first1=Patricia |date=2 April 2012 |title=Belle de Jour: Catherine Deneuve and Her Shades of Grey |url=https://www.huffingtonpost.com/patricia-zohn/catherine-deneuve_b_1395172.html |access-date=29 October 2014 |work=HuffPost}}</ref> Roger Ebert described it as "possibly the best-known erotic film of modern times, perhaps the best",<ref>{{cite web |last1=Ebert |first1=Roger |title=Belle de Jour |url=https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/great-movie-belle-de-jour-1967 |access-date=29 October 2014 |work=Chicago Sun Times}}</ref> even though, as another critic has written, "in terms of explicit sexual activity, there is little in ''Belle de jour'' we might not see in a [[Doris Day]] comedy from the same year".<ref>{{cite web |last1=Melville |first1=David |date=9 September 2013 |title=Who Let the Cats Out? Buñuel, Deneuve and Belle de jour |url=http://sensesofcinema.com/2013/cteq/who-let-the-cats-out-bunuel-deneuve-and-belle-de-jour/ |access-date=29 October 2014 |website=Senses of Cinema |publisher=Film Victoria}}</ref> It was Buñuel's most successful film at the box office.<ref name="anderson belle" />

Critics have noted Buñuel's habit of following up a commercial or critical success with a more personal, idiosyncratic film.<ref name="Polizzotti milky way">{{cite web |last1=Polizzotti |first1=Mark |title=The Milky Way: Easy Striders |url=https://www.criterion.com/current/posts/611-the-milky-way-easy-striders |access-date=11 December 2014 |website=Criterion Collection}}</ref> After the worldwide success of ''Belle de Jour'', and upon viewing [[Jean-Luc Godard]]'s film ''[[La Chinoise]]'', Buñuel, who had wanted to make a film about Catholic heresies for years, told Carrière: "If that is what today's cinema is like, then we can make a film about heresies."<ref name="supernal dreams">{{cite web |last1=French |first1=Lawrence |title=Supernal Dreams: Jean-Claude Carriere on Luis Bunuel's Sublime Fantasy, "The Milky Way" |url=http://cinefantastiqueonline.com/2009/02/supernal-dreams-jean-claude-carriere-on-luis-bunuels-sublime-fantasy-the-milky-way/ |access-date=11 December 2014 |website=Cinefantastique Online}}</ref> The two spent months researching Catholic history and created the 1969 film ''[[The Milky Way (1969 film)|The Milky Way]]'', a "picaresque road film"<ref name="Nochimson">{{cite book |last1=Nochimson |first1=Martha |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DXK5gkQwAs8C |title=World on Film: An Introduction |date=2010 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |isbn=978-1405139793 |location=New York |page=294 |access-date=11 December 2014}}</ref> that tells the story of two vagabonds on [[Camino de Santiago|pilgrimage to the tomb of the Apostle James]] at [[Santiago de Compostela]], during which they travel through time and space to take part in situations illustrating heresies that arose from the six major Catholic dogmas.<ref name="mazur">{{cite book |last1=Mazur |first1=Eric Michael |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JPNfox6H5qwC |title=Encyclopedia of Religion and Film |date=2011 |publisher=ABC-CLIO |isbn=978-0313330728 |location=Santa Barbara, CA |page=101 |access-date=11 December 2014}}</ref> [[Vincent Canby]] compared it to [[George Stevens]]'s blockbuster ''[[The Greatest Story Ever Told]]'', in that Buñuel had made a film about Jesus casting nearly all the famous French performers of the time in cameo roles.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Canby |first1=Vincent |date=27 January 1970 |title='The Milky Way':Bunuel Weaves Surreal Spiritual Journey |url=https://www.nytimes.com/movie/review?res=990CE5D8123AE03BBC4F51DFB766838B669EDE |access-date=11 December 2014 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> ''The Milky Way'' was banned in Italy, only to have the Catholic Church intervene on its behalf.<ref name=durgnat />{{rp|p.152}}

{{quote box|bgcolor=#CCDDFF|align=right|width=25%|quote=A few great directors have the ability to draw us into their dream world, into their personalities and obsessions and fascinate us with them for a short time. This is the highest level of escapism the movies can provide for us – just as our elementary identification with a hero or a heroine was the lowest. |source=Film critic [[Roger Ebert]], on ''Tristana''<ref name="ebert tristana">{{cite news |last=Ebert |first=Roger |title=Tristana |url=https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/tristana-1970 |access-date=12 December 2014 |work=Chicago Sun Times}}</ref>}}

''[[Tristana (film)|Tristana]]'' (1970) is a film about a young woman who is seduced and manipulated by her guardian, who attempts to thwart her romance with a young artist and who eventually induces her to marry him after she loses one of her legs due to a tumor. It has been considered by scholar Beth Miller the least understood of Buñuel's films, and consequently one of the most underrated, due to a "consistent failure to apprehend its political and, especially, its socialist-feminist statement".<ref name="beth miller">{{cite book |last1=Miller |first1=Beth |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8cCIcUaEznYC |title="From Mistress to Murderess," in Women in Hispanic Literature: Icons and Fallen Idols, edited by Beth Kurti Miller |date=1983 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=978-0520043671 |pages=340–41 |access-date=12 December 2014}}</ref> Buñuel had wanted to make a film of [[Benito Pérez Galdós]]'s novel ''[[Tristana (novel)|Tristana]]'' as early as 1952, even though he considered Galdós's book the author's weakest.<ref name="fujiwara">{{cite web |last1=Fujiwara |first1=Chris |title=Tristana |url=https://www.tcm.com/this-month/article/449958 |access-date=12 December 2014 |website=TCM Summer Under the Stars |publisher=Turner Entertainment Network}}</ref> After finishing ''Viridiana'' and in the wake of the scandal its release caused in 1962, the Spanish censor turned down this project,<ref name=durgnat />{{rp|p.152}} and Buñuel had to wait for 8 years before he could receive backing from the Spanish production company Época Films.<ref name=fujiwara /> The censors had threatened to deny permission for the film on the grounds that it encouraged dueling, so Buñuel had to approach the subject matter very gingerly, in addition to making concessions to his French/Italian/Spanish producers, who insisted on casting two of the three primary roles with actors not of Buñuel's choosing: [[Franco Nero]] and Catherine Deneuve.<ref name="faulkner literary adaptations">{{cite book |last1=Faulkner |first1=Sally |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yeMgJsea3-8C |title=Literary Adaptations in Spanish Cinema |date=2004 |publisher=Tamesis |isbn=978-1855660984 |location=London |page=128 |access-date=20 September 2014}}</ref>{{rp|p.128}} On this occasion, however, Deneuve and Buñuel had a more mutually satisfactory working relationship, with Deneuve telling an interviewer, "but in the end, you know, it was actually rather a wonderful shoot. ''Tristana'' is one of my favorite films. Personally, as an actress, I prefer ''Tristana'' to ''Belle de Jour''."<ref name=fujiwara />

The idea for their next film, ''[[The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie]]'' (1972) came from Buñuel and Silberman discussing uncanny repetition in everyday life; Silberman told an anecdote about how he had invited some friends for dinner at his house, only to forget about it, so that, on the night of the dinner party, he was absent and his wife was in her nightclothes.<ref name="pinkos">{{cite web |last1=Pinkos |first1=Jefferey |title=Dinner Is Served |url=http://lonestarfilmsociety.com/discreet-charm-of-the-bourgeoisie/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141223031928/http://lonestarfilmsociety.com/discreet-charm-of-the-bourgeoisie/ |archive-date=23 December 2014 |access-date=12 December 2014 |website=Lone Star Film Society}}</ref> The film tells of a group of affluent friends who are continually stymied in their attempts to eat a meal together, a situation that a number of critics have contrasted to the opposite dilemma of the characters in ''The Exterminating Angel'', where guests of a dinner party are mysteriously unable to leave after having completed their meal.<ref name=lim /> For this film, Buñuel, Silberman and Carrière assembled a top-flight cast of European performers, "a veritable rogues' gallery of French art-house cinema", according to one critic.<ref name="budd wilkins">{{cite web |last1=Wilkins |first1=Budd |date=21 November 2012 |title=The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie |url=https://www.slantmagazine.com/film/review/the-discreet-charm-of-the-bourgeoisie-6699 |access-date=12 December 2014 |website=Slant Magazine}}</ref> For the first time, Buñuel made use of a [[video monitors|video-playback monitor]], which allowed him to make much more extensive use of [[crane shot]]s and elaborate [[tracking shot]]s, and enabled him to cut the film in the camera and eliminate the need for [[Re-shoot|reshoots]].<ref name=pinkos /> Filming required only two months and Buñuel claimed that editing took only one day.<ref name=pinkos /> Silberman decided to skip the Cannes Festival in order to concentrate on getting it nominated for the [[Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film]], which it won, leading Buñuel to express his contempt for a process that relied on the judgment of "2500 idiots, including for example the assistant dress designer of the studio".<ref name=pinkos />

Buñuel took advantage of the popular success of ''Discreet Charm'' to make one of the "puzzling, idiosyncratic films he ''really'' wanted to make".<ref name="Polizzotti milky way" /> In 1973, at the [[Monastery of El Paular|Monastery of Paular]] in the Spanish [[Somosierra]], he wrote the screenplay for ''[[The Phantom of Liberty]]'' (1974) with Carrière for production by Silberman and his Hollywood partners.<ref name=aranda />{{rp|p.249}} The resulting film is a series of 12 distinctive episodes with separate protagonists, linked together only by following a character from one episode to another in a relay-race manner.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Lanzagorta |first1=Marco |date=4 October 2002 |title=The Phantom of Liberty |url=http://sensesofcinema.com/2002/cteq/phantom/ |access-date=15 December 2014 |website=Senses of Cinema |publisher=Film Victoria, Australia}}</ref> Buñuel has stated that he made the film as a tribute to poet [[Benjamin Péret]], a founding member of French Surrealism,<ref name="bill krohn" />{{rp|p.170}} and called it his "most Surrealist film".<ref name=aranda />{{rp|p.249}}

Buñuel's final film,  ''[[That Obscure Object of Desire]]'' (1977), was adapted by Buñuel and Carrière from an 1898 novel by [[Pierre Louÿs]] called ''[[La Femme et le pantin]]'', which had already been used as the basis of films directed by [[Josef von Sternberg]] (''[[The Devil Is a Woman (1935 film)|The Devil Is a Woman]]'', 1935) and [[Julien Duvivier]] (''[[La Femme et le Pantin]]'', 1959). The film, which tells the story of an older man who is obsessed by a young woman who continually evades his attempts to consummate a sexual relationship, starred the Spanish actor [[Fernando Rey]], appearing in his fourth Buñuel film. Initially, the part of the young woman was to be played by [[Maria Schneider (actress)|Maria Schneider]], who had achieved international fame for her roles in ''[[Last Tango in Paris]]'' and ''[[The Passenger (1975 film)|The Passenger]]'',<ref>{{cite news |last1=Grimes |first1=William |date=4 February 2011 |title=Maria Schneider, Actress in ''Last Tango'', Dies at 58 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/02/04/movies/04schneider.html |access-date=16 December 2014 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> but once shooting started, according to Carrière, her drug usage resulted in a "lackluster and dull" performance that caused tempestuous arguments with Buñuel on the set and her eventual dismissal.<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Thomson |first1=David |date=8 February 2011 |title=David Thomson on Films: Remembering Maria Schneider |url=https://newrepublic.com/article/books-and-arts/82975/david-thomson-films-remembering-maria-schneider |access-date=16 December 2014 |magazine=New Republic}}</ref> Silberman, the producer, decided to abandon the project at that point, but was convinced by Buñuel to continue shooting with two different actresses, [[Ángela Molina]] and [[Carole Bouquet]], playing the same role in alternating sequences throughout the film. In his autobiography, Buñuel claimed that this unusual casting decision was his own idea after drinking two dry martinis, saying: "If I had to list all the benefits derived from alcohol, it would be endless".<ref>{{cite web |last1=Pinkos |first1=Jefferey |date=24 May 2014 |title=Buñuel's Pursuit of That Obscure Object |url=http://lonestarfilmsociety.com/that-obscure-object-of-desire/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141223155848/http://lonestarfilmsociety.com/that-obscure-object-of-desire/ |archive-date=23 December 2014 |access-date=17 December 2014 |website=Lone Star Film Society}}</ref> Others have reported that Carrière had first broached the idea while developing the film's scenario, but had been brushed off by Buñuel as "the whim of a rainy day".<ref>{{cite web |last1=Gonzalez |first1=Ed |date=17 September 2003 |title=That Obscure Object of Desire |url=https://www.slantmagazine.com/film/review/that-obscure-object-of-desire |access-date=17 December 2014 |website=Slant Magazine}}</ref>

After the release of ''That Obscure Object of Desire'', Buñuel retired from filmmaking.<ref name="McAdam">{{cite web |last1=McAdam |first1=Conor |date=19 February 2017 |title=Outtake: Luis Buñuel is a Walking Contradiction |url=https://medium.com/outtake/the-man-y-luis-bu%C3%B1uel-s-8260076236f0 |access-date=11 June 2020 |website=[[Medium (website)|Medium]]}}</ref><!-- original url: https://outtake.tribecashortlist.com/the-man-y-luis-bu%C3%B1uel-s-8260076236f0 which now redirects to Medium website --> In 1982, he wrote (along with Carrière) his autobiography, ''Mon Dernier Soupir'' (translated as ''My Last Sigh'' in the U.S., ''My Last Breath'' in the UK), which provides an account of his life, friends and family as well as a representation of his eccentric personality. In it, he recounts dreams, encounters with many well-known writers, actors and artists such as [[Pablo Picasso]] and [[Charlie Chaplin]] as well as antics, like dressing up as a nun and walking around town.<ref name="my last sigh" />{{rp|p. 83}}

==Personal life==
{{quote box|bgcolor=#CCDDFF|align=right|width=25%|quote=Luis waited for death for a long time, like a good Spaniard, and when he died he was ready. His relationship with death was like that one has with a woman. He felt the love, hate, tenderness, ironical detachment of a long relationship, and he didn't want to miss the last encounter, the moment of union. "I hope I will die alive," he told me. At the end it was as he had wished. His last words were "I'm dying".<ref name="carriere flickhead" />  |source=Long-time friend and collaborator, [[Jean-Claude Carrière]]}}

Starting at age 17, Buñuel steadily dated the future poet and dramatist [[Concha Méndez]], with whom he vacationed every summer at [[San Sebastián]]. He introduced her to his friends at the Residencia as his fiancée.<ref name="bellver">{{cite book |last=Bellver |first=Catherine Gullo |title=Absence and Presence: Spanish Women Poets of the Twenties and Thirties |publisher=Bucknell University Press |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-8387-5463-4 |location=Lewisburg, PA |pages=232}}</ref><ref name="wilcox">{{cite book |last=Wilcox |first=John Chapman |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=i8RlmBiUl68C&q=concha+mendez+bunuel&pg=PA125 |title=Women Poets of Spain, 1860–1990: Toward a Gynocentric Vision |publisher=University of Illinois Press |year=1997 |isbn=978-0-252-06559-0 |location=Urbana and Chicago |pages=125}}</ref> After five years, she broke off the relationship, citing Buñuel's "insufferable character".<ref name="agonia.net">{{cite web |title=Biografia Concha Mendez Cuesta |url=http://portugues.agonia.net/index.php/author/0028634/index.html |access-date=30 July 2012 |publisher=Agonia.Net}}</ref> Fetishism, especially of feet, is a theme in his work. Pauline Kael wrote "That was a wonderful afternoon little Luis spent on the floor of his mother’s closet, and he has never allowed us to forget it."<ref name="ebert viridiana">{{cite news  | last=Ebert | first=Roger | author-link=Roger Ebert | title=The mischievous charm of Luis Buñuel  | date=April 29, 2010  |  work=[[Chicago Sun Times]] | url=https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/great-movie-viridiana-1961}}</ref>

During his student years, Buñuel became an accomplished hypnotist. He claimed that once, while calming a hysterical prostitute through [[hypnosis|hypnotic]] suggestion, he inadvertently put one of the several bystanders into a trance as well.<ref name="my last sigh" />{{rp|p.67}} He was often to insist that watching movies was a form of hypnosis: "This kind of cinematographic hypnosis is no doubt due to the darkness of the theatre and to the rapidly changing scenes, lights, and camera movements, which weaken the spectator's critical intelligence and exercise over him a kind of fascination."<ref name="my last sigh" />{{rp|p.69}} Referring to Buñuel's interest in hypnosis, [[Anthony Lane]] wrote, "You can easily picture yourself being hypnotized by this man; sit through a sample of his movies, and you will think you have been."<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Lane |first=Anthony |date=10 December 2000 |title=In Your Dreams |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2000/12/18/in-your-dreams-2 |magazine=[[The New Yorker]]}}</ref>

=== Marriage ===
In 1926 he met his future wife, Jeanne Rucar Lefebvre,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Trébede |url=http://www.redaragon.com/trebede/feb2000/articulo2.asp |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924085450/http://www.redaragon.com/trebede/feb2000/articulo2.asp |archive-date=24 September 2015 |access-date=7 September 2014}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=6 November 1994 |title=Jeanne Rucar, viuda de Luis Buñuel |url=https://elpais.com/diario/1994/11/07/agenda/784162802_850215.html |access-date=20 March 2021 |work=El País |language=es |issn=1134-6582}}</ref> a [[gymnastics]] teacher who had won a bronze medal at the 1924 Paris Olympics.<ref name="edwards 2009">{{cite book |last1=Edwards |first1=Gwynne |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CA34AgAAQBAJ&q=Olympic+bronze+medal+jeanne+rucar&pg=PT72 |title=Lorca, Buñuel, Dalí: Forbidden Pleasures and Connected Lives |date=2009 |publisher=I.B. Tauris |isbn=978-1848850071 |location=London |page=86 |access-date=15 August 2019}}</ref><ref name="max aub 2017">{{cite book |last1=Aub |first1=Max |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1sm4DgAAQBAJ&q=Olympic+bronze+medal+jeanne+rucar&pg=PA154 |title=Conversations with Bunuel: Interviews with the Filmmaker, Family Members, Friends and Collaborators |date=2017 |publisher=McFarland |isbn=978-1476668222 |location=Jefferson, NC |page=154}}</ref> Buñuel courted her in a formal Aragonese manner, complete with a chaperone,<ref name="bbc world service">{{cite web |date=19 September 2000 |title=Luis Buñuel: In The Directors' Chair |url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/worldservice/arts/highlights/000919_bunuel.shtml |access-date=30 July 2012 |publisher=BBC World Service}}</ref> and they married in 1934<ref name="brain juice" /> despite a warning by Jean Epstein when Buñuel first proposed in 1930: "Jeanne, you are making a mistake.... It's not right for you, don't marry him."<ref name="jeanne rucar">{{cite book |last=Rucar de Buñuel |first=Jeanne |author-link=Jeanne Rucar |title=Memoirs of a Woman Without a Piano: My Life with Luis Buñuel |publisher=Five Ties Publishing |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-9794727-6-3 |location=Brooklyn |pages=43}}</ref> The two remained married throughout his life and had two sons, [[Juan Luis Buñuel|Juan Luis]] and Rafael.<ref name="Centro Virtual Cervantes">{{cite web |title=Rafael Bunuel, Escultor |url=http://cvc.cervantes.es/actcult/bunuel/entrevistas/r_bunuel.htm |access-date=23 July 2012 |website=Centro Virtual Cervantes |publisher=Instituto Cervantes}}</ref> [[Diego Buñuel]], filmmaker and host of the [[National Geographic Channel]]'s ''[[Don't Tell My Mother]]'' series, is their grandson.<ref name="nat geo">{{cite web |title=Nat Geo Adventure |url=http://natgeoadventure.tv/int/user.aspx?userid=10703 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120813071957/http://natgeoadventure.tv/int/User.aspx?userId=10703 |archive-date=13 August 2012 |access-date=23 July 2012 |publisher=NGC-UK Partnership}}</ref>

=== Illness and death ===
In his 70s, Buñuel once told his friend, novelist [[Carlos Fuentes]]: "I'm not afraid of death. I'm afraid of dying alone in a hotel room, with my bags open and a shooting script on the night table. I must know whose fingers will close my eyes."<ref name="fuentes discreet charm">{{cite web |last1=Fuentes |first1=Carlos |date=18 December 2000 |title=The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeosie |url=https://www.criterion.com/current/posts/109-the-discreet-charm-of-the-bourgeosie |access-date=12 December 2014 |website=Criterion Collection}}</ref> In his autobiography, ''My Last Sigh'', he wrote, "I'd love to rise from the grave every ten years or so and go buy a few newspapers. Ghostly pale, sliding silently along the walls, my paper under my arm, I'd return to the cemetery and read about all the disasters in the world before falling back to sleep, safe and secure in my tomb."<ref>{{cite news |last=Thomson |first=David |author-link=David Thomson (film critic) |date=20 February 2000 |title=FILM; In Bunuel's Dreams Began Film's Liberation |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/02/20/movies/film-in-bunuel-s-dreams-began-film-s-liberation.html |work=The New York Times}}</ref>

According to his wife, Jeanne, Buñuel died in Mexico City in 1983 from diabetes complications.<ref>Reference Jeanne Rucar, "Memorias de una mujer sin piano".
