=== Accolades ===

Crew members [[Robert Knudson]], [[Robert Glass (sound engineer)|Robert Glass]], [[Richard Tyler (sound engineer)|Richard Tyler]] and [[Jean-Louis Ducarme]] were nominated for the [[Academy Award for Best Sound]] at the [[50th Academy Awards]] in 1978 for work on this film.<ref name="Oscars1978">{{cite web |url=http://www.oscars.org/oscars/ceremonies/1978 |title=The 50th Academy Awards (1978) Nominees and Winners |access-date=2011-10-05 |work=oscars.org |archive-date=April 2, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402004056/http://www.oscars.org/oscars/ceremonies/1978 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== International and home releases ===

==== International cuts ====
[[File:Wages of Fear (1978).png|thumbnail|right|UK newspaper advert for Sorcerer retitled 'Wages of Fear' in 1978]]
The film's European as well as Australian<ref>{{cite news | url=http://www.smh.com.au/articles/2002/11/28/1038386261243.html | work=smh.com.au | first=Garry | last=Maddox | title=Hollywood Sorcerer Is Casting His Old Spell | date=2002-11-29 | access-date=2013-05-25 | archive-date=July 20, 2013 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130720122300/http://www.smh.com.au/articles/2002/11/28/1038386261243.html | url-status=live }}</ref> cinema release cut 28 minutes from the original (but not in France, where the movie was distributed in its full-length version). In most regions of the world it was also retitled as ''Wages of Fear'' and distributed by [[Cinema International Corporation]] (later renamed as [[United International Pictures]]),<ref name="jclark" /> a joint venture between Universal and Paramount specifically established for overseas distribution.<ref name="variety1" /> This version opens in the village with the drivers already present, and ends with the delivery of explosives. The cuts were made by the international distributor Cinema International Corporation, without Friedkin's consent<ref name="filmjournal">{{cite journal|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050903045506/http://www.thefilmjournal.com/issue10/sorcerer.html|archive-date=2005-09-03|url=http://www.thefilmjournal.com/issue10/sorcerer.html |title=On Wages of Fear and Sorcerer|issn=1542-0868 |journal=The Film Journal| first=Tim| last=Applegate| date=October 2004|access-date=2012-10-27}}</ref> in order to obtain more screenings.<ref name="urban">{{cite news| url=http://www.urbancinefile.com.au/home/view.asp?a=6832 | work=Urban Cinefile | title=Friedkin, William: Sorcerer / Shooting with Guns | date=2002-12-05|access-date=2013-06-03}}</ref> Friedkin referred to this cut as a "mutilated" version of his work.<ref name=":0" /> The opening vignettes are somewhat retained, albeit heavily shortened and inserted as flashbacks.<ref name="jclark" /> Although the European cut is shorter, there is almost sixteen minutes of unique footage not shown in the original American theatrical version.<ref name="moviecensorship" />

The aforementioned changes were approved by Verna Fields and commissioned to Jim Clark, who reluctantly agreed, and Cynthia Scheider. Fields was a Universal Studios executive who thought shortening and restructuring the movie would increase the film's commercial potential. Scheider was also interested in applying those changes, offering his cooperation. Jim Clark was reportedly assured by Fields that Friedkin permitted changes, but was very suspicious about the authenticity of this claim. Therefore, Clark wrote an indemnity preventing Friedkin from any form of interference. Some additional dialogue written by Clark and Ken Levinson was later dubbed in. The studio did not possess the original work print; hence it was forced to work on the combined print. Jim Clark said the cut was "at best, passable" and was of the opinion that if he "had left Friedkin's version alone, it would have had exactly the same fate."<ref name="jclark" />

==== Home media ====
The film's release on video was held up for many years; executives at Paramount and Universal argued it was ownership issues that was preventing a release, though a Universal spokesperson suggested that a lack of public interest might be another reason.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-04-30-ca-1813-story.html|title=Film Classics Still Eluding Video Viewers|last=BENESCH|first=CONNIE|date=1988-04-30|work=Los Angeles Times|access-date=2018-08-04|language=en-US|issn=0458-3035|archive-date=December 11, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151211174204/http://articles.latimes.com/1988-04-30/entertainment/ca-1813_1_warner-home-video|url-status=live}}</ref> A [[VHS]] version of ''Sorcerer'' was released on October 4, 1990.{{sfn|Kachmar |2002|page=144}} A [[laserdisc]] release followed on December 15, 1990.<ref name="lddb">{{cite web| url=http://www.lddb.com/laserdisc/02992/12009/Sorcerer-%281977%29| title=LaserDisc Database – Sorcerer (1977) [12009]| work=lddb.com| access-date=2013-06-23| archive-date=July 7, 2022| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220707035809/https://www.lddb.com/laserdisc/02992/12009/Sorcerer-(1977)| url-status=live}}</ref> The DVD was released in the U.S. and Canada on November 17, 1998,<ref name="tomatoes" /> and used the laserdisc transfer<ref name="obscure">{{cite web| url=http://knifeinthehead.blogspot.com/2009/02/not-so-obscure-trailer-but-still-mia-on_18.html| title=Not So Obscure Trailer, But Still MIA on DVD in Widescreen: Sorcerer (1977, William Friedkin)| work=Obscure One-Sheet| first=Ned| last=Merrill| date=February 18, 2009| access-date=2013-06-23| archive-date=December 22, 2014| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141222053606/http://knifeinthehead.blogspot.com/2009/02/not-so-obscure-trailer-but-still-mia-on_18.html| url-status=live}}</ref> presented in a 1.33:1<ref name="sorcererdvd">{{cite AV media notes |title=Sorcerer DVD |others=[[William Friedkin]] |type=Liner notes |publisher=[[Universal Home Video]] |location=Hollywood, California |year=1998}}</ref> non-widescreen version, which is not its original theatrical aspect ratio; it was shown in cinemas at a ratio of 1.85:1.<ref name="twitch" /> However, since widescreen televisions have become popular, Friedkin has allowed many of his other films to be released on DVD in their original widescreen formats (''[[The French Connection (film)|The French Connection]]'', ''[[Cruising (film)|Cruising]]'', ''[[To Live and Die in L.A. (film)|To Live and Die in L.A.]]'').

==== 2014 US home video re-release and 2017 UK home video release ====
In September 2013, Friedkin announced that new, remastered home video releases on Blu-ray and DVD<ref name="twitter4" /> were supposed to be released on April 14, 2014,<ref name="twitter10">{{cite tweet|user=WilliamFriedkin|number=378371860150231040|author=William Friedkin|date=2013-09-12|access-date=2013-09-22|title=Friends. Sorcerer will be on WB blu-ray April 14. In theatres before that, from Paramount, Then TV from Universal. The print is Fantastic.}}</ref> however, both ended up being pushed to April 22.<ref name="twitch2" /> While the 2014 Blu-ray release contains a new, digitally remastered version of the movie, its DVD counterpart is simply a reissued version of the previous DVD release, and has not been authorized by Friedkin, who himself disowned it, and advised to avoid purchasing it.<ref name="twitter12">{{cite tweet|user=WilliamFriedkin|number=459122505626943488|author=William Friedkin|date=2014-04-24|access-date=2014-05-15|title=The Rotten Tomatoes review of SORCERER is the Bad unauthorized DVD, not the new remastered WB Blu-ray. Don't buy the DVD until corrected.}}</ref> Furthermore, the director announced that he would supervise the remastering process for its proper DVD re-release,<ref name="twitter13">{{cite tweet|user=WilliamFriedkin|number=461991723325865984|author=William Friedkin|date=2014-05-01|access-date=2014-05-15|title=Next week I'll make the new SORCERER DVD. Warner's hopes to release it on or about June 5. I'll keep you all posted.}}</ref> which hit US stores in August.<ref name=wb>{{cite press release|url=http://www.warnerbros.com/studio/news/william-friedkin%E2%80%99s-remastered-%E2%80%9Csorcerer%E2%80%9D-blu-ray-scores-solid-success|title=William Friedkin's Remastered "Sorcerer" Blu-ray Scores Solid Success|publisher=Warner Bros.|date=April 30, 2014|access-date=April 7, 2016|archive-date=April 21, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160421202815/http://www.warnerbros.com/studio/news/william-friedkin%E2%80%99s-remastered-%E2%80%9Csorcerer%E2%80%9D-blu-ray-scores-solid-success|url-status=live}}</ref> In the US Blu-ray had no extra features, but was accompanied by a booklet with production stills and an excerpt of Friedkin's memoir ''The Friedkin Connection'',<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nola.com/movies/index.ssf/2014/04/sorcerer_william_friedkins_los.html|title='Sorcerer,' William Friedkin's lost 1977 'magnum opus,' makes Blu-ray debut (full home-video listings)|date=April 22, 2014 |publisher=NOLA.com|access-date=April 8, 2016|archive-date=April 14, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160414200310/http://www.nola.com/movies/index.ssf/2014/04/sorcerer_william_friedkins_los.html|url-status=live}}</ref> and was well-received upon release, with good reviews praising the quality of the transfer and reaching #1 in drama and # 2 in action/adventure on [[Amazon.com]].<ref name=wb /> In the UK, the Blu-ray was released on November 6, 2017, and included a 74-minute ‘In Conversation’ film with the director, conducted by director [[Nicolas Winding Refn]].

====2025 Criterion Collection release====

''Sorcerer'' was released on Blu-ray and 4K [[Ultra HD Blu-ray]] June 24, 2025, by [[The Criterion Collection]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sorcerer |url=https://www.criterion.com/films/34370-sorcerer |access-date=2025-04-24 |website=The Criterion Collection |language=en}}</ref> This release, based on a new 4K restoration, marked the film's first release on the 4K Blu-ray format. Supplemental material for the film includes the conversation with Friedkin and Refn from the 2017 UK Blu-ray, a new conversation between filmmaker [[James Gray (director)|James Gray]] and [[The Ringer (website)|The Ringer]] editor-in-chief Sean Fennessy, interviews with screenwriter Walon Green and editor Bud Smith, behind-the-scenes footage, an original theatrical trailer, and a printed essay by film critic [[Justin Chang]].

== Legacy ==
''Sorcerer''{{'}}s box office flop status had since led to comparisons with other financial failures of the time, particularly [[Michael Cimino]]'s ''[[Heaven's Gate (film)|Heaven's Gate]]'', [[Francis Ford Coppola]]'s ''[[One from the Heart]]'', and [[Martin Scorsese]]'s ''[[New York, New York (1977 film)|New York, New York]]''. Critics argued that the fiasco of these films, among others, contributed to ending a period of auteur approach to the American cinema that was prominent in the 1970s.<ref name="highconcept">{{cite book | title=High Concept: Movies and Marketing in Hollywood | url=https://archive.org/details/highconceptmovie00wyat | url-access=registration | year=1994| publisher=University of Texas Press| first=Justin|last=Wyatt|page=[https://archive.org/details/highconceptmovie00wyat/page/75 75]}}</ref>

In the opinion of several critics, the release of ''Star Wars'' marked a distinctive demographic shift among the audiences, as well as altering trends in the movie industry drastically, which at the same time contributed to ''Sorcerer''{{'}}s financial and critical fiasco. Sean Macaulay notes that ''Star Wars'' changed the movie-going demography, considerably "reset[ting] American cinema back to comforting fantasy".<ref name="telegraph">{{cite news | url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/film/10118338/William-Friedkin-interview-You-dont-need-to-know-about-my-sexual-liaisons.html | work=The Sunday Telegraph | first=Sean | last=Macaulay | title=William Friedkin Interview: 'You Don't Need to Know About My Sexual Liaisons' | date=2013-06-18 | access-date=2013-07-01 | archive-date=February 19, 2018 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180219150633/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/film/10118338/William-Friedkin-interview-You-dont-need-to-know-about-my-sexual-liaisons.html | url-status=live }}</ref> According to reviewer [[Pauline Kael]], ''Star Wars'' contributed to "infantilizing the audience", as well as "obliterating irony, self-consciousness, and critical reflection",{{sfn|Biskind|1998|p=344}} and to Tom Shone, who drew from Kael, was impossible to compete with by Friedkin and ''Sorcerer''.<ref name="blockbuster">{{cite book | title=Blockbuster: How Hollywood Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Summer | year=2004| publisher=Simon & Schuster| page=10 | first=Tom|last=Shone}}</ref> Biskind also thought the American movie-going demographic had changed considerably since ''The French Connection'', and ''Sorcerer'' was "too episodic, dark, and star-challenged" to achieve mainstream appreciation.{{sfn|Biskind|1998|p=338}} RH Greene argues that ''Star Wars'', which in his opinion was "pure escapism", made intellectually demanding films like ''Sorcerer'' obsolete.<ref name="scpr">{{cite news | url=http://www.scpr.org/programs/offramp/2013/05/02/31615/rh-greene-reevaluates-wm-friedkin-s-flop-sorcerer/ | work=Southern California Public Radio | first=RH | last=Greene | title=RH Greene reevaluates Wm Friedkin's 'flop,' 'Sorcerer' | date=2013-05-02 | access-date=2013-07-01 | archive-date=July 28, 2013 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130728050953/http://www.scpr.org/programs/offramp/2013/05/02/31615/rh-greene-reevaluates-wm-friedkin-s-flop-sorcerer/ | url-status=live }}</ref>

Bill Gibron marks the demise of unrestrained writer-director creative control in favor of studio-governed film-making with ''Heaven's Gate'', and adds that ''Sorcerer'' also significantly contributed to this trend.<ref name="popmatters">{{cite news | url=http://www.popmatters.com/pm/post/162300-craftsmanship-vs.-crap-criterions-planned-released-of-heavens-gate/ | work=PopMatters | first=Bill | last=Gibron | title=Craftsmanship vs. Crap: Criterion's Planned Re-release of 'Heaven's Gate' | date=2012-08-27 | access-date=2013-07-01 | archive-date=January 30, 2013 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130130161451/http://www.popmatters.com/pm/post/162300-craftsmanship-vs.-crap-criterions-planned-released-of-heavens-gate/ | url-status=live }}</ref> [[Sheldon Hall (film historian)|Sheldon Hall]] theorizes that success of films like ''Jaws'' and ''Star Wars'' set the trends in Hollywood cinema for the decades to come. This was, in contrast to the "subversive attitude" which then journalists heralded as the pinnacle of filmmaking. Hall observes that films such as ''[[MASH (film)|M*A*S*H]]'', ''[[Deliverance]]'', ''[[One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest (film)|One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest]]'', ''[[Dog Day Afternoon]]'' and ''[[All the President's Men (film)|All the President's Men]]'' "have few equivalents in Hollywood after the 1970s". Furthermore, he states that the last favorable year for New Hollywood was 1976, and "socially critical, stylistically adventurous cinema" would soon be substituted by "ideologically and formally conservative work" of directors like Steven Spielberg and George Lucas. The critic holds the opinion that several financial fiascoes, including ''Sorcerer'', ''New York, New York'', ''One From the Heart'', and ''Heaven's Gate'', were auteur movies aspiring to achieve mainstream success but were panned by the movie-goers and critics alike.<ref name="contusacinema">{{cite book | title=Contemporary American Cinema | url=https://archive.org/details/contemporaryamer00will | url-access=limited | year=2006| publisher=McGraw-Hill International| page=[https://archive.org/details/contemporaryamer00will/page/n205 180] | first=Sheldon|last=Hall|editor=Linda Ruth Williams, Michael Hammond}}</ref> This belief is also held by J. Hoberman to whom the period immediately following 1975's ''One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest'' marked the point when "experimental films became less and less able to recoup their costs".<ref name="hoberman">{{cite news | work=American Film | first=J. | last=Hoberman| title=1975-1985:Ten Years That Shook the World |page=38| date=June 1985}}</ref>

Justin Wyatt concludes that the downfall of "the experimental period" was followed by a retreat to "large-scale grand filmmaking", a Hollywood staple from early to mid-1960s and adds that filmmakers such as [[Peter Bogdanovich]], Friedkin, and [[Arthur Penn]] still continued their cinematic involvement but their most ambitious work had been produced during the peak of [[New Hollywood]] era, which was characterized by "financial experimentation".<ref name="highconcept" />{{rp|page=77}} Nat Segaloff observes that cinematic trends presented in ''Sorcerer'' were later abandoned by the studio system,<ref name="harvard" /> an opinion mirrored by Phil Mucci, who holds the opinion that ''Sorcerer'' stands for a cinematic style that is unlikely to be seen again".<ref name="twitch" /> William Friedkin states in the 2003 documentary ''[[A Decade Under the Influence (film)|A Decade Under the Influence]]'' that cynicism was a ubiquitous attitude in the country during the 1970s, so the studios were receptive to it, which made "filmmakers and the studio heads be in sync" and added that artistic content was never questioned, only the costs. On the other hand, the director thinks this trend is impossible to return, because he feels that nowadays "a film has to serve the greater good of the corporation in order to get made and it cannot be subversive in nature. As well as, has to have the broadest possible appeal, so that it will help other divisions of the corporation".<ref name="influence">{{cite AV media | people=Demme, Ted (director) | date=2003-01-19 | title=A Decade Under the Influence | medium=Motion picture | publisher=Constant Communication}}</ref>

Friedkin sat for an interview with the Danish director [[Nicolas Winding Refn]] in February 2015, in which they discussed the film at length. It was produced by the French distribution company La Rabbia.<ref>{{cite web |title=Sorcerers: A Conversation with William Friedkin and Nicolas Winding Refn |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BOc__mvXcOg& |website=YouTube |access-date=26 August 2022}}</ref>

The film was selected for screening as part of the Cannes Classics section at the [[2016 Cannes Film Festival]].<ref name="Classics">{{cite web |url=http://www.festival-cannes.fr/en/article/62136.html |title=Cannes Classics 2016 |access-date=21 April 2016 |date=20 April 2016 |work=Cannes Film Festival |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170210012746/http://www.festival-cannes.fr/en/article/62136.html |archive-date=February 10, 2017 |url-status=dead |df=mdy-all }}</ref>

In 2017, Friedkin described ''Sorcerer'' as "the only film I’ve made that I can still watch."<ref name="indiewire-2017">{{cite web |url=https://www.indiewire.com/features/general/william-friedkin-hollywood-blockbusters-exorcist-sorcerer-lumiere-festival-1201889301/ |title=William Friedkin Says Hollywood Has Been 'Reduced to Blockbusters' |access-date=13 August 2023 |date=20 October 2017 |work=IndieWire }}</ref>

== Court case, restoration, and re-release ==
In April 2012, it was reported that Friedkin was suing Universal and Paramount over the domestic rights of ''Sorcerer'' for a share of the movie's profits. In a July 2012 interview, Friedkin said that the film's case was pending at the [[Ninth District Court of Appeals]] in California with a settlement to be announced by November 26. Had no settlement been reached by that time, the jury would have to set a trial date for March 2013. The director emphasized that his intent was not dictated by profits but by the desire to have it released on DVD and [[Blu-ray]], and to have a film print for various outlets, such as [[film society|film societies]] and universities. He also noted that if the case were to become precedential, he hoped it would help other pictures in a similar situation.<ref name="avclub">{{cite news | url=https://www.avclub.com/william-friedkin-talks-killer-joe-and-shares-some-choic-1798232491 | work=[[The A.V. Club]] | first=Sam | last=Adams | title=Interview: William Friedkin Talks Killer Joe and Shares Some Choice Words About Hollywood | date=2012-07-27 | access-date=2013-06-28 | archive-date=July 30, 2012 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120730075204/http://www.avclub.com/articles/william-friedkin-talks-killer-joe-and-shares-some%2C83023/ | url-status=live }}</ref>

In a July 2012 interview, Friedkin said Universal and Paramount both claimed they did not own the film and did not know who did, a consequence of the bankruptcy of [[Cinema International Corporation]], a company granted an ownership by Universal Studios and Paramount Pictures, and commissioned to release films in international markets. Friedkin said he believed any issues related to the matter were of bookkeeping nature.<ref name="avclub" />

In December 2012, Friedkin revealed that the film rights were in fact owned by Universal, as the Paramount lease had expired after 25 years. He also added he would meet [[Warner Bros.]], which wanted a sublease, and also announced that he would be meeting with the head of [[Universal Studios, Inc.|Universal Studios]]; if the outcome was negative, he would have to resort to a legal case. Friedkin also indicated that restoration of ''Sorcerer'' would require a considerable amount of work, stating that he did not, at the time, possess any prints of good quality. He added that Paramount had made a print around the beginning of 2012, which was shown at the [[American Cinematheque]]'s [[Aero Theatre]], and he was trying to locate it, noting difficulties related to obtaining the print as the studio no longer possessed an adequate capacity to deal with the matter, and off-shore companies involved in the legal matters were now greatly reduced in staff. He said that was why acquiring the film's print was time-consuming.<ref name="AICN">{{cite news | url=http://www.aintitcool.com/node/60117 | work=Ain't It Cool News | first=Jeremy | last=Smith | title=AICN Legends: William Friedkin Talks KILLER JOE, Clarence Carter, SORCERER And More With Mr. Beaks! | date=2012-12-20 | access-date=2013-06-28 | archive-date=December 30, 2012 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121230195729/http://www.aintitcool.com/node/60117 | url-status=live }}</ref>

On February 11, 2013, Friedkin announced that money had been budgeted to create a new, digital master copy of ''Sorcerer''. He also asserted that the original negative is in a good state.<ref name="twitter1">{{cite tweet|user=WilliamFriedkin|number=301145196299694080|author=William Friedkin|date=2013-02-11|access-date=2013-06-28|title=Re: SORCERER. The original negative is in good condition And it's now being budgeted to make a new digital master. I'll keep you updated.}}</ref> He followed this with a statement that [[The Criterion Collection]] would not be the film's publisher.<ref name="twitter2">{{cite tweet|user=WilliamFriedkin|number=301147716245942272|author=William Friedkin|date=2013-02-11|access-date=2013-06-28|title=Guys I can only tell you that SORCERER will not be Released by Criterion. More info as it develops.}}</ref>

In March 2013, Friedkin revealed that he had dropped his lawsuit against Universal and Paramount, and that he and a "major studio" were involved in the creation of a new, recolored digital print of ''Sorcerer'', to be tentatively screened at the [[Venice Film Festival]] and to receive a [[Blu-ray]] release:
{{blockquote|We're working off the original negative, which is in pretty good shape, but without changing the original concept we have to bring it back in terms of color saturation, sharpness and all the stuff... The film been in a legal whirlpool for 30 or 35 years. And a lot of people have come and gone from the studios during that time, so it just takes awhile to unravel everything, but we're very close to announcing a premiere date.<ref name="The Wrap" />}}

On April 14, 2013, the aforementioned 35&nbsp;mm print of ''Sorcerer'' from the Paramount archives was screened at the [[Chicago Film Critics Association]]'s first annual film festival, with Friedkin in attendance. He remarked that the film "hasn't dated... It's set in a kind of limbo and neither the haircuts nor the wardrobes nor the sets have aged poorly."<ref name="The Wrap">{{cite news | url=http://www.thewrap.com/movies/article/william-friedkins-misunderstood-1977-sorcerer-getting-re-release-exclusive-81966 | work=The Wrap | first=Brent | last=Lang | title=William Friedkin's Misunderstood 1977 'Sorcerer' Getting Re-Release (Exclusive) | date=2013-03-21 | access-date=2013-06-28 | archive-date=April 20, 2013 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130420135810/http://www.thewrap.com/movies/article/william-friedkins-misunderstood-1977-sorcerer-getting-re-release-exclusive-81966 | url-status=live }}</ref>

On May 2, 2013, the director announced the pending re-release, a new, digital print, and a premiere at the [[Venice Film Festival]] on August 29.<ref name="twitter3">{{cite tweet|user=WilliamFriedkin|number=329957029651288066|author=William Friedkin|date=2013-05-02|access-date=2013-06-28|title=SORCERER will be rereleased this year with a new digital Print. The world premiere is on my birthday, Aug.29, At the Venicice festival.}}</ref> where he would also receive a lifetime achievement award.<ref name="variety1" />

Restoration of the print was supervised by Friedkin himself, along with Ned Price<ref name="twitter4">{{cite tweet|user=WilliamFriedkin|number=329959260953931776|author=William Friedkin|date=2013-05-02|access-date=2013-06-28|title=In answer to your questions, yes there will be a DVD and a blu-ray Supervised by my friend Ned Price, and me.}}</ref> and a [[Color grading|colorist]], Bryan McMahan, Friedkin's collaborator since 1994.<ref name="variety1" /> In addition, Friedkin also confirmed there would be DVD and Blu-ray disc releases.<ref name="twitter4" /><ref name="twitter5">{{cite tweet|user=WilliamFriedkin|number=329958038595330048|author=William Friedkin|date=2013-05-02|access-date=2013-06-28|title=Warner Bros and Universal will share the release In all media. Gratitude to all of you who lobbied for this.}}</ref> Friedkin also stated that Warner Bros. financed the restoration, and that the distribution rights would be split between Paramount for theatrical, Warner Bros. for home and streaming media, and Universal for television.<ref name="HBF" /> According to Friedkin, making of the new print was to commence in June 2013.<ref name="twitter6">{{cite tweet|user=WilliamFriedkin|number=332575007408529408|author=William Friedkin|date=2013-05-09|access-date=2013-06-28|title=I LOVE Patton Oswalt but the Aero screening tonite is Not a restored print. It's the best 35&nbsp;mm available. We Make a new digital copy in June}}</ref> The director described his efforts to restore and re-release ''Sorcerer'' as "a truly Lazarus moment" and said he was gratified that "it’s going to have a new life in cinema".<ref name="variety1" />

On June 4, 2013, the director declared that the [[color grading]] would commence on June 10, 2013,<ref name="twitter7">{{cite tweet|user=WilliamFriedkin|number=342130591178833920|author=William Friedkin|date=2013-06-04|access-date=2013-06-28|title=Color timing for the digital print of Sorcerer starts on Monday, June 10th. Premiere at Venice Film Festival, August 29th.}}</ref> which said was completed by June 25. There was no distortion of original colors, he said, and a [[5.1 surround sound]] transfer was planned for June 28, 2013.<ref name="twitter8">{{cite tweet|user=WilliamFriedkin|number=349689587708338176|author=William Friedkin|date=2013-06-25|access-date=2013-06-28|title=SORCERER color timing, first pass is complete. Color has not been altered, just restored. Friday, the sound transfer to 5.1 begins.}}</ref> Moreover, he also revealed an [[audio commentary]] and extra features would be part of the Blu-ray release.<ref name="twitter9">{{cite tweet|user=WilliamFriedkin|number=349696059674607616|author=William Friedkin|date=2013-06-25|access-date=2013-06-28|title=I will do a commentary for Sorcerer, there will be a blu-ray And extras; first, the theatrical.}}</ref> On July 17, 2013, Friedkin announced that the film's soundtrack has been remastered.<ref name="twitter11">{{cite tweet|user=WilliamFriedkin|number=357673303814574080|author=William Friedkin|date=2013-07-17|access-date=2013-09-22|title=Sorcerer soundtrack remastered. Sounds great.}}</ref> Two days before the Venice screening, Friedkin announced that a theatrical screening had been booked at Los Angeles' [[Cinefamily]] for spring 2014.<ref name="HBF">Turan, Kenneth (August 27, 2013). [http://www.latimes.com/entertainment/movies/moviesnow/la-et-mn-william-friedkin-20130827,0,2521372.story William Friedkin celebrates a Golden Lion, restored 'Sorcerer.'] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130905082453/http://www.latimes.com/entertainment/movies/moviesnow/la-et-mn-william-friedkin-20130827,0,2521372.story |date=September 5, 2013 }} ''[[Los Angeles Times]]''.</ref> On September 12, 2013, Friedkin revealed April 14, 2014 would be the release date of the film's Blu-ray home video version.<ref name="twitter10" />

'''''The Gardener's Son''''' is a 1977 American [[Historical drama|historical]] [[crime drama|crime]] [[Drama (film and television)|drama]] [[television film]] directed by [[Richard Pearce (director)|Richard Pearce]] and written by [[Cormac McCarthy]]. Set in the [[company town]] of [[Graniteville, South Carolina]] during the [[Reconstruction era]], the story is based on a real historical 1876 murder and subsequent trial. ''The Gardener's Son'' dramatizes the tensions between the working-class McEvoy family and the wealthy Greggs, whose patriarch owned the town [[cotton mill]]. [[Brad Dourif]] stars as Robert McEvoy, a disgruntled amputee who in 1876 killed James Gregg ([[Kevin Conway (actor)|Kevin Conway]]). The plot presents the complex material and psychological conditions for the crime while leaving the ultimate question of [[Motive (law)|motive]] ambiguous.

The [[Public broadcasting in the United States|public television]] station [[KCET]] produced the film as the twelfth entry in its anthology series ''[[Visions (1976 TV series)|Visions]]''. Pearce, known as a [[documentary film|documentarian]], was new to filming a fictionalized story. He learned of the story of the McEvoys and Greggs in a footnote from a biography of [[William Gregg (industrialist)|William Gregg]], an influential industrialist and father of James. Impressed by McCarthy's novel ''[[Child of God]]'' (1973), Pearce asked the author to write what would be his first screenplay. While developing the screenplay, McCarthy and Pearce spent several months researching the circumstances of the murder, the community's reaction to the crime, and the socioeconomic conditions in Graniteville during the period.

Though set in South Carolina, ''The Gardener's Son'' was mostly filmed around [[Burlington, North Carolina]] and partly in [[Virginia]]. It was shot [[location shooting|on location]] at historical sites that had been scouted for their period accuracy, far from the visible encroachments of modern technology like [[Overhead power line|powerlines]]. Other members of the cast included [[Nan Martin]], [[Jerry Hardin]], Anne O'Sullivan, [[Penelope Allen|Penny Allen]], [[Ned Beatty]], and [[Paul Benjamin]], plus 34 nonprofessional actors from around North Carolina cast in [[bit part]]s. [[Charles Gross]] composed the spare, [[Appalachian music|Appalachian]]-influenced [[Film score|score]].

''The Gardener's Son'' premiered on [[PBS]] stations on January 6, 1977, to positive reviews. It has remained [[out of print]] on [[home video]] for decades, seeing a small-scale [[DVD]] release in 2010. [[The Gardener's Son (screenplay)|McCarthy's screenplay]] was published as a book by [[Ecco Press]] in 1996, containing scenes and lines cut from the film version. Because of its general unavailability, ''The Gardener's Son'' is commonly experienced only as a [[closet drama]] to be read, rather than a film to be watched. The film is remembered for its pivotal place in McCarthy's career as his first dramatic work, his first work of historical fiction, and his first time participating in a film production. Despite several further efforts at screenwriting, McCarthy would not get a second original screenplay made into a film until ''[[The Counselor]]'' (2013).

==Plot==
[[File:William Gregg (undated portrait).jpg|thumb|left|upright=0.8|alt=Photographic portrait at bust length of a bearded man|Undated portrait of [[William Gregg (industrialist)|William Gregg]] (1800–1867), industrialist and patriarch of the Gregg family]]
Dr. Perceval makes a [[house call]] to the Gregg estate in the company town of [[Graniteville, South Carolina]]. [[William Gregg (industrialist)|William Gregg]], the owner of the town cotton mill, is declared dead following an illness. The doctor and Mrs. Gregg then visit the home of Patrick McEvoy, a gardener employed by the Greggs, to attend to his son Robert. Robert's leg had earlier been broken in an industrial accident, for which William's son James may be at fault. Seeing that the leg has become badly infected, Mrs. Gregg convinces Robert to assent to [[amputation]]. William Gregg is buried in a well-attended ceremony with an adulatory [[eulogy]].

Robert, now equipped with a prosthetic leg and crutch, takes a job sweeping up at the mill. A group of impoverished people come by train to Graniteville seeking work but James, now the mill's owner, turns them away. Over supper, with Robert absent, the McEvoys discuss his perplexing, troubled nature. Mrs. Gregg and James visit the grave of an unnamed boy who died visiting Graniteville in 1855. James chides his mother for her paternalistic concern for the poor. Robert's 14-year-old sister Martha, who works [[Spinning mule|spinning cotton]], goes looking for Robert and finds James, who makes lewd remarks and offers to pay her a [[Gold coin|gold piece]], prompting her to flee. Mr. Giles, an assistant at the mill, finds Patrick in his [[greenhouse|glasshouse]] and inquires after Robert, who has been absent from work. Patrick answers that he does not know his son's whereabouts.

Some time later, Martha writes a letter to Robert telling him "mama has took sick again" and that she and her father wish he would return home. Robert hops off a horse-drawn cart and drives away two black gravediggers when he discovers they are burying his mother, who he says "don't belong to the mill." Robert finds his father's glasshouse barren and learns he is no longer employed as a gardener. That night Robert drinks whiskey and commiserates with employees of the mill, including Pinky. The next morning, Robert wakes up in a barn. As Patrick starts his shift at the mill, he learns his son has returned. Robert confronts James in his office. After an argument ensues, James surmises that Robert is there begging for money and offers him a gold piece. Robert draws a pistol. James reaches for a desk drawer. Robert shoots him in the stomach and exits the mill. James stumbles outside and fires at Robert, missing. Robert returns fire, killing James. Patrick and other mill employees walk outside.

Robert stands trial, accused of murder. The prosecutor reads an opening statement before a majority-black jury. Mr. Giles and another witness testify. After trial, Robert's attorney O. C. Jordan speaks with a discouraged Patrick, telling him that he is confident Robert will go free, and that it would be unwise for Robert to testify as doing so would risk an unpopular sullying of the Gregg name. Jordan also reveals that the defense has agreed with Mrs. Gregg to avoid calling any female witnesses. A constable asks Patrick to return home to bury his wife, as neighbors can smell her corpse 4 houses away. Patrick breaks down and cries. Starks Sims, a boy who works for Mr. Giles, testifies that he witnessed Robert shoot James. W. J. Whipper, a black attorney for Robert's defense, cross-examines Starks; Whipper asks if Starks had ever read any notes written by James to any female employees of the mill. Starks replies that he had never done so because he is illiterate. That night, Patrick goes to ask Whipper to have Robert testify and Whipper responds that it would not be possible because of Robert's erratic nature, but reassures Patrick and counsels him about the limitations of the law.

At trial, Robert is sentenced to death. Martha goes to Mrs. Gregg, apparently to plead her brother's innocence, but then tells Mrs. Gregg that James "never done nothing" to her. Believing Martha is there to console her, Mrs. Gregg takes ease and asks her servant Daphne to bring tea. Martha says that the Greggs "must have failed him somewhere". Martha says she wonders what she would have said if asked to testify and speculates that she would have told about the gold piece, but downplays its significance. Enraged, Mrs. Gregg orders her to leave.

Robert poses in a [[Photographic studio|studio]] for a portrait photograph taken, seated, from the waist up, taking care that his legs not be shown. The photographer asks if copies might be made to print for sale, with half of the proceeds to go to his family. Robert replies that he does not mind if people are ignorant enough to buy his image, but does not want his family to know where any proceeds are sent from. In the street, Martha encounters Robert, who says he was never meant to be hanged and should have gone to the penitentiary. Martha says she would have testified and told "any kind of lie" in his defense. Robert tells her to forget she had a brother and to find the best man she can and make him treat her right. Robert is executed by hanging. Dr. Perceval declares the time of death. Patrick takes his son's body in a coffin onto a cart and rides away.

[[Cormac McCarthy]] makes a brief, uncredited [[cameo appearance]] in a non-speaking role as a stockholding investor in the mill.{{sfn|Frye|2020|p=xix}} His cameo occurs just before the scene of the killing. Dressed in a dark coat and [[top hat]], he can be spotted within a crowd of fellow businessmen on a tour of the mill, distinguishable as the youngest-looking member of the group. Stacey Peebles—a scholar of McCarthy's works—likened his small role to [[Alfred Hitchcock]]'s [[List of cameo appearances by Alfred Hitchcock|famous cameos]] in his own films, though rendered ironic by the fact that the obscure author would have been unrecognizable to the viewing audience.{{sfn|Peebles|2017|p=15}}

==Development==
===Background on ''Visions'' series===
{{Main|Visions (1976 TV series)}}
{{Image frame|content=[[File:Visions (1976 TV series logo).png|frameless|upright=1.3|alt=Logo; see caption]]|caption={{center|''Visions'' series logo with slogan:<br/>"It's [[off-Broadway]] television."}}|align=left|border=no}}

''The Gardener's Son'' was produced by [[KCET]], a Los Angeles-based [[PBS]] affiliate station, as the twelfth installment in its ''[[Visions (1976 TV series)|Visions]]'' series of made-for-television drama films.{{sfn|Krafft|1991|pp=100, 102}} The series sought out original [[teleplay]]s by American writers with no prior experience in television.{{sfn|Kriegsman|1977}} Many of the films were [[historical drama]]s, like ''The Gardener's Son''.{{sfn|Peebles|2017|p=15}} ''Visions'' often addressed serious social issues with "a deliberate pace far removed from the forced urgency of commercial television", and served as "a proving ground for drama on public television as well as for talented actors, directors and writers".{{sfn|Krafft|1991|p=100}} Advertising materials pitched ''Visions'' as "[[Off-Broadway]] television".{{sfn|Josyph|2010|p=40}}

Production of ''The Gardener's Son'' cost $200,000.{{sfn|Pearce|1996|p=vi}} Its budget reflected the average expenditure for entries in the ''Visions'' series, each made with much less money than the typical hour-long episode of major [[network era]] dramas.{{efn|By comparison, in 1977 the cost to produce a one-hour episode of the hit police procedural ''[[Hawaii Five-O (1968 TV series)|Hawaii Five-O]]'' was $385,000.{{sfn|Kriegsman|1977}}}} Funding was provided by the [[National Endowment for the Arts]], the [[Ford Foundation]], and the [[Corporation for Public Broadcasting]].{{sfn|Kriegsman|1977}}

===Conception===
In the mid-1970s, [[Richard Pearce (director)|Richard Pearce]] was known for his work as a cinematographer on [[documentary film]]s such as ''[[Hearts and Minds (film)|Hearts and Minds]]''&nbsp;(1974). Pearce had come across the story of while conducting research on a journalism [[Grant (money)|grant]] from the [[Alicia Patterson Foundation]].{{sfn|Cook|1976|p=29}} He was using the grant funds to research the lives of Southern [[Textile industry|textile workers]] in the late 19th century.{{sfn|''Statesville Record & Landmark''|1977|loc=front page}} He became interested in the 1876 murder of James Gregg by Robert McEvoy after reading about it in the footnote of a history book, later learning that the story had endured in local [[folklore]].{{sfn|O'Connor|1977|p=59}} Pearce went to Graniteville and spoke with many descendants of the original textile workers who came to the town in the 1840s, who he said "still tell Robert McEvoy's story—stories, I should say, because there are now at least eight or nine different versions."{{sfn|''The Daily Times-News''|1977|p=10}} Pearce pitched the story to ''Vision'', and he was commissioned to direct and co-produce an episode.{{sfn|''Statesville Record & Landmark''|1977|loc=front page}} It would mark his first effort in fictional filmmaking.{{sfn|Pearce|1996|pp=v–vi}}

{{Quote box
|quote = It is not about one character. It is about two families and the strange circumstances surrounding the death of James Gregg. It is really the story of the mill in those times. And it is very much the story of William Gregg, who was very much beloved by his mill-town people. The town was his garden.
|author = Pearce
|source = speaking to the press, 1977{{sfn|''Statesville Record & Landmark''|1977|loc=front page}}
|bgcolor = 
|width = 25em
|align = right
|salign  = right
}}

Pearce consulted Tom Terrill, an economic historian at [[University of South Carolina]]. Terrill later published the article "Murder in Graniteville", giving an authoritative account of McEvoy's murder of Gregg.{{sfn|Luce|1999|p=75}} Terrill identified Pearce's source for the McEvoy–Gregg story as [[Broadus Mitchell]]'s 1928 biography of [[William Gregg (industrialist)|William Gregg]], owner of the Graniteville mill and one of the most significant industrialists of the [[Antebellum South]].{{sfn|Luce|1999|p=72}} Mitchell's biography is a flattering portrayal of the elder Gregg, with a highly positive assessment of his patricianly leadership during the period of rapid [[Industrialisation|industrialization]]. Gregg viewed the South's transition from an agrarian to a manufacturing-based economy as a means of enriching the [[Common good|general welfare of ordinary people]] and [[Poverty reduction|reducing poverty]].{{sfn|Peebles|2017|p=23}} Mitchell's biography characterized Robert McEvoy's crime as an act of thoughtless violence perpetrated by the "bad boy of the village". Contrarily, Terrill analyzed it as a vindictive eruption of [[class consciousness]] by an alienated worker against a capitalist.{{sfn|Peebles|2017|p=25}} Pearce conducted and taped original interviews with Graniteville residents in 1974 and exchanged research materials with Terrill.{{sfn|Terrill|1982|p=218 (fn.&nbsp;18)}}

===Research and screenwriting===
{{multiple image
| align = left
| total_width = 268
| caption_align = center
| image1 = Cormac McCarthy (Child of God author portrait - high-res).jpg
| alt1 = Photo portrait of Cormac McCarthy from the first edition of ''Child of God''.
| caption1 = 
| image2 = Child of God - Cormac McCarthy.jpg
| alt2 = First-edition dust cover jacket for ''Child of God''
| caption2 = 
| footer = McCarthy was asked to write a screenplay on the strength of his third novel, ''[[Child of God]]'' (1973). Pearce had been impressed by its demonstration of McCarthy's "[[Negative capability|Negative Capability]]".{{sfn|Pearce|1996|p=v}}}}

Pearce asked the novelist [[Cormac McCarthy]] to adapt the story of the McEvoys and the Greggs into a dramatic [[screenplay]].{{efn|Pearce also claimed to have reached out to [[Eudora Welty]] as a potential screenwriter.{{sfn|Pearce|1996|p=v}}}} To reach the author, whom he did not know personally, he sent a postcard to a [[Post office box|P.O. box]] in [[El Paso, Texas]].{{efn|According to a January 1977 newspaper article, McCarthy had been in [[Mexico]] "working on a novel".{{sfn|''Statesville Record & Landmark''|1977|loc=front page}} He was then a resident of Tennessee, though he would later move to El Paso full-time. The novel in question would be ''[[Blood Meridian]]'' (1985), which McCarthy started researching in the Southwest in 1974.{{sfn|Frye|2020|p=xix}}}}{{sfn|Pearce|1996|p=v}} McCarthy was an obscure novelist at the time and had no prior experience in filmmaking.{{efn|McCarthy had taken an active interest in managing the [[film rights]] of his first two novels, ''[[The Orchard Keeper]]'' (1965) and ''[[Outer Dark]]'' (1968), which had been considered for cinematic adaptation but ultimately passed over.{{sfn|Peebles|2017|pp=15, 22}} He also claimed "motion picture acting" among various odd jobs he claimed to have held in a questionnaire submitted to his publisher, [[Random House]], in 1964.{{sfn|Peebles|2017|pp=21}}}} Pearce had been impressed by McCarthy's third and most recent novel, ''[[Child of God]]''&nbsp;(1973), which tells the story of an alienated Appalachian man's descent into [[necrophilia]] and murder.{{sfn|Mitchell|2020|pp=249–250}} Already acquainted with the author's early work, Pearce felt especially impressed by the latest novel:

{{blockquote|''Child of God'', the oddest of a wonderfully odd lot, had been the one that struck me. It was easily the most cinematic, but not in the conventional sense of the term. It had a rigor about it, a way of not taking the easy, 'novelistic' route. By never presuming an [[Artistic license|author's license]] to enter the mind of his protagonist, McCarthy had been able to insure the almost complete inscrutability of his subject and subject matter, while at the same time thoroughly investigating it. Here was "[[Negative capability|Negative Capability]]" of a very high order. I was hooked.{{sfn|Pearce|1996|p=v}}}}

Pearce and McCarthy collaborated on the screenplay, working between [[motel]]s in South Carolina and McCarthy's residence in [[Blount County, Tennessee]]. Research lasted from early April to November 19, 1975, as documented in a series of "research newsletters" sent by Pearce to the Alicia Patterson Foundation.{{sfn|Luce|1999|pp=73–74}} Pearce had already found many [[primary source]]s and [[public records]] for McCarthy to use as reference material. McCarthy's primary responsibility was [[dramatization]] of the historical material, though he soon became just as engaged with the research as Pearce.{{sfn|Josyph|2010|pp=139–140 (fn.&nbsp;5)}} The work brought them to the courthouse in [[Aiken, South Carolina|Aiken]] and newspaper archives housed in [[Augusta, Georgia]]; McCarthy remarked that the latter were more useful.{{sfn|''Statesville Record & Landmark''|1977|loc=front page}}

{{Quote box
|quote = We used all the facts—all the names are those of actual people involved. It is as accurate as possible, but it was a reconstruction of the events.
|author = McCarthy
|source = speaking to the press, 1977{{sfn|''Statesville Record & Landmark''|1977|loc=front page}}
|bgcolor = 
|width = 25em
|align =
|salign = right
}}

As their work continued, Pearce and McCarthy uncovered numerous historical details that complicated Mitchell's rosy narrative of the Gregg family and their impact on the regional economy. They learned of an 1875 [[Strike action|labor strike]] responding to docked wages and an 1877 petition to the governor, bearing hundreds of signatures, requesting that he [[Commutation (law)|commute]] McEvoy's death sentence.{{sfn|Peebles|2017|p=25}} "We spent four weeks," McCarthy said, "in South Carolina researching the thing—in Columbia I even found a 22-page letter McEvoy had written [[Wade Hampton III|Gov. Wade Hampton]]. And even then no one was quite sure why McEvoy did it. He just came into Gregg's office one day and shot him."{{sfn|Carr|1976|p=A15}}

Pearce and McCarthy decided to leave the question of Robert McEvoy's [[Motive (law)|motive]] purposely ambiguous.{{sfn|Peebles|2017|p=25}} McCarthy told the Burlington ''[[Times-News (Burlington, North Carolina)|Daily Times-News]]'' that the killing happened for no apparent reason, or "at least no single, clearly-defined reason, but obviously occurred because of a multiplicity of intertwined ideas and relationships that took their toll on the boy who was to become a murder".{{sfn|Blanchard|1976c|p=6D}}{{efn|A nearly identical statement appears in the ''[[Knoxville News Sentinel|Knoxville News-Sentinel]]''{{'}}s January 1977 profile of McCarthy, though it is presented within the journalist's prose as part of the article text itself, not as a quote attributed to McCarthy nor anyone else: "The killing apparently took place for no reason, at least no single, clearly-defined reason, but obviously occurred because of a multiplicity of intertwined ideas and relationships that took their toll on the boy who was to become a murderer." See {{harvnb|Luce|Turpin|2022|p=127}}.}} Pearce aimed to achieve a plausible, authentic portrayal of the character's emotional state without definitively spelling out the factors that cause the killing.{{sfn|Josyph|2010|p=157 (fn.&nbsp;3)}} The narrative's uncertainty and complexity, Pearce said, were "a reaction against the type of movies on TV" in which {{nowrap|"[n]othing}} is left open to several interpretations, nothing is left to the imagination. I bent over backwards to avoid doing that. In so many movies, the motives and characters are too clearly defined. Life isn't that way."{{sfn|Lester|1978|p=1-C}}

McCarthy valued [[verisimilitude (fiction)|verisimilitude]] and drew every named character in ''The Gardener's Son'' from a verifiable person in the historical record.{{sfn|''Statesville Record & Landmark''|1977|loc=front page}} Beyond historical and literary influences, McCarthy likely drew cinematic inspiration from film titles listed in his archived notes, such as ''[[Black Orpheus]]'' (1959), ''[[La Dolce Vita]]'' (1960), ''[[In Cold Blood (film)|In Cold Blood]]'' (1967), and ''[[The Great Gatsby (1974 film)|The Great Gatsby]]'' (1974).{{sfn|Crews|2017|p=39}} Like the McEvoys, McCarthy remarked he too had grown up [[Irish Catholic]] in the South within majority-Protestant communities. Regarding Robert McEvoy's status as "a [[black sheep]], the bad boy of the town," McCarthy said: "That was familiar to me, too. The kid was a natural rebel, probably just a troublemaker in real life. But in our film he has a certain nobility. He stands up and says, 'No, this is intolerable and I want to do something about it!{{' "}}{{sfn|Luce|Turpin|2022|p=127}}

==Production==
===Casting===
[[File:Dourif Pearce Hausman McCarthy (1976-03-23 photograph - crop).jpg|thumb|left|alt=Photograph of four men standing indoors|upright=2.4|Top cast and crew (''left to right'': Dourif, Pearce, Hausman, and McCarthy) at a press conference in [[Graham, North Carolina]] on March 23, 1976, promoting local auditions.{{sfn|Blanchard|1976a|p=1B}}]]

[[Casting (performing arts)|Casting]] was primarily handled by co-producer Michael Hausman, whose previous experience included [[Miloš Forman]]'s ''[[Taking Off (film)|Taking Off]]'' (1971) and [[Elaine May]]'s ''[[The Heartbreak Kid (1972 film)|The Heartbreak Kid]]'' (1972) and ''[[Mikey and Nicky]]'' (1976).{{sfn|''Statesville Record & Landmark''|1977|loc=front page}} "We stressed to the actors," Hausman said, "that this is a 'prestige' venture rather than a profit-making one, since we obviously couldn't offer larger salaries."{{sfn|Blanchard|1976a|p=1B}} Despite the modest budget, Pearce said he found casting straightforward because the quality of writing provided by McCarthy drew actors' attention.{{sfn|Cook|1976|p=30}}

[[Brad Dourif]], cast in the lead role of Robert McEvoy, told the press he chose to join the project for its screenplay.{{sfn|Blanchard|1976a|p=1B}} Dourif had [[48th Academy Awards|recently]] been nominated for the [[Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor]] for his role in ''[[One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest (film)|One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest]]'' (1975).{{sfn|Cook|1976|p=30}} Hausman convinced [[Ned Beatty]] to play the role of Pinky by scheduling his scene to be filmed when he could stop en route to New York from an unrelated shoot further south.{{sfn|''Statesville Record & Landmark''|1977|loc=front page}} The main cast is rounded out by [[Kevin Conway (actor)|Kevin Conway]], [[Nan Martin]], Anne O'Sullivan, [[Penelope Allen|Penny Allen]], [[Jerry Hardin]], and [[Paul Beatty]].{{sfnm|1a1=Cook|1y=1976|1p=30|2a1=Blanchard|2y=1976a|2p=1B}}

More than 100 North Carolinians participated as [[Extra (acting)|extras]], while another 34 locals had [[bit part]]s.{{sfn|Newton|1976|p={{nowrap|C-1}}}} [[Audition]]s were held in [[Winston-Salem, North Carolina|Winston-Salem]], [[Charlotte, North Carolina|Charlotte]], [[Raleigh, North Carolina|Raleigh]], and [[Chapel Hill, North Carolina|Chapel Hill]].{{sfn|''The Sentinel''|1977|p=20}} With less than a week before filming, the production still needed more adult men as extras for crowd shots, so Pearce, McCarthy, Dourif, and Hausman held a [[press conference]] on March 23, 1976, at the arts center in [[Graham, North Carolina]] to publicize further auditions in the area.{{sfn|Blanchard|1976a|p=1B}} Some parts—like those of the black gravediggers—were cast informally through a truck driver Pearce met at a gas station in Burlington, who he called his "unofficial casting agency" and "one of [his] most valuable contacts".{{sfn|''Statesville Record & Landmark''|1977|loc=front page}}

|caption=Map of [[filming location]]s in North Carolina and Virginia (plus the story's historical setting of Graniteville, South Carolina)}}

Though the story is set in South Carolina, ''The Gardener's Son'' was mostly filmed in [[North Carolina]].{{sfn|Josyph|2010|p=145}} The [[location scouting]] process had led Pearce and McCarthy to consider sites in South Carolina and [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]]. Their main concern was period accuracy, without for example visible [[Overhead power line|power lines]] in the background or modern [[aluminum siding]] on buildings. The crew and lead cast used the city of [[Burlington, North Carolina|Burlington]] as their central base from which to travel for [[location shooting|locations shoots]].{{sfn|Blanchard|1976c|p=6D}}

Cinematographer [[Fred Murphy (cinematographer)|Fred Murphy]] shot ''The Gardener's Son'' [[Color motion picture film|in color]] on [[16 mm film|16&nbsp;mm film]].{{sfn|Josyph|2010|p=145}} Other major crew members on set included [[art director]] [[Patrizia von Brandenstein]] and [[costume designer]] [[Ruth Morley]].{{sfn|David|1978|p=98}} [[Principal photography]] lasted from March 29 to May 7, 1976,{{sfn|Blanchard|1976c|p=6D}} amid an unseasonably warm spring [[heat wave]].{{sfn|''Statesville Record & Landmark''|1977|loc=back page}}

Filming began at [[Glencoe Mill Village Historic District|the restored cotton mill]] in [[Glencoe, North Carolina|Glencoe]], where the majority of the shoot occurred. The Glencoe mill came to the crew's attention through [[Brent Glass]],{{efn|Glass was then employed by the [[State Archives of North Carolina]].{{sfn|Malone|1976|p=20}}}} who was conducting a survey of the region's historic industrial architecture.{{sfn|Blanchard|1976a|p=1B}} Glencoe was used for exterior scenes at the mill, while mill interiors were shot at Baxter, Faust & Kelly Co. [[textile mill]] in Worthville near [[Asheboro, North Carolina|Asheboro]].{{sfn|Lougee|1977|p=1B}} Other [[filming location|shooting locations]] in the Burlington area included a local greenhouse and the cemetery at St. Paul's Episcopal Church{{efn|Most sources describe it as St. Paul's ''Episcopal'' Church,{{sfn|Newton|1976|p=C-6}}{{sfn|''Statesville Record & Landmark''|1977|loc=front page}}{{sfn|Leland|1977|p=1F}}{{sfn|Lougee|1977|p=1B}} though one labels it St. Paul's ''Lutheran'' Church.{{sfn|Blanchard|1976c|p=6D}}}} in [[Alamance, North Carolina|Alamance]] near the [[Alamance Battleground]].{{sfnm|1a1=Blanchard|1y=1976c|1p=6D|2a1=Leland|2y=1977|2p=1F}} Farther locations were the [[Caswell County Courthouse]] and city jailhouse in [[Yanceyville, North Carolina|Yanceyville]];{{sfn|Carr|1976|p=A15}} and the [[Prestwould]] [[Plantation complexes in the Southern United States|plantation]] across the state border in [[Clarksville, Virginia]].{{sfn|Blanchard|1976c|p=6D}}

===McCarthy on set===
McCarthy was present on set for the duration of shooting and became involved with many facets of production. Pearce estimated that he and McCarthy met with more than 1,000 people throughout the process.<ref name="KNS 128">{{harvnb|''Knoxville News-Sentinel''|1977|p={{nowrap|G-7}}}} (reprinted at {{harvnb|Luce|Turpin|2022|p=128}}).</ref> McCarthy endeared himself to the cast and crew with his humorous impromptu storytelling.{{sfn|Josyph|2010|pp=116, 156–157 (fn.&nbsp;2)}} Dourif recalled the author's fascinated appreciation for the particularities of local dialect:
{{blockquote|I guess there's something about the way characters use language. You know, [[Charles Dickens|Dickens]] always defined his characters so well with language. And I'm just remembering what a kick it was. We were out looking at locations, and this old guy was showing us around and he'd say: "Well, y'know, th'other day... went over, got in m'car, so t'speak... turned on the engine, so t'speak..." And I remember McCarthy's ''delight'' at that. He was describing it to somebody, saying: "My God—this guy was talking about things that'd really happened, but he'd always say ''so to speak'' as if it were a metaphor, as if it didn't happen!" There it is. There's the writer. How the way this guy used the language was telling you so much about him. So easy to do, so easy to write—but so clear.{{sfn|Josyph|2010|p=147}}}}

However, McCarthy did not much enjoy making ''The Gardener's Son''. While the experience satisfied his curiosity to observe and participate in filmmaking up close, its difficulties clarified his preference for the writer's life. "It's back-breaking work," McCarthy told his local Knoxville newspaper. "On location for 30 days, and the last week we were working 16 to 18 hours a day. You've got to be some kind of weirdo to think that it's fun. But it sure kept my interest up—and writers are basically pretty lazy people."<ref name="KNS 128" /> More than three decades later, he had similar recollections for ''[[The Wall Street Journal]]'': "Dick Pearce and I made a film in North Carolina about 30 years ago and I thought, 'This is just hell. Who would do this?' Instead, I get up and have a cup of coffee and wander around and read a little bit, sit down and type a few words and look out the window."{{sfn|Jurgensen|2009}} Asked if there was "something compelling about the collaborative process compared to the solitary job of writing", McCarthy replied: "Yes, it would compel you to avoid it at all costs."{{sfn|Jurgensen|2009}}

===Music===
[[Charles Gross]] composed the [[Film score|score]]. The music is influenced by traditional [[Appalachian music]].{{sfn|Kriegsman|1977}} Among the instruments heard are [[banjo]], [[fiddle]], [[Jew's harp]], [[acoustic guitar]], and [[Brass instrument|brass]], such as a [[Muted trumpet|muted]] [[trumpet]]. Aside from the [[theme music|themes]] heard during the opening and closing credits, the drama makes spare use of [[background music]], reserving it mostly for transitions between scenes. Describing the score as "[[Psychedelic music|acid]] [[Bluegrass music|bluegrass]]", Eli Friedberg of ''The Film Stage'' said its sound unmistakably dated the film to the late 1970s, yet at the same time gave the 19th century period piece a timeless feel.{{sfn|Friedberg|2023}} {{As of|2017}}, Gross's music for ''The Gardener's Son'' had not been released as a [[soundtrack album]] or other audio media.{{sfn|Greve|Wierschem|2017|p=22 (fn.&nbsp;2)}}

==Release and reception==
===Broadcast===
[[File:The Gardener's Son (1977 WNET Channel 13 PBS advertisement).png|thumb|upright=1.2|alt=Newspaper advertisement; see file page for full text.|Print ad in the ''New York Times'' on January 6, 1977, promoting that night's premiere broadcast of ''The Gardener's Son'' on [[WNET]].]]

''The Gardener's Son'' premiered on [[PBS]] stations at 9&nbsp;p.m. on Thursday, January 6, 1977.{{sfn|O'Connor|1977|p=59}} Initial reviews were generally enthusiastic.{{sfnm|1a1=Vieth|1y=2012|1pp=31–32|2a1=Peebles|2y=2017|2p=40}} In ''[[The New York Times]]'', [[John J. O'Connor (journalist)|John J. O'Connor]] noted the film's unconventional narrative, its historical authenticity, and the passionate quality of Dourif's performance. O'Connor wrote that the film "strays far from the path of standard television. It refuses to be hurried; it fails to tie up loose ends and refuses to send us off to bed secure in the knowledge that everything in this life has a defined beginning, middle and end."{{sfn|O'Connor|1977|p=59}} [[Alan M. Kriegsman]] of ''[[The Washington Post]]'' hailed ''The Gardener's Son'' as the standout from the ''Visions'' series to date, writing that the drama "reflect[s] a writer's accurate ear for local vernacular, and a filmmaker's grasp of the revelatory power of imagery," with further praise for the cast and score.{{sfn|Kriegsman|1977}} In the [[Winston-Salem, North Carolina|Winston-Salem]], North Carolina paper ''The Sentinel'', Genie Carr highlighted the [[Climax (narrative)|climactic]] scene when "16-year-old Martha McEvoy pleads in vain with her older brother Bobby—handcuffed and guarded by a burly deputy sheriff—for understanding of her life, and his own," saying the moment "brings tears in a film that for more than an hour has emphasized the deadly placid surface stretched tightly over controlled feelings". In Carr's reckoning, the storytelling was true to the emotionally repressed realities of life in the old mill town. He applauded the cast, particularly Martin (who he wrote "controls each of her scenes") and O'Sullivan (who "combines the face of a young worker—beautiful but quickly becoming too old and weary—with the depth of a tender, but wise-too-early girl").{{sfn|Carr|1977|p=36}}

At the [[29th Primetime Emmy Awards]] in September 1977, ''The Gardener's Son'' received one [[Emmy Awards|Emmy Award]] nomination—recognizing Gene Piotrowsky in the category [[Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Main Title Design|Graphic Design and Title Sequences]]—although many sources have erroneously claimed it received two nominations.{{efn|According to scholarly sources like {{harvnb|Arnold|Luce|1999|p=5}} (citing {{harvnb|Pearce|1996|p=vi}}) and {{harvnb|Peebles|2017|p=40}}, ''The Gardener's Son'' received ''two'' Emmy nominations. Pearce's foreword mentions two Emmy nominations, but specifies neither category.{{sfn|Pearce|1996|p=vi}} Sources published before Pearce's foreword mention only one Emmy: both the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' article announcing the nominees for the [[29th Primetime Emmy Awards|1977 Emmy Awards]]{{sfn|Margulies|1977|p=16}} and the 1989 edition of ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'s Directory of Major U.S. Show Business Awards''{{sfn|Kaplan|1989|p=[https://archive.org/details/varietysdirector0000kapl/page/196/mode/1up 196] {{nowrap|(E-1294)}}}} list only one nomination for ''The Gardener's Son'', for Gene Piotrowsky in graphic design. According to the earlier sources, the ''Visions'' series did receive a nomination in the light direction category, but it was for Ken Dettling and Leard Davis for their work on another episode, titled ''Gold Watch''—not for ''The Gardener's Son''.{{sfnm|1a1=Margulies|1y=1977|1p=16|2a1=Kaplan|2y=1989|2p=[https://archive.org/details/varietysdirector0000kapl/page/196/mode/1up 196] {{nowrap|(E-1295)}}}}}} ''[[The Village Voice]]'' named it one of the best films of 1977 in a write-up by Tom Allen.<ref>{{harvnb|Allen|1978|p=45}} (cited in {{harvnb|Josyph|2010|pp=145, 229}}; {{harvnb|Peebles|2017|pp=40, 224}}; and {{harvnb|Luce|Turpin|2022|pp=130, 133 [fn.&nbsp;41]}}. However only {{harvnb|Josyph|2010}} identifies Tom Allen as the author of the ''Village Voice'' piece.)</ref> He said it was the year's "most provocative unknown American movie", worthy of comparison to ''[[The Battle of Algiers]]'' (1966), and a fine example of "class-conscious filmmaking, a rarity in this country, that is squeezed for humanistic insights rather than doctrinaire propaganda".<ref>{{harvnb|Allen|1978|p=45}} (quoted by {{harvnb|Peebles|2017|p=40}}).</ref> Later, in an essay for ''[[Film Comment]]'' asking if the medium of "[[Television film|telefilm]]" had experienced its own "[[Golden Age of Television|Golden Age of TV Drama]]" yet, Allen cited Pearce as one of the two "most promising" directors working in TV since 1975 (alongside [[Robert Markowitz]]), writing that ''The Gardener's Son'' and his later TV film ''Siege'' (1978) had "demonstrated more of an engaged social conscience wed to a commendable level of craft than any other active filmmaker in America."{{sfn|Allen|1979|p=23}}

Critical response was not unanimously positive. In the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'', the critic James Brown dismissed ''The Gardener's Son'' as too dreary and directionless for audiences to connect with its historical themes on its own terms. "McCarthy and Pearce have asked the audience to determine Robert's motivations," Brown said, but he found this was "a less than compelling task" given the drama's reliance on vague [[Symbolism (arts)|symbolism]] and emotional detachment from its central character. Brown said Dourif "alternately underplays and overstates the role", though he commended much of the rest of the cast, particularly Hardin and O'Sullivan.{{sfn|Brown|1977|p=18}} A reviewer for the North Carolina newspaper ''[[The Greensboro Record]]'' said the film "contained dialogue gross enough to make an [[alderman]] blush, to say nothing of repeated blasphemies of the commoner sort" and objected so strongly offended to its content that he called for its permanent removal from the airwaves, invoking [[United States obscenity law|obscenity law]] via the [[Communications Act of 1934]] and [[Title 18 of the United States Code|Title 18 of the U.S. Code]].{{sfn|Snider|1977|p=A14}}

===Screenings===
The premiere screening of ''The Gardener's Son'' took place at the [[Hugh M. Cummings High School]] auditorium in Burlington on December 17, 1976, ahead of its broadcast premiere, with seating by invitation only.{{sfnm|1a1=Blanchard|1y=1976b|1p=9A|2a1=Blanchard|2y=1976c|2p=6D}} More than 400 people attended the screening,{{sfnm|1a1=Malone|1y=1976|1p=20|2a1=Newton|2y=1976|2p={{nowrap|C-1}}}} including more than 100 people who had played bit parts or appeared as extras.{{sfn|Blanchard|1976c|p=6D}} A local journalist reported locals had been "looking forward to [the screening] with mixed feelings of trepidation and pride."<ref>{{harvnb|Blanchard|1976b|p=9A}} (quoted by {{harvnb|Williams|2017}}).</ref>

Encouraged by critics' favorable response to the broadcast, McCarthy and Pearce explored the possibility of a [[limited theatrical release]]. However, they learned that a theatrical version would be expected to undergo [[Re-edited film|re-editing]] for a shorter runtime. The [[Film format|format]] would need to be converted from 16&nbsp;mm to [[35 mm movie film|35&nbsp;mm film]]. Such a process "takes money", as McCarthy noted in a 1981 letter.{{sfn|Peebles|2017|p=40}} The film never reached a cinematic release.{{sfn|Josyph|2010|p=145}} However, the film did screen out of competition at the [[Berlin International Film Festival]] and [[Edinburgh International Film Festival]].{{sfn|Pearce|1996|p=vi}} Reviewing the film at Edinburgh, ''[[The Observer]]''{{'}}s [[Russell Davies]] dubbed it a "nice art-house job" and detected a modern subtext in "the [[Thousand-yard stare|shell-shock-eyed]]" expression worn by Dourif throughout the historical drama: "Whether or not the derangements of [[Vietnam War|Vietnam]] were uppermost in the director's mind, they are certainly outermost in Dourif's face."{{sfn|Davies|1977|p=26}}

Through 1978, the film also screened at a [[San Francisco]], California showcase for independent filmmakers;{{sfn|Stanley|1977|p=25}} at the [[Winthrop University]] in [[Rock Hill, South Carolina]]; at the [[University of South Carolina]] in the state capital of [[Columbia, South Carolina|Columbia]];{{sfn|Benarde|1978|p=11}} at the [[Columbia Museum of Art]];{{sfn|Lester|1978|p=1-C}} and for a senior citizens club in Graniteville, where the film takes place.{{sfn|Benarde|1978|p=11}} North Carolina newspapers reported that the film would screen at the [[1977 Cannes Film Festival|30th]] [[Cannes Film Festival]],{{sfnm|1a1=''The Chapel Hill Newspaper''|1y=1977|1p=6A|2a1=Gardner|2a2=Gardner|2y=1977|2p=2}} but this did not materialize. Years hence, McCarthy scholars have occasionally organized screenings at [[academic conference]]s devoted to the author's literature.{{sfn|Cant|2008|p=136}}

===Cast and crew response===
Dourif later revealed he felt the film was, despite its merits, fatally flawed by McCarthy's [[Anticlimax (narrative)|anticlimactic]] ending: "If he had had a really good resolving third act, he'd have had a movie. It was close."{{sfn|Josyph|2010|pp=115–116, 139 (fn.&nbsp;4)}} [[Jerry Hardin]], who played the McEvoys' gardening father, had voiced strong disagreements with Pearce during filming about the emotional handling of the plot development and maintained strong feelings about these differences decades later.{{sfn|Josyph|2010|pp=116}} McCarthy said he felt mostly satisfied with the film but regretted that it had been filmed in color on 16&nbsp;mm instead of [[black-and-white]] on 35&nbsp;mm film.{{sfn|Josyph|2010|p=140 (fn.&nbsp;5}} In Pearce's [[foreword]] to the published screenplay, he called ''The Gardener's Son'' "my education as a filmmaker" and said McCarthy had become a [[godparent|godfather]] to his daughter and, "in many ways, to all the films I've made since."{{sfn|Pearce|1996|p=vi}}

==Screenplay publication==
{{Main|The Gardener's Son (screenplay)}}
In September 1996, [[Ecco Press]] published a hardcover edition of McCarthy's screenplay, with a foreword by Pearce.{{sfn|Arnold|Luce|1999|p=11}} It was reprinted in its first [[Paperback#Trade paperback|trade paperback]] edition in 2014.{{sfn|Hoffert|2014|p=54}} There are lines and scenes in the screenplay as published that were cut from the film. The differences between the screenplay and film have been described in an article by Dianne C. Luce.<ref>{{harvnb|Cant|2008|pp=136, 303 (fn.&nbsp;3}} (see {{harvnb|Luce|1999}}).</ref> The published screenplay differs yet again from the final [[shooting script]], stored in Pearce's archives, and its differences have also been evaluated by Luce.{{sfn|Luce|2000|p=29}} The screenplay's publication prompted little critical attention.<ref>{{harvnb|Arnold|Luce|1999|pp=11–12}} "The book received almost no attention from reviewers&nbsp;..."; {{harvnb|Vieth|2012|p=32|ps=: "Ecco Press published the script in 1996, though in contrast to the film's numerous positive reviews, it received almost no reviews of any sort"}}; {{harvnb|Frye|2022|loc="Articles on Individual Works: ''The Gardener's Son''"|ps=: "Luce 1992 [reprinted as {{harvnb|Luce|1999}}] offers the only assessment of the produced screenplay to date."}}</ref> A review in ''[[Booklist]]'' called it "lesser in scope and impact than his ''[[All the Pretty Horses (novel)|All the Pretty Horses]]'' (1992) or ''[[The Crossing (McCarthy novel)|The Crossing]]'' (1994) but bearing in full measure his gift—that ability to fit complex and universal emotions into ordinary lives and still preserve all of their power and significance."{{sfn|Smothers|1996|p=200}}

==Home video==
{{Quote box
|quote = But the story of ''The Gardener's Son'' and McCarthy's mark on the [Glencoe] village has been buried over time. Filming locations have been demolished, remodeled, rebuilt, or fallen into disrepair. Even the film, itself, is impossible to find online or in stores.
|author = ''[[Times-News (Burlington, North Carolina)|Times-News]]''
|source = {{" '}}The Gardener's Son' 40 years later" (January 2017){{sfn|Williams|2017}}
|bgcolor = 
|width = 25em
|align = right
|salign = right
}}

''The Gardener's Son'' remained unavailable on [[home video]] formats for many years.{{sfn|Vieth|2012|p=32}} It is generally considered [[out of print]].{{sfn|Jagernauth|2013}} Because video copies have been scarce and generally unavailable, the published text of the screenplay is typically read in isolation as a [[closet drama]]. In 2008, the scholar John Cant wrote:

{{blockquote|''The Gardener's Son'' ought to be evaluated and analyzed as a television film. This was the form in which it was conceived and indeed brought into being.&nbsp;... In order to perform this critical task adequately it would be necessary to have access to repeated viewings of the film itself, but this is not possible. A video does exist but copyright conditions are such that it is not available, even to academics.{{sfn|Cant|2008|p=136}}}}

[[Direct Cinema Limited]], a company based in [[Santa Monica, California]], released the film on [[DVD]] in 2010.{{sfn|Jillett|2016|p=232}} Unofficial uploads of the complete film have circulated online.{{sfn|Jagernauth|2013}}

==Legacy==
{{Quote box
|quote = The screenplay suggests that while records and artifacts may embody the distorted views of their creators, they are nonetheless the fragments out of which we may apprehend the past if we read them closely, sympathetically, and in context.
|author = Dianne C. Luce
|source = in ''Myth, Legend, Dust: Critical Responses to Cormac McCarthy'' (2010){{sfn|Luce|2000|p=34}}
|bgcolor = 
|width = 25em
|align = left
|salign = right
}}

McCarthy scholars distinguish McCarthy's screenplay and Pearce's film as distinct works to be evaluated separately. The Southern author [[Robert Morgan (poet)|Robert Morgan]] saw the film the night it premiered on PBS and was inspired by its [[social realism]] and close attention to regional [[dialect]].{{sfn|Josyph|2010|p=146}} "In typical McCarthy style," [[Richard B. Woodward]] wrote in his 1992 profile of the author, "the amputation of the boy's leg and his slow execution by hanging are the moments from the show that linger in the mind."{{sfn|Woodward|1992}} [[Peter Josyph]] praised the acting and cinematography but found McCarthy's writing below the standard of his finest works, though he also described the screenplay as "certainly sympathetic to the screen", concluding that it was certainly "better than most of the crap that was made at the time."{{sfn|Josyph|2010|pp=115–116}}

By 2020, [[Lee Clark Mitchell]] claimed the film version "now sustains interest solely for being the first of McCarthy's ventures into cinematic writing."{{sfn|Mitchell|2020|p=250}} ''The Gardener's Son'' represented a noteworthy turning point in McCarthy's development as a writer not only as his first attempt at screenwriting, but also as his first rigorously researched work of historical fiction, anticipating his Western novel ''[[Blood Meridian]]'' (1985) in this respect.{{sfn|Luce|1999|p=72}} ''Blood Meridian'' is noted for its remarkable historical authenticity and rich detail drawing from various fields of knowledge. Luce said that ''Blood Meridian'' initially seemed like a radical stylistic break for McCarthy, but ''The Gardener's Son'' shows it had precedent. For Luce, both works are "everywhere informed by McCarthy's mastery of the history, geology, botany, cultural anthropology, language—all the physical and human textures" of their respective regions.{{sfn|Luce|1999|pp=71–72}}

McCarthy would go on to write several more screenplays, most unpublished, and several of his novels have been adapted into films by others.{{efn|McCarthy's three unpublished screenplays are two drafts that, over time, became the novels ''[[Cities of the Plain (novel)|Cities of the Plain]]'' (1998) and ''[[No Country for Old Men (novel)|No Country for Old Men]]'' (2005), plus an abandoned drama titled ''Whales and Men''. Manuscripts of these unpublished screenplays are held with the archive of McCarthy's papers at the [[Wittliff Collections]]. Though ''No Country for Old Men'' was adapted into a [[No Country for Old Men|film in 2007]], its screenplay was written by the [[Coen brothers]] and is unrelated to McCarthy's early draft version.{{sfn|Peebles|2017|pp=41–42}}}} Decades after ''The Gardener's Son'', McCarthy got a second original screenplay made into a motion picture with ''[[The Counselor]]'' (2013), directed by [[Ridley Scott]]. In addition to writing the screenplay, McCarthy took a hands-on role in development of ''The Counselor'' just as he had on ''The Gardener's Son'', this time as an [[executive producer]], weighing in during pre-production, casting, filming, and editing.{{sfn|Peebles|2017|p=167}}

McCarthy received sole official credit on the screenplay, but the background research undertaken in the writing ''The Gardener's Son'' was a collaborative effort between McCarthy and Pearce, and to an extent Pearce can be considered as a coauthor or at least influence.{{sfn|Luce|1999|pp=73–74}} Rick Wallach regarded Pearce, not McCarthy, as "the real author" of the film in terms of vision and ultimate artistic responsibility, a position aligned with the tenets of [[auteur theory]].{{sfn|Josyph|2010|p=101}} Writing in an unfamiliar medium, McCarthy restrained some of the more challenging avant-garde tendencies of his prose style. Mitchell claimed McCarthy "reined in the pyrotechnics, perhaps uncertain about the ways in which experimental techniques might alter visual possibilities as thoroughly as his lexical experiments were already recasting [[Late modernism|late modernist]] expectations," adding that "nothing [in ''The Gardener's Son''] suggests the [[Surrealism|surreal]], contorted vision evoked by his novels."{{sfn|Mitchell|2020|p=249}} On the other hand, Luce judged the screenplay "in every way consistent with McCarthy's treatments of characters, theme and the spoken language in his novels," even as its interpretation of historical events demonstrates Pearce's input and approval.{{sfn|Luce|1999|pp=73–74}}

Both Pearce's and McCarthy's research materials can be found in [[archive]]s held by [[Academic library|university libraries]]. McCarthy's research materials, rough drafts, and correspondence related to ''The Gardener's Son'' have been held by the [[Wittliff Collections]] at the [[Alkek Library]] of [[Texas State University]] in [[San Marcos, Texas]] since December 2007.{{sfn|Crews|2017|pp=1–2, 6}} Pearce's original [[shooting script]] and research newsletters are held at the [[University of South Carolina Libraries]].{{sfn|Luce|1999|p=74}}
